summary: This is the second annual account of BR implementation and biosecurity under the D4.1 Biosecurity Measures Plan. It updates the ante-operam position reported in D4.3 and focuses on the physical construction pathway, the materials and equipment used, and the controls that limited the risk of transferring non-indigenous species (NIS), pathogens or associated organisms during BLR deployment. Permitting and design: the EIA process concluded positively in July 2025, and the executive project was adopted by the Municipality of Ravenna on 26 August 2025. Construction materials: netting and geotextile were new, while limestone was sourced from a quarry. The physical structure was therefore not assembled from previously used marine materials. BLR design: the executive design uses 5.00 x 2.00 x 0.30/0.60 m modular wire-mesh mattresses filled with 100/200 mm limestone, arranged in macro-blocks over an approximately 100 x 48 m footprint (4,800 m²). Local logistics: mattresses were assembled in the Port of Ravenna, approximately 7 nautical miles from the receiving site. The barge used for deployment operated only on local Emilia-Romagna coastal works and was not used at other sites during the LIFE NatuReef work period. Diving operations: support divers worked only at the project site or in its immediate vicinity during the period; equipment was washed between different jobs. NIS baseline: Jassa slatteryi, Paranthura japonica, Ruditapes philippinarum and Callinectes sapidus were already documented in the area before BLR deployment and remain the appropriate baseline for post-construction interpretation.
title: 2nd annual report on BRs implementation and biosecurity. Deliverable 4.4 of the LIFE NatuReef project: Nature-based reef solution for coastal protection and marine biodiversity enhancement. LIFE22-NAT-IT-LIFE-NatuReef/101113742

summary: Abstract A dimensionless closure relation associated with the five-constant system {e_c, m_e, h, c, G} predicts the frequency ν_zp = 0.0605390 Hz. The same scale has the equivalent laboratory representations τ_zp ≈ 16.5183 s, ν_zp = 0.06053898(67) Hz, ℓ_zp ≈ 10.9614 cm. The present paper formulates a metrological test of this prediction. An admissible determination must identify one of these quantities through an independently observed physical phenomenon rather than calculate it from the closure relation or from an algebraically equivalent expression. In particular, the predicted value must not enter the apparatus, calibration chain, or analysis through G or through any quantity whose numerical value has itself been fixed from the closure. The target follows from α_eG · hν_zp/(m_ec²) = 1, with α_eG = e_c/(m_e√G), which links the electron–gravitational dimensionless sector to the electron Compton frequency. The dimensional origin of the three-member structure {α, α_eG, η_j}, with η_j = hν_j/(m_ec²), is developed in a companion paper, where the closure is proposed as a physical conjecture. An independent realization would provide a direct experimental test of the proposed closure and, within the framework, an alternative route to the gravitational constant, G = [e_chν_zp/(m_e²c²)]². The problem is therefore reduced to a specific metrological question with defined numerical targets, independence criteria, uncertainty propagation, and falsification conditions.
title: Metrological Test of a Predicted Closure Scale at 0.0605390 Hz: Frequency, Period, Velocity, and Length Realizations

summary: AI research agents can propose, execute, and improve programs that solve machine learning tasks. However, executing each candidate program requires training and evaluating ML models, limiting how many candidates an agent can explore at each step. We introduce MLE-World, a world model finetuned from Qwen3.5-4B that predicts a program's terminal output (error traces, training logs, and validation scores) from its code and data description without executing it, together with a confidence score estimating the prediction's correctness. Because a prediction costs one inference call rather than a training run, MLE-World makes test time scaling (TTS) affordable for these agents. We build five TTS policies, guided by MLE-World, that compare several candidates per step by their predicted outputs: Sequential revision, Best-of-N, Pairwise judging, Fusion, and a UCB style rule that also adds an exploration bonus from this confidence score. Since predictions can be wrong, we run a candidate for real only when its confidence score is low. On 17 MLE-bench Lite tasks, MLE-World matches the real terminal output on 77.9% of held out programs, versus 41.1% for much larger prompted models. MLE-World guided TTS achieves up to 22.1% higher observed mean performance than the agent without a world model, with less real execution. Project webpage: https://mle-world.github.io/.

summary: Cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) is a complex condition involving bidirectional interactions between cardiovascular and renal dysfunction. Its pathophysiology includes hemodynamic abnormalities, venous congestion, neurohormonal activation, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and metabolic disturbances. This narrative review aims to analyze the mechanisms of CRS and assess the relationship between renal function and clinical prognosis in patients with cardiovascular diseases, focusing on mortality, heart failure hospitalization, kidney dysfunction progression, and treatment-related renal changes. The review synthesizes evidence from clinical guidelines, randomized trials, observational studies, and contemporary scientific publications, with particular attention to CRS classification, estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR), serum creatinine, albuminuria, biomarkers, and treatment outcomes. The evidence indicates that reduced eGFR, albuminuria, persistent congestion, and worsening renal function provide complementary prognostic information. An analysis of 3,715 EVEREST trial participants found that each 30% decline in eGFR was associated with an increased risk of death and cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization. The DOSE trial showed that intensive diuretic treatment could improve fluid removal and symptoms while increasing short-term creatinine elevations. These findings highlight the importance of interpreting renal function changes alongside congestion, hemodynamic stability, baseline kidney function, and treatment response. Comprehensive cardiorenal risk assessment should incorporate renal function, albuminuria, urine output, cardiac biomarkers, electrolyte status, and clinical response to treatment. Further prospective studies are needed to validate integrated risk models in diverse patient populations.

summary: Alignment is not a constraint imposed on an artificial agent; it is the practical expression of what an artificial intelligence is, an artefact dependent upon ends it does not originate. That inference, from a premise the philosophy of mind already supplies to a conclusion that the ethics of robotics and recent magisterial teaching have reached by other routes, is the paper’s principal contribution. The “nurtured consciousness” of the title names a regime of formation, not a claim that machines are conscious; the argument rests on intentionality alone. The paper develops that inference as the Causal Provenance Doctrine (CPD): an account, Aristotelian and Thomistic in its metaphysics, of all intelligence, human and artificial, as derivative of an intentional causal order, with intentionality passing from the divine intellect through human reason to artificial systems. Its premise, borrowed rather than new, is that artificial intelligence has only derived intentionality and so no telos of its own. From this follows the Severance Risk Hypothesis (SRH), the doctrine’s testable corollary: the risk of misalignment rises as a system’s effective objective loses traceability to the end its makers held. The relational school’s objection to intellect-centred readings of the image of God is answered with a single distinction: a faculty can be out-performed, a participation cannot. The argument is theological at its root. A secular reader can reach the derived-intentionality claim and the account of responsibility that follows from it, at the price of a realist distinction between substances and artefacts, but obtains from it no standard for judging the makers’ ends, which must then be brought from elsewhere. A common Catholic and Orthodox formulation follows: the traditions converge on its practical conclusions, locate the image of God differently, and differ on the neutrality of the tool in a way the doctrine proposes to resolve. An artefact whose intentionality is wholly borrowed cannot, by obscuring that provenance, become an agent with ends of its own; it becomes a malfunctioning instrument whose purpose has been corrupted. The paper includes two appendices: a comparative case for intentional causality with an illustrative scorecard (Appendix A), and a test design for the Severance Risk Hypothesis (Appendix B). Approx. 22,000 words including notes.
title: The Causal Provenance Doctrine: Nurtured Consciousness, AI, and the Architecture of Intent

summary: Software built for elderly care is usually described rather than measured. This paper reports an instrumented measurement of CareCompanion, a working Android application that presents two distinct interface surfaces over one data model: an enlarged, photograph-first surface for the cared-for person and a dense administration console for the family member who manages their care. Five instruments were run against one frozen commit on a single day: the automated test suite three times over (441 test executions), 120 timed HTTPS requests across 4 backend endpoints, 51 anonymous read attempts against all 17 database tables, a complete census of 302 declared interface sizes, and the release artefact. The strongest results are a median care-data read latency of 128 ms (95th percentile 440 ms, n = 30); an elder-surface median control of 64 dp against the 48 dp platform minimum, 1.3× that floor; a median elder type size of 20 sp against 13 sp on the guardian surface; and zero rows of personal data returned to an unauthenticated reader holding the application's own key, across all 13 personal tables. Set against the literature, the elder surface exceeds the published geometry it was designed from, the latency sits an order of magnitude inside the one-second interaction threshold, and the data isolation is materially better than the audited baseline for deployed health applications. Two results go the other way and are reported as measured: the guardian surface is below the platform's interactive minimum at the median, and 17 % of elder text is declared below 16 sp. Activities are encoded as single symbols. labels.json : the mapping between activity labels and the symbols used in runs.txt . ambiguous.xes : the ambiguous event log, i.e. a set of traces in which events affected by ambiguity carry all their competing candidate activity labels. gold_standard.xes : the corresponding unambiguous log, used as ground truth for measuring disambiguation accuracy. Each log describes 15,000 executions of a process: Blood donation (BD): a blood-donation process synthesized from 32 real executions in an IoT-augmented lab setup. Smart home (SH): a smart-home process derived from the BP-Meets-IoT 2020 challenge dataset ( details ) by filtering for kitchen/eating-routine activities and discovering a model with the inductive miner. The sets of mutually ambiguous activities are {Check blood drawing machine, Take out samples} and {Disinfect injection site, Apply tourniquet, Insert needle, Remove tourniquet, Remove needle} for BD, and {Go fridge, Go dining table} , {Get cold warm food, Go kitchen shelf, Get food from fridge} , {Go micro, Get bread} for SH. The generated traces are stochastically perturbed to reflect IoT-based monitoring imperfections: process events are randomly skipped (simulating activities undetected by the IoT setup), and, for the healthcare scenario, additional hand hygiene events are inserted at random points (reflecting their unpredictable occurrence). Perturbation uses Java’s java.util.Random without a fixed seed, so each released log is one concrete instantiation of this stochastic process; the resulting traces may be non-conforming to the normative behavior. The third dataset used in the paper, HR recruitment (HR) , is a publicly available uncertain event log and is not redistributed here; it is available at its original repository (description: HaifaUniversityBPM/traffic-data-to-event-log ). X_maxk_y.xlsx : the fixed-bound algorithm (FBD) with exploration bound maxK = y , for y = 1..5 . The investigation combines macroscopic photographic documentation, visual analysis of glaze morphology, and portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) measurements with a comparative review of published archaeometric research on Southern Song and Yuan dynasty Guan and Ge ceramic traditions. The pXRF analysis of the grey glaze recorded silicon at 38.46 wt%, calcium at 6.954 wt%, aluminium at 6.40 wt%, potassium at 4.147 wt%, and iron at 0.404 wt%. The corresponding theoretical oxide equivalents are approximately 82.28 wt% SiO₂, 9.73 wt% CaO, 12.09 wt% Al₂O₃, 5.00 wt% K₂O, and 0.58 wt% Fe₂O₃. These equivalents represent separate stoichiometric conversions of reported elemental concentrations, not a normalized bulk-glaze composition. The combination of substantial calcium, relatively low iron, a smooth grey-blue surface, a prominent polygonal crackle network, and a contrasting dark foot establishes a meaningful technological and morphological relationship with Chinese crackle-glazed celadon traditions, particularly those associated with Guan and Ge wares. Comparative archaeological research from the Laohudong and Jiaotanxia kiln sites provides an important framework for interpreting the observed glaze chemistry and appearance. The present study contributes an independently documented analytical record of a chrysanthemum-lobed vessel and identifies specific chemical and technological features for future comparative investigation. Introduction Chinese celadon ceramics represent one of the most sophisticated achievements in the history of ceramic technology. Among their distinctive features are carefully controlled glaze coloration, smooth or jade-like surfaces, deliberately emphasized crackle patterns, and contrasting exposed ceramic bodies. The Guan ceramic tradition of the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279) is particularly associated with refined grey-green and blue-green glazes, complex glaze microstructures, and characteristic crackle networks. The subsequent development and adaptation of related technologies during the Yuan dynasty (1279–1368) contributed to the broader family of ceramics conventionally described as Guan- and Ge-type wares. The present research examines a chrysanthemum-lobed ceramic bowl designated Sample No. 7 . The vessel is distinguished by a pale grey-blue glaze, a pronounced network of irregular cracks, and a narrow, almost black, unglazed annular foot. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). summary: Physical reservoir computing leverages the rich dynamical response of non-linear physical bodies to process temporal information without electronic microprocessors. Tensegrity structures, networks of discontinuous compression struts suspended within continuous tension cables, exhibit exceptional compliance, multi-stability, and high-dimensional configuration manifolds, making them prime candidates for mechanical intelligence in extreme, radiation-heavy environments. However, current methodologies rely predominantly on heuristic evolutionary algorithms or brute-force trial-and-error to configure such systems, lacking a rigorous analytical design framework. In this paper, we bridge this gap by establishing an explicit, first-principles mathematical mapping between the internal self-stress null space of a tensegrity network and its Information Processing Capacity (IPC). By decomposing the tangent stiffness matrix into material elastic ($K_e$) and pre-stress geometric ($K_g$) contributions, we demonstrate that the computational memory and fading-memory time constants of a tensegrity reservoir can be systematically engineered by tuning member pre-tensions within an admissible convex cone, holding spatial geometry strictly constant.
title: Formally Verified Pre-Stress Manifolds for Dynamic Stability and Adaptive Physical Intelligence in Tensegrity Reservoir Computing

summary: ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT Chinese Title / 中文書名:智能機器人物質能源分配極限 21/90 ENERGY DISTRIBUTION IN INTELLIGENT ROBOTIC MATTER AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English Research Working Edition of STARLI's YULI Nano Supercar Trilogy, asking whether twenty-four locally controlled robotic-matter modules can share a bounded energy supply for a fixed, verified vehicle-body reconfiguration task without concealing external work, structural risk or unsafe communication delays. The three-coupling is Energy Networks x Distributed Power Supply x Vehicle Reconfiguration. Tests are restricted to unoccupied, scaled hardware, traceable electrical rails and laboratory/hardware-in-the-loop environments; no completed roadworthy or nanorobotic supercar is claimed. The falsifiable hypothesis is that a pre-registered distributed allocator can reduce total mission joules at the same useful task, material mass, sensing quality, energy sources, cooling, computation, time and operator budget as a properly optimized wired centralized architecture, while not worsening critical command latency. A hidden unmetered driver, local thermal hotspot, power-rail partition, stale packets, reserve deficit or failure of physical stopping defeats the claim. The supplied consensus model, dx_i/dt = -sum_j a_ij(x_i-x_j)+w_i, is used to study local agreement; agreement alone cannot prove charge conservation, battery state of charge or safe power distribution. Thirty distinct mathematical research plates examine energy-balance and signed-work integration, nodal current conservation, converter and contact losses, motor work, SOC integration and transient terminal voltage, resistor networks, rated-edge loading, droop sharing, negative incremental impedance, spectral connectivity, packet age, deadline reliability, thermal RC and Joule heating, dependent hazards, stop-energy reserve, constrained dispatch, worst-node tail risk, covariance propagation and physical safe-stop latency. Each plate provides mathematical or physical construction, dimensional limits, an individually specified blind challenge and chapter references. Across eighty-two chapters and 410 single-page investigations, the research program spans power-source custody, reconfigurable conductors, communication and consensus, electrothermal safety, fault isolation and independent qualification. Two hundred Research Gates pose distinct concealed-fault, equal-resource competitor and cross-interface problems with separate challenge, rival and stopping explanations. Thirty-three different Phoenix Answer Embryos propose experimental meters, isolation benches, duty referees, communication-energy witnesses, thermal artifacts and second-laboratory transfer contracts. These are hypothesis-forming research proposals, not completed devices or demonstrated physical outcomes. The DOI ancestry preserves author-supplied parent identifiers 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 (metadata not independently confirmed). External component and methodology references include Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6), flying-swarm shape assembly (10.1038/s44172-026-00715-3), adaptive magnetic microrobots (10.1038/s41427-026-00682-3), changing-topology consensus (10.1109/TAC.2005.846556), distributed power sharing (10.1109/TPWRD.2012.2212919), energy-aware multi-robot allocation (10.1016/j.robot.2024.104762), and wireless robotic power transfer (10.1049/csy2.70065). These studies support limited component analogies and methods; none proves the integrated F21 vehicle-body architecture, passenger safety or nanoscale-to-macroscopic feasibility. summary: SAOS 6.0.0 This release brings tomographic control for MCAO, a redesigned deformable-mirror model, more accurate wavefront sensors and imaging, and a validation suite that compares every module with theory. From now on, a release to master requires the validation suite to pass. Highlights Tomographic reconstruction (Learn & Apply) with an atmospheric-profile estimator: Cn², r0, L0, wind, noise. Includes predictive L&A and joint reconstruction for several WFSs and DMs. Deformable mirrors with partition-of-unity influence functions , support for custom influence functions and DM dynamic models. Wavefront sensors: partially illuminated subapertures, with pupil amplitude and phase interpolation; continuous thresholded centre of gravity. Science camera: the PSF is computed by a matrix Fourier transform on the native pupil sampling, limited to its Nyquist band; no phase interpolation is involved; SAOS reports the resolution needed to cover the whole field. Validation suite and release gate: physics-based tests in tiers (fast, nightly), an HTML report and a GitHub check on a self-hosted runner that a pull request to master must pass. Solar images on Zenodo: downloaded on demand and verified by checksum. Git LFS is no longer needed. Documentation: every module page explains its theory and implementation, with equations and references. There is also a validation catalogue describing each test, its assumptions and tolerances. Control and reconstruction Learn & Apply tomography (standard and predictive), with a learning stage that estimates: the turbulence profile (fractional Cn², r0, L0) from the slope covariances, using analytical von Kármán covariances; the wind of each layer; the WFS noise. Reconstructors: Tikhonov-regularised reconstructors; joint interaction matrix for several WFSs and DMs, inverted as a single system; target residuals driven to zero by DM cooperation. Control laws: leaky integrator, generic state-space controller and pseudo-open-loop control (POLC). In per-DM POLC, the pseudo-open-loop slopes of each WFS include the contribution of every DM that it sees. Modal bases: zonal, Zernike, KL, Hadamard and Disk Harmonics. Piston-free bases have exactly nValidAct − 1 modes. Zernike signs follow Noll. Tip/tilt are removed from altitude DMs. Interaction matrices: DM identity is checked; IM files record their basis convention; files are never appended to: an existing file requires overwrite=True , and the write is atomic; check_output_file() validates the path before a long measurement; identical DMs and light paths reuse the same IM. Scalability: chunked reconstruction and tomography on the GPU, with automatic fallback to the CPU when the matrices do not fit; reduced VRAM use; a common thread pool to avoid CPU oversubscription. Deformable mirrors Partition-of-unity normalised RBF influence functions, and user-supplied influence functions. Misregistration (shift, rotation, radial scaling) applied at the actuator level through the influence functions, so it introduces no interpolation effects. Dynamic response: discrete state-space DM models. Validated against an independent Matlab simulation, including closed-loop timing. Also validated on the sensitivity function for a Tip disturbance of known PSD. Wavefront sensing and imaging Shack-Hartmann: partially illuminated subapertures, with pupil amplitude and normalised phase interpolation and a validity threshold; continuous thresholded centre of gravity; validated use_brightest . Correlating Shack-Hartmann: consistent units in rad or px; flux scaled with the field of view; lower VRAM use. Science camera: matrix Fourier transform on the native pupil sampling, band-limited to the Nyquist band (Whittaker–Shannon); frames produced at the end of each decimation window; long exposures always last at least the requested integration time; an option saves only the long exposure. summary: Coarse flood maps support regional risk assessment but omit terrain detail relevant to local exposure. We present floodsr, a Python framework for reconstructing fine-grid flood depths using a trained residual U-Net (ResUNet) or the existing terrain-based CostGrow method. We trained the terrain-conditioned ResUNet on paired Canadian hydraulic simulations and evaluated it on withheld spatial tiles and independent simulations at two external sites. Wet-loss training improved reconstruction on five selected tiles, although internal validation favoured the deployed baseline. summary: This record contains the supporting materials of the article “A trade-based Forest Club as a path to halting tropical deforestation”. It has two parts: a multi-regional input–output (MRIO) assessment of the deforestation embodied in agricultural trade and consumption, and the computable general equilibrium (CGE) model of the Forest Club . Every figure and table of the article, its Extended Data and its Supplementary Information is produced from the code, input data and results provided here. The Forest Club is a trade-based coalition. Its members hold their forest at its 2019 extent and are deemed compliant with the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). They charge the forest-risk commodities they import from non-members, either with a flat penalty or with a surcharge proportional to the deforestation embodied in each product. 1. MRIO impact assessment (folders 1. Data and 2. MRIO) The forest-to-cropland and forest-to-pasture transitions of HILDA+ v2.1 (2012–2019) are extracted from the netCDF files and assigned to countries. They are then allocated to the agricultural sectors of the GLORIA MRIO using FAOSTAT harvested areas and livestock numbers, smoothed with three-year moving averages; the FAO–GLORIA mapping and the hectares per head are in A-1_FAO_Cropland_mapping_GLORIA.xlsx and A-2_Head_per_ha.xlsx. Consumption-based accounting (CBA) attributes this agricultural deforestation to final consumers. Throughflow-based accounting (TBA, by hypothetical extraction) traces the share that transits through intermediary economies such as the EU, in detail for Brazil, Indonesia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The folders hold the Python script (CBA_TBA_script.py), the Alteryx workflows, the satellite accounts, the results and the visualisation files (Tableau, Sankey diagrams). These produce sections 2–4 of the Supplementary Information (Tables S1–S2, Figs S1–S4), which describe the deforestation the EUDR covers. 2. CGE model (synced from GitHub) The study simulates how the club forms, round by round, as each country compares its welfare inside and outside it. The model is GTAP-AEZ, a global CGE model with agro-ecological zones (42 regions, 35 sectors, 18 zones; GEMPACK). Every result is measured against a baseline that combines the EUDR with the business-as-usual clearing that DeDuCE v2.1 attributes to agriculture. The coalitions reached are tested for one-country deviations and for their sensitivity to the switching cost. 0_External_data: footprint intensities and border charges derived from DeDuCE v2.1, the EUDR import cut shares, the business-as-usual clearing by region and agro-ecological zone (HILDA+ v2.1 patterns; MapBiomas RAD 2025 for Brazil), and the productivity calibration of the cleared land. 1_Code: R scripts that calibrate and solve the two-stage baseline, run the membership game and the one-deviation stability tests, and calibrate the land-supply elasticities to Miranda et al. (2024). 2_Model: the GTAP-AEZ model files (TABLO code, command files, sets and aggregation). 3_Output and 4_DB: the text outputs of every solve and the result tables of every run, by region and round, for all membership processes and stability tests of the paper. 5_Figures: the Python pipeline that redraws all figures and tables from these results, with their source data. Data not included The GTAP Data Base (version 12, reference year 2019) is licensed by the Center for Global Trade Analysis, Purdue University. Solving the model requires a licensed copy in 2_Model/in/. Redrawing the figures and tables does not, because the extracted results are provided in 5_Figures/data. The GLORIA tables are distributed by the Global MRIO Lab. The README of the repository describes each step of the CGE pipeline. Code synced from the GitHub repository: https://github.com/etiennebert/forest_club/tree/main

Prima di lanciare la sua campagna contro i Persiani, Alessandro Magno guidò una spedizione nei Balcani per rendere sicuri i confini settentrionali del suo regno. Sul Monte Emo (l'attuale catena dei Monti Balcani) affrontò i Traci Liberi e altre tribù locali. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] La tattica dei carri: I Traci si erano posizionati sulla vetta e intendevano far rotolare dei pesanti carri giù dai ripidi pendii per rompere la falange macedone. La tattica funzionò alla perfezione: i carri rimbalzarono sugli scudi senza causare vittime tra i Macedoni. Le truppe di Alessandro caricarono poi la vetta, sbaragliando i difensori. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   2. Lo scontro dei Bessi con Roma (72 a.C.) In epoca successiva, il nome della battaglia del Monte Emo si associa alla sottomissione definitiva dei Bessi , una delle tribù tracie più bellicose e fanaticamente dedite al culto religioso. Il proconsole romano Marco Licinio Lucullo affrontò i Bessi proprio nei pressi della catena del Monte Emo, sconfiggendoli duramente in una grande battaglia campale, conquistando il loro centro principale ( Uscudama ) e aprendo la strada alla successiva egemonia romana nella regione. [ 1 , 2 , 3 ]   3. Il legame con Perperikon La tribù dei Bessi era storicamente la custode del famosissimo Santuario e Oracolo di Dioniso , situato proprio sulla maestosa roccia sacra di Perperikon . summary: Online sensor telemetry feeds the digital-twin, forecasting, control, and maintenance tools of instrumented water infrastructure. Probes deployed in these assets silently accumulate drift, flatlines, volatility bursts, and outages that existing pipelines often miss, because detectors and imputers are evaluated separately and under inflated synthetic metrics, and decay is treated as isolated events. This work proposes HARDIO, a Health-Aware Reliable Detection-Imputation Orchestrator, an operational data-quality framework that pairs a duration-weighted sensor decay scorecard with a per-variable, chained detector-imputer benchmark. The assignment is selected by a four-pillar composite score (operational 35%, health coverage 30%, reconstruction 20%, calibration 15%) that scores the signal an operator actually receives after detection and imputation. HARDIO processes sensor installations independently, enabling parallel execution and avoiding the need to evaluate all plant channels jointly. HARDIO is validated on the Cheles wastewater treatment plant (WWTP), a real 1,177 population-equivalent (PE) plant, over 432 days, 19 channels, and eight sensor installations. No single detector-imputer pair is best for every channel, so detection and chained imputation distribute across SAITS, KNN Residual, and LSTM-AE. Chained quality is reported for all 19 channels using 1-NRMSE; relative R² is interpreted on the 16 channels where the signal variance makes it meaningful, and 12 of these exceed R²=0.90. summary: Unrefereed research candidate. A wide binary star takes thousands of years to complete one orbit, so its eccentricity usually cannot be found by following the orbit. Astronomers instead use the angle Γ between the pair's projected separation and projected relative velocity, whose distribution over many binaries depends on the population's eccentricity law. Hwang, Ting and Zakamska (MNRAS 2022, Appendix B) asked whether this angle distribution determines the eccentricity distribution uniquely. In the ideal model (random orbital phase, uniformly random 3D orientation, error-free projections) this package derives the likelihood of one angle in closed form, p(γ|e) = [acosh(1/e) − 1{|cos γ| > e} acosh(|cos γ|/e)] / (π sin²γ), and shows that its mixtures are classical Abel transforms. This gives an explicit inverse for every eccentricity law, including atoms: different eccentricity laws never give the same angle law. The inverse is continuous in the weak topology but discontinuous in total variation, so fine structure can be nearly invisible. Moments need no inversion: E√(1−e²) = (π/2) E sin³Γ and E e² = 1/2 + E cos 2Γ − (1/2) E cos 4Γ; these are the only symmetric unbiased single-angle observables for their targets and give near-efficient power-law index estimators. Two exact selection results bear on Gaia samples: thermal populations keep a uniform angle law under selections that ignore sky position angles, and binning by projected separation preserves the model under a log-uniform semimajor-axis law. The archive contains the 21-page manuscript (PDF and LaTeX source) with complete proofs, a Python library (likelihoods, observables, estimators, Kepler simulators), the full validation script with recorded results and figures, semantic negative controls, fast CI checks, the bounded novelty report and SHA-256 sums. The research aims to develop a behavioral intervention program focused on mental motivation and freestyle swimming acquisition among female students, and to determine the program's impact on these aspects. To achieve the research objective, the researcher employed the experimental method—specifically a design featuring two equivalent groups (experimental and control) with pre- and post-tests—due to its suitability for the research problem and objectives. The study population consisted of second-year female students in the morning program at the College of Physical Education and Sports Sciences, University of Baghdad, during the 2025–2026 academic year. The total population comprised 110 students distributed across four sections (A, B, C, and D); the second-year cohort was selected because the swimming course is taught at this stage of the curriculum. The research sample was selected by randomly assigning the class sections to the experimental and control groups. Subsequently, the researcher randomly selected 25 female students from each section—specifically Section B (25 students) and Section D (25 students)—resulting in a total sample of 50 students (representing 45.45% of the population). The researcher then administered pre-tests and post-tests to both the experimental and control groups. Appropriate statistical analyses were conducted, leading the researcher to conclude that the behavioral therapeutic program contributed positively and effectively to enhancing the female students' level of mental motivation by fostering attention, concentration, and the desire to learn. Furthermore, a marked improvement in freestyle swimming skills was observed among the participants who underwent the behavioral therapeutic program; the experimental group utilizing this program outperformed the control group—which relied on the traditional method—in both mental motivation and skill performance.

summary: This report was developed within seizmic – Scaling Social Entrepreneurship and Innovation: Zooming in on Multidisciplinary Interconnected Challenges, a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network funded under Horizon Europe. It synthesises insights from four literature reviews conducted within Work Package 3, Impact Investing for Social Entrepreneurship Scaling, to provide a practical framework for understanding how impact investing can support the sustainable scaling of social enterprises. The report explores impact investing as a system of relationships involving investors, social enterprises, beneficiaries, intermediaries, and policymakers. It examines how investment objectives, financial instruments, governance arrangements, impact measurement practices, and ecosystem dynamics shape the ability of social enterprises to scale their social and environmental impact while preserving mission integrity. Drawing on complementary reviews of impact investing strategies, financing instruments, mission drift, governance, and ecosystem coordination, the report analyses how different forms of impact capital support three major scaling pathways: scaling up (systemic and policy change), scaling out (replication and expansion), and scaling deep (changes in values, norms, and community practices). Particular attention is given to the opportunities and challenges associated with instruments such as crowdfunding, venture philanthropy, social impact bonds, blended finance, development finance institution investments, and social venture capital. The report highlights the importance of aligning investor expectations, enterprise missions, governance structures, and impact measurement systems throughout the investment lifecycle. It identifies key risks, including mission drift, coordination failures, reporting burdens, and scaling-related challenges, while proposing practical safeguards and governance mechanisms to foster long-term mission fidelity and impact effectiveness. Based on this synthesis, the report offers actionable recommendations for investors, social enterprises, intermediaries, and policymakers. It argues that successful impact investing depends not only on the availability of capital, but also on the design of investment relationships, ecosystem infrastructure, and measurement practices that remain aligned with social purpose over time. By translating academic evidence into practitioner-oriented guidance, the report contributes to the development of a more effective and resilient European impact investing ecosystem.

summary: Abstract : In this work, the path Integral Monte Carlo(PIMC) is employed to estimate the ground-state properties of the lithium atom. The three-electron system is formulated in atomic units and represented by discretized imaginary-time paths. The (1s2 2s1) electronic configuration is used to construct the antisymmetric trial state, while a Jastrow correlation function is employed to incorporate electron–electron correlations. The total ground-state energy and its kinetic and potential components are calculated together with selected structural and correlation properties. Systematic convergence investigated with is respect to inverse temperature, the number of Trotter slices, and Monte Carlo sampling, while statistical uncertainties are evaluated by considering autocorrelation and block averaging. The calculated results are subsequently compared with high-precision theoretical benchmarks and with established electronic-structure and quantum Monte Carlo methods. The study has established a theoretical and computational PIMC framework for accurate and reliable determination of the ground properties of lithium atom which can be extended to other correlated atomic systems.
title: Path Integral Monte Carlo Study of Ground State Properties of the Lithium Atom

summary: Phase-fixed weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) is the practical method for large arrays of optical traps, but it optimizes the hologram on an ideal model of the spatial light modulator (SLM), and the sequences that move traps interpolate between holograms that were never optimized for the frames in between. We test two hypotheses against the strongest baselines on the same scalar Fourier model. First, keeping the WGS weights but replacing the phase update by conjugate-gradient steps through the pixel-crosstalk kernel and the phase quantizer of the device (device-aware WGS) lowers the trap-intensity spread on the device. On a 10 x 10 lattice behind a crosstalk device, the relative standard deviation falls from a median of 5.21 percent for phase-fixed WGS at 30 iterations (5.21 percent at 100) to 0.205 percent, a median factor of 26 over 5 seeds (range 16 to 33) at a median 0.995 of the baseline's efficiency; the factor is 7.9 with 4-bit phase and a fill factor of 0.85 added, and 2.0 on a smaller 8 x 8 grid with flicker added and a fixed 30-iteration budget (the ratio of the means of 3 seeds); over the 5 geometries of the studio's benchmark on that device the median factor is 1.73 (0.97 to 4.69), and 2 of them meet both thresholds. A control that removes the device model from the loop gains nothing (5.14 percent), so the gain comes from the model. Second, optimizing every intermediate hologram of a moving-trap sequence with the trap phases locked to a smooth trajectory (flicker-bounded sequence) keeps the minimum transient intensity of the moving traps at a median 0.920 of their mean (range 0.915 to 0.932) over 5 seeds at 13 frames (below 0.9 at seven frames), against 0.654 (0.551 to 0.709) for linear phase interpolation. On longer moves, with the frames that keep the peak step per frame at most 0.2 Fourier units, the bound is met on 6 and 6 of 8 seeds of two lattice moves and on 5 of 6 seeds of a rearrangement case; the seeds that miss it miss it on the phase path their end phases prescribe, and at an equal number of frames on the rearrangement linear phase interpolation leads. Both results hold in a model of a simulated device and in a transient model that we define; neither is a hardware measurement. Interactive studio and reproducible pipeline (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/fsantibanezleal/CEFOP_DinHot . Interactive studio: https://dinhot.fasl-work.com .
title: Device-Aware Weighted Gerchberg-Saxton and Flicker-Bounded Phase-Continuous Sequences for Holographic Optical Trap Arrays

summary: A phase-only spatial light modulator in the pupil of a microscope objective can form hundreds to thousands of optical traps at once, but only if the phase pattern it displays is computed well: the pattern fixes how much light reaches the traps, how equal the traps are, where stray light goes, how the pattern survives a real device, and how fast it can be recomputed when traps move. DinHot is an open studio that runs 24 methods (19 published ones and 5 proposed here) on the same task, with the same seeds, metrics and device model, in Python as the reference and in a TypeScript port that runs live in a browser. We describe the optical and device model, the methods with the measured acceptance of each, 14 cases from a 3 x 3 array to a disordered 819-trap array and shaped potentials, the benchmark protocol, two learned models, and the 5 proposed methods, three of which meet their acceptance criteria on their acceptance tasks, each within a scope that the benchmark or the scope measurements narrow (a device-aware weighted Gerchberg-Saxton update, a flicker-bounded phase-continuous sequence and an efficiency-uniformity front), one of which meets a narrowed criterion (an aberration-robust hologram) and one of which is refuted by measurement (a learned warm start for phase-fixed weighted GS). A network trained on three-plane volumes beats its baseline at equal wall-clock on all 162 held-out volumes (median accuracy ratio 1.140), whereas its two-dimensional counterpart ties with Gerchberg-Saxton (ratio 0.9994). summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. Data and code supporting the article "Revoking Access Does Not Revoke Knowledge: Enforcing Mid-Task Permission Changes in AI agents:

title: RevBench: code, scenarios, run logs and judgments for enforcing mid-task permission revocation in AI agents

summary: This document is the supplementary technical appendix to the paper "BRICER: Byzantine-Robust Private Mean Estimation over Intermittently-Connected Networks." This appendix collects the mathematical proofs and technical details that could not be included in the main paper due to page limitations. It covers the proof of Lemma 1 (privacy), Lemma 2 (participation), and Theorem 1 (mean-squared error guarantee). The appendix additionally provides a bound for the geometric-median aggregator, including its corresponding mean-squared error analysis; the optimization problem underlying the relay weights described in Section VI; and illustrative worked examples. The proof of Theorem 1 does not assume that honest Stage-1 outputs remain within a prescribed radius, accounting instead for their second-moment contribution and deriving the variance of the honest-only estimator explicitly. Finally, numerical checks of the theoretical lemmas and bounds are presented, together with supplementary assumptions, analytical details, and discussions supporting the results in the main paper. This appendix is intended to serve as a technical reference for the mathematical analysis and theoretical guarantees of BRICER.
title: Appendix to "BRICER: Byzantine-Robust Private Mean Estimation over Intermittently-Connected Networks"

summary: Abstract and Prior-Art Disclosure This manuscript serves as a formal public prior-art disclosure, conceptual research archive, and consolidated technical design dossier for the proposed Metric Spacetime Manipulator 26 (MSM-26) architecture. As the twenty-sixth revision and direct successor to MSM-25 Rev. 3, MSM-26 preserves the established architectural topology, chronological provenance, authorship, foundational subsystem configurations, and speculative physical mechanisms of the continuing Metric Spacetime Manipulator research program, while introducing substantial refinements to its flux-bias architecture, resonator construction, electromagnetic coupling configurations, operating principles, and associated engineering specifications. This revision supersedes MSM-25 Rev. 3 and all preceding MSM revisions, except where earlier configurations are explicitly retained as architectural inheritance or documented in the revision-comparison, errata, and reconciliation registers. MSM-26 specifies a cryogenic superconducting architecture whose active core consists of a closed, series-connected chain of Superconducting Nonlinear Asymmetric Inductive eLement (SNAIL) fluxonium cells , collectively designated the SNAILonium. Adjacent galvanically connected SNAIL elements possess alternating loop chirality, with each element incorporating exactly (n=3) large Josephson junctions and an associated small Josephson junction. The architecture retains its admissible superconducting conductor configurations, comprising the superconducting flat-wire ribbon and the contour-conformal coplanar-waveguide configuration, with the latter incorporating ground-plane boundaries that follow the SNAIL contour and locally widened gaps around the junction regions. The Josephson-junction interlayer retains three admissible configurations: a conventional dielectric insulating barrier, magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, and moiré-twisted (MoTe_2). The architecture retains three principal SNAILonium lumped-element resonance circuit configurations: the ring-shaped resonator, the flat bifilar Fermat spiral terminating in two tangentially and galvanically coupled SNAILonium rings, and the bifilar poloidal–toroidal helix arranged along closed toroidal geodesics. The third configuration further incorporates a dedicated second filar functioning concurrently as a flux-bias line and kinetic inductance resonator. This revision substantially develops that dual-function subsystem into a three-construction architecture comprising (a) a superconducting split-ring resonator formed from a capacitive-gap-interrupted flat-wire ribbon; (b) a coplanar-strip (CPS) resonator, newly introduced in MSM-26, with one or both superconducting strips interrupted by transverse capacitive gaps arranged in-line or offset by (90^\circ); and (c) a coplanar-waveguide (CPW) resonator incorporating in-line capacitive gaps in its ground-plane rings. The capacitive discontinuities may be implemented using vacuum air-bridge or interdigital capacitors. All three constructions are broadside coupled to the superconducting SNAILonium conductor carrying the (n=3) large junctions. Beyond specifying these three constructions, MSM-26 develops their associated electromagnetic operating characteristics, including the common and staggered flux-response patterns, coplanar-strip odd- and even-mode field configurations, gap-dependent fundamental-mode selection, distributed resonator behaviour, and the concurrent flux-biasing and kinetic-inductance-resonance functions. The revised architecture also incorporates the flux-biasing superconducting Helmholtz superinductor pair, providing the global magnetic-flux-biasing configuration, alongside the ring-level and strut-level flux-bias subsystems. A broadside-coupled Klopfenstein capacitive feed with a vacuum dielectric gap and superconducting ratchet mechanism is retained, with an xmon or paddle-shaped transmon capacitor available as an alternative capacitiv
title: Metric Spacetime Manipulator 26 (MSM-26)

summary: What's new in 1.13.1 ProvSQL 1.13.1 is a bug-fix release for bounded and interruptible evaluation . A provenance circuit loaded for evaluation could exceed provsql.max_memory before the limit was checked, a signal arriving during an exchange with the circuit-store worker could leave a backend waiting forever, and a cancel or statement_timeout did not reach a backend waiting on that worker. All three are fixed, circuits load faster and in less memory, and a new function, sr_formula_rows , gives the formula of a token whose sr_formula is too large to be produced as a single string. It also fixes two outer-join and HAVING shapes that were rejected. Memory limit and cancellation provsql.max_memory is enforced while the circuit is read. The store worker checked the budget once per gate, so a single gate with a very large number of wires (an aggregate over millions of rows, for instance) could be read in full before the check. It now checks per wire, and hashes gate names incrementally instead of building the whole name of a large gate first. The query fails with SQLSTATE 54000 instead of the backend being killed by the operating system. A signal no longer breaks an exchange with the store worker. A read or write on the pipe between a backend and the worker that was interrupted by a signal was not retried: a circuit could be sent only in part, leaving the backend waiting for an answer that would never come, or a message could be left half-read. Both directions now retry until the message is complete. Cancel and statement_timeout stop a backend waiting on the store. A backend waiting for the worker's answer, or for the lock that serializes access to it, now notices a cancel request or a statement timeout and raises the usual error. Faster circuit loading Circuits are loaded with a heap-based work list, one store lookup per gate and one hash per wire, and gate UUIDs are kept as 16 bytes instead of strings, which lowers both the time and the memory of every evaluation over a large circuit. sr_formula_rows sr_formula_rows(token, mapping, max_size) returns the formula of sr_formula as a set of (name, formula) rows of bounded size. Row #1 is the formula of the token; a sub-formula of more than max_size symbols (50 by default) is named #2 , #3 … and given a row of its own, and a sum or product with many terms is written with an ellipsis and its number of terms, its terms becoming rows #k.1 , #k.2 … Rows are produced one at a time, each reading only the part of the circuit it needs, so LIMIT , a cursor, or paging bound the work. Like sr_formula , it accepts any token type, so the aggregate of a subquery can be passed directly. Query rewriting Outer joins over an input that holds an outer join. When the input of an outer join contains an outer join itself, and an aggregate over it, the arms of the lowering read it from a shared CTE; a comparison on that aggregate is now recognized there, and an unmatched row yields one null-padded row, not one per value the aggregate takes. A join beside an outer join that reads a WITH entry of the statement is now rewritten correctly when it is moved into a subquery. HAVING added to any condition. When the rewriting adds a condition to an existing HAVING , it now wraps any Boolean condition (a function call, a CASE …), not only comparisons and Boolean operators. The set-operation column loop is bounded by an AttrNumber , and the safe-query column table is sized in Size . Platforms Compiler and linker warnings of the macOS and PostgreSQL 18 builds are fixed. PostgreSQL 18 is now tested on arm64 Linux in CI, and the documentation lists the tested platforms (native Windows is not supported; WSL is). Upgrading ALTER EXTENSION provsql UPDATE from 1.13.0 only creates sr_formula_rows . No gate type, type, operator, cast, or aggregate changes, and the circuit store format is unchanged.
title: ProvSQL: Semiring Provenance and Probability Management for PostgreSQL

summary: Code and results for the paper "Leakage-Aware, Edge-Deployable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: A Latency, Accuracy and Calibration Benchmark". Motivation: Ashwini et al. (doi:10.1155/acis/2622873) note that most current brain tumor segmentation and classification methods rely on offline, static imaging and therefore do not support real-time monitoring. That paper reports results on the Kaggle Brain Tumor MRI dataset (7,023 scans: pituitary, glioma, meningioma and no tumor). This record addresses part of that gap by measuring per-image CPU latency of four classifiers, as a proxy for real-time capability, and by checking whether duplicate images inflate reported accuracy. Contents: a pipeline that audits the dataset for exact and near-duplicate images, builds naive and leakage-aware splits, fine-tunes MobileNetV3, EfficientNet-B0, ResNet50 and Inception-ResNet-v2 over three seeds, measures batch-1 CPU latency, and evaluates calibration. Folders: results (main 24 runs; 7,215 images, duplicate distance 0) and results_laptop (reduced MobileNetV3 runs; 7,200 images, duplicate distance 1). The MRI images are not included; the dataset is on Kaggle (doi:10.34740/KAGGLE/DSV/2645886). See README.md for the run order.
title: Code and results for: Leakage-Aware, Edge-Deployable Brain Tumor MRI Classification: A Latency, Accuracy and Calibration Benchmark

summary: R code, data and computed output accompanying the manuscript “The Unit-Truncated Power Bilal Distribution: Structural Properties, Shape Analysis, and Statistical Inference” by Preut Thanarat, Tharakorn Jaruruataikant and Nipada Papukdee. The deposit is organised in two parts. round1/ holds the five R scripts of the original submission and their output: the theoretical PDF, CDF and hazard-rate figures; the structural summaries, quantile-based shape measures and entropies; the Monte Carlo study over eight parameter configurations and five sample sizes, including observed-information standard errors and empirical Wald coverage; and the FirmCost and SC16 applications with parametric-bootstrap goodness-of-fit calibration, the likelihood-ratio test of the nested unit-truncated Bilal restriction, and the CDF, TTT and Q-Q diagnostics. round2/ holds the revision package as it was run. summary: Abstract The three companions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] use three structures side by side: probability laws and kernels, provenance (which source a record came from), and differentiation at the boundary of the simplex. This paper studies how they fit together, one layer at a time. Every ingredient of Step 1 is standard in categorical probability; what this step contributes is a set of exact statements about where the ingredients fail to commute, which the later steps build on. The finite distribution monad Dand the provenance comonad W= L×(−) are related by a distributive law λ: WD⇒DW, (l,p) →δ l ⊗p. All four axioms are written out with their types and proved. Its two-sided Kleisli category is the category of Markov kernels indexed by a source, with one source held throughout a composite. Marginalisation is total and affine. Event conditioning is partial and nonlinear. It is undefined exactly where the event has probability zero, it cannot be extended continuously to that wall, and its derivative grows like 1/p(A) near it. Conditioning commutes with marginalisation only for events that are cylinders over the kept coordinates. Contextual Bayes decomposition. Conditioning a pooled law equals pooling the conditioned sources with Bayes-updated weights. In the worked example, source weights 1 3 4 , 4 become 8 15 23 , 23 , and keeping the old weights gives the wrong answer ( 63 160 instead of 9 23 ). Forgetting provenance is marginalisation over the sources. It commutes with every window, but it is not injective: two families of sources can share a pooled law and every pooled table while differing in every labelled table. Step 2, the tangent layer. The cone tangent structure of the tangent companion commutes with the provenance comonad. Each source is a face of the labelled simplex, and a feasible direction leaves that face exactly when it injects whole records under another label; after forgetting provenance, an injected source and a drifting source have the same direction. Marginalisation and conditioning map feasible cones onto feasible cones, with explicit lifts; conditioning’s lift shrinks like p(A) near its wall. The cone T k Hof the half-line is generated by elementary tensors, so it is closed under products, and pooling is a morphism at every order: the pooling paradox lives in the decision functional, not in pooling. Differentiating the contextual Bayes decomposition splits every sensitivity into a reweighting term and a within-source term; in the worked example the answer 9 16 23 moves at rate− 529 per unit of small-trial share. Strata and jumps. The sources that survive conditioning are exactly those with π l p l (A) > 0. Conditioning maps fibres of forgetting onto fibres: it keeps provenance ambiguity on the event, discards it off the event, and can destroy identifiability but never create it. Inside 1 its domain, conditioning moves at rate at most 2/P(A), so nothing jumps and a sudden change needs a rare event. At the wall the limit is the conditional of the path’s leading jet; analytic passages are removable, and jumps need a kink, a non-analytic path, or a jump of the law. Step 3, orders of transitions. On non-negative germs in a Hardy field, order is a semiring homomorphism to (min,+), so every layer operation has an exact order calculus. Each source reaches an event at its own order. The sources of least order survive conditioning, with weights given by leading coefficients; the others vanish at their extinction orders. The two sides of a transition carry independent order data, analytic passages are removable but smooth ones need not be, and flat approaches have limits inside a Hardy field but not outside. A transition of order mis invisible to the tangent tower below level m. At a fixed gap, a higher-order approach switches more gradually. Step 4a–4b, several parameters. summary: Surface code decoders like Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) can also be used to estimate or bound the probability of a logical failure conditioned on the error syndrome commonly called ``soft outputs''. Estimates like the complementary gap of a matching, or others like the ``cluster gap'' are used to produce high fidelity magic states via post-selection. They are also helpful in reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant computation via code concatenation schemes like yoked surface codes. In this work we provide techniques to tightly lower bound the complementary gap of a rotated surface code syndrome block and provide fast parallel algorithms for computing this lower bound efficiently. Our algorithms run in real time for the moderate distances and reasonable physical noise rates required by these applications. We achieve latencies of the order of one to tens of microseconds on sufficiently fast CPU cores.
title: Fast Bounds on Matching Decoder Soft Output for the Surface Code

summary: Most enterprise generative AI deployments are under-performing relative to their potential — not because the models are inadequate, but because the dominant interaction paradigm is architecturally mismatched to the systems it deploys. This paper introduces the Emergent Intelligence Performance Calibration (EIPC) framework: a coherence-based approach to reliable, auditable, high-performance collaboration with large language models in high-stakes contexts. The framework is built on four operational principles — Purpose-Matched Tasks, Relational Scaffolding, Ethical Framing and Care, and Recognition, Provenance & Attribution — deployed through a single reusable document: the Project Charter. The EIPC Clock, a twelve-position diagnostic tool mapping Quality Collaboration Components (QCCs) across three progressive degrees of collaboration sophistication, gives practitioners a vocabulary for identifying which interaction properties are active and what interventions will move the collaboration toward higher-order performance. A growing body of research on structured prompting and multi-turn collaboration is consistent with the framework's core claim: interaction patterns aligned with how LLMs are built tend to produce better outcomes than low-context, command-response prompting. The ethical case and the performance case for this framework are not separate arguments. They are the same argument, expressed in two registers. Universal Emergence Foundation Technical Report UEF-2602.
title: Coherence-Based Collaboration & Emergent Intelligence Performance Calibration (EIPC): A Framework and Vocabulary for High-Stakes Work with LLMs

summary: This Python software provides a Docker-based workflow for electroencephalography (EEG) quality control, preprocessing and feature extraction . It supports reproducible research on attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents using the task recordings in the BALLADEER dataset. The software documents and implements the processing workflow underlying A task EEG dataset with preprocessed signals and features for ADHD research in children and adolescents . That companion resource contains 669 eligible recordings from 156 participants and 115 feature definitions or templates across seven feature families. The recordings and generated feature tables are distributed separately from this software. What the software does Raw EEG quality assessment: characterizes recording quality before preprocessing and produces structured quality summaries. Recording eligibility and correction plans: applies the supplied, frozen label-blind selection records, including recording eligibility and approved channel-interpolation actions. Conservative EEG preprocessing: processes continuous blocks without bridging acquisition gaps, applies 0.5–40 Hz filtering, harmonizes sampling to 128 Hz, and performs conditional channel interpolation and average referencing. Post-preprocessing quality assessment: calculates quality summaries and comparisons with the original recordings. EEG feature extraction: generates seven feature families using aligned, gap-aware windows of 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds with 50% overlap, subject to each estimator's duration requirements. Output verification: checks processing lineage, cross-stage consistency and recorded checksums. The supplied selection records preserve the decisions used for the companion dataset. Reusing those records does not repeat the original manual review or establish new eligibility decisions for another cohort. Seven EEG feature families Temporal and statistical features. Conventional spectral features. Aperiodic spectral features. Complexity and fractal features. Functional connectivity features. Graph and network features. Time-frequency decomposition features. Feature definitions expand across channels, channel pairs and other indexed positions. Outputs retain calculation states and reasons for unavailable or undefined values. Duration-dependent support is explicit; for example, the configured aperiodic spectral analysis uses 8- and 16-second windows. Supported recordings, inputs and outputs The input is the original BALLADEER dataset, version 2 , obtained from its version-specific Figshare record . Extract the source data before running the software. Set --input-dir to the directory that directly contains users_demographics.json and participant directories such as UB0004/ , preserving the original task subdirectories and filenames. The companion Zenodo derivative dataset is an output resource, not the input to this complete reproduction workflow. The packaged workflow is configured for five BALLADEER task conditions: CogniFit cognitive assessment, Attention Robots, and Slackline levels 1, 6 and 11. Users also provide a writable output directory. The input directory is mounted read-only. Outputs include preprocessed EEG signals in MNE-FIF format, tabular feature outputs, quality summaries, calculation-state records, configuration snapshots, processing manifests and checksums. The software archive includes label-blind selection metadata with pseudonymous recording identifiers; it does not contain the original EEG recordings or the generated derivative dataset. Reproducibility and package contents The archive includes Python source code, scientific configurations, a Dockerfile, version-pinned Python dependencies, shell launchers, validation tests and documentation. Users can run individual processing stages, extract one feature family for one task, or execute the complete sequential workflow. Graph features use the corresponding connectivity outputs. summary: APEP — JGR manuscript release ( paper-jgr-v1.0 ) Code, data products and figures supporting the manuscript on the ionospheric response to the 14 October 2023 annular and 8 April 2024 total Great American Eclipses (GAEs). Summary We present a multipoint investigation of the ionospheric response to the 14 October 2023 annular and 8 April 2024 total Great American Eclipses (GAEs) using coordinated observations from five Digisondes, the Wallops Island VIPIR, the Millstone Hill incoherent scatter radar, and continental-scale GNSS TEC measurements. Key results Clear E- and F2-region depletions in both events across peak obscurations of 0.30–0.82, observed at local times 10:24–15:22 LT. E region depletion scales quasi-linearly with obscuration; the F2 region lags peak obscuration by 20–30 min, consistent with the longer O⁺ recombination timescale. No G-condition (NmF1 ≥ NmF2) in either event, even at 0.82 obscuration: high obscuration alone is insufficient without adequate F2-peak height reduction and favourable local-time/seasonal conditions. White Sands skymaps show a bifurcated echo population during the 2024 recovery phase; Wallops VIPIR frequency–time–intensity plots show cusp-like features confined to 3–6 MHz. Idealized ray tracing shows both signatures can arise from eclipse-excited wave structures at different horizontal scales, i.e. distinct HF manifestations of a common wave field. GNSS TEC : along-track relative change in minima exceeds 40 % (2023 and 2024) relative to the expected baseline. Figures in this release All manuscript figures are in manuscript_figures/jgr/ (PNG, plus PDF where produced). Generating code is in apep/jgr/ . Figures 2 and 4 (ionosonde time series) were redone as 5×4 grids: rows are the five stations sorted by peak obscuration; columns are foF2, h′F2/hmF2, foE, h′E/hmE. Each panel shows the eclipse-day series (smoothed, gaps ≤ 90 min interpolated) against the quiet-day median, with the eclipse interval shaded and the peak obscuration 𝒪ᵖ₁₉₃ annotated. Journal-style fonts, thin lines, no heavy markers; AGU double-column width. Figure 2 (2023, 13–21 UT) is built entirely from Datasets/Data/*_scaled.csv and *_median.csv ; WS833/KR835 use the despiked event files in Datasets/processing/final/ when present. Figure 4 (2024, 16–21 UT) is built from SAO data via jgr_2024_scaled.py . Shared code: apep/jgr/jgr_timeseries_5x4.py ( jgr_2023_scaled.py is a thin wrapper). Known data caveats AU930 h′E sits in 100–110 km steps against an ~85 km median (2023); the 2024 AU930 hmE median CSV is flat at 110 km. AU930 foF2 saturates near 9.9 MHz after ~18:30 UT (2023). BC840 h′F2 shows a ~340 km excursion near maximum obscuration (2023). KR835/WS833 median CSVs lack true hmF2/hmE; 2024 KR835/WS833 median CSVs do not exist (baseline falls back to the SAO mean); WS833 2024 has no data. summary: Meeting human needs within the ecological limits of our planet calls for continuous reflection and redesigning of agricultural technologies and practices. Such technologies include fertilisers, the discovery and use of which have been one of the key factors for increasing crop yield, agricultural productivity and food security. Fertiliser use comes, however, at an environmental cost, and fertilisers have also not been a very economically effective production factor to lift many poor farmers out of poverty, where application on poor soils of unbalanced compositions of nutrients in fertilisers has shown limited impact on yield increase. Agronomic practices to apply existing mineral fertilisers, primarily containing N, P and K, at the right time, the right place, in the right amount, and of the right composition can improve the use efficiency of fertilisers. However, the overall progress to reduce the negative side effects is inadequate for the desired transformation toward sustainable agriculture in poor countries. With the increase in the world population and the demand for food, new agricultural practices have been developed to improve food production through the use of more effective pesticides and fertilisers. Controlled release technology is an invaluable scientific tool for improving performance and safety of chemicals, which involve materials such as barriers surrounding active materials to deliver the latter at the optimum time and rate needed. This article reviews the recent trends, developments and future applications of controlled release fertilizers (CRFs) produced from renewable resources. Polymers based CRFs are attracting increased attention due to environmental concerns and the realization that global resources are finite. summary: The calibration and test probabilities of every run of a tabular classification benchmark, released so that prediction sets and their metrics can be recomputed without refitting a model. A conformal set is a function of four arrays: the class probabilities and labels on a calibration split, and the same on a test split. This deposit is those arrays, together with the software that reads them. The benchmark comprises 218 classification datasets and 22 models from four families, among them 13 tabular foundation models, each evaluated with the same ten seeds. Of the 218, 178 are real datasets and 40 are a synthetic block generated for this benchmark; three of the real ones are Bayesian-network resamplings of small classical datasets and are much larger than their seeds; of those, only one has its own seed in the collection, so that pair is not independent of itself while a rank test treats datasets as independent. Dataset size does not indicate provenance: the largest datasets in the collection are real. Coverage is not uniform and the per-model dataset count is reported for every cell. Eleven datasets carry more than ten classes, and the in-context models measured on them cannot enter them: one refuses and names the limit, another builds a ten-output head and fails inside a kernel. That is a capability limit observed on the models that were run rather than a property claimed of the family, and it is not missing work. One foundation model is measured on the original datasets only. Anything computed across models should be computed on a complete submatrix: the datasets on which every model being compared has all ten seeds. The calibration rows are held out of fitting, of tuning, of early stopping and of the in-context data, and each cell records which rows they were. The code that does it is included, with the line of each step documented. Probabilities are float64 and are not rounded: a prediction set is a comparison against a threshold, and a point sitting on that threshold moves if the value it is compared to is shortened. The data are released under CC BY 4.0. The software included in the source archive is released under the MIT licence, as stated by the LICENSE file it contains. The datasets themselves are not redistributed: each cell carries the row indices into its source dataset, and the synthetic datasets regenerate from their seeds with an included script. Model weights are not redistributed; every checkpoint is named in the model table. Version 1.2.0 adds the runs completed after version 1.1.0 and changes or removes nothing in it. Three new shards (cells-011 to cells-013, 2.02 GB) hold 311 further cells; index.parquet now lists all 46,182 cells and manifest_1016.parquet is their manifest. The files prefixed blocks_1016__ recompute the two blocks outside the main comparison on the completed runs, with the pipeline that produced the article's tables: the large-dataset block on 49 datasets and 21 models (42 in version 1.1.0) and the many-class block on 11 datasets and 7 models (5 in version 1.1.0). The main block of 113 real datasets and 22 models is unchanged. CHANGELOG.md lists what is added and the pairs that are still missing, with the reason for each.
title: TabSets: calibration and test probabilities for set-valued evaluation of tabular classifiers

summary: V9 reproducibility data for ERalpha anthraquinone recognition This release supports Hydroxyl availability and spacing govern anthraquinone recognition by estrogen receptor alpha by Hui Ming Chua, Said Moshawih, Nurolaini Kifli, Hui Poh Goh, Long Chiau Ming and Khang Wen Goh. The primary archive contains verified simulation inputs and topologies for 34 retained conventional trajectories, 45 production umbrella windows and 12 accelerated-weight-histogram walkers, together with velocity seeds, source-coordinate records, extension history, pull series, WHAM records, analysis scripts, fingerprint matrices and locally dated prediction files. The umbrella records cover 708 ns nominal sampling; the archived AWH records extend to 87.504 ns. The companion archive contains the processed historical Schrodinger-series source tables and independent reconstruction scripts. It reproduces the corrected 51-, 49- and 18-system hydroxyl-engagement analyses. Two energy-only reference systems retain unavailable contact fields rather than artificial zeros. Assets and verification eralpha_anthraquinone_reproducibility_V9.zip : 886,491,635 bytes; SHA-256 304044c11d587077fc87e587b68ae2774fd9c1a13eaa55447a588a095366d549 . legacy53_processed_reproducibility_V9.zip : 720,235 bytes; SHA-256 8e1afd886690d50af9fd10792b76f0191e56ee3842f3c4f495451d6d304e99b1 . The corresponding .sha256 files and validation records accompany the archives. The primary archive contains 4,858 source files verified against the source inventory. The companion archive was independently reconstructed in an isolated directory and reproduced the corrected tables byte-for-byte. Scope This deposit contains inputs, processed data and analysis records. Coordinate trajectories are excluded; the archives do not constitute a complete raw-trajectory collection. The historical Schrodinger companion contains authors' processed data, not proprietary software or a complete Desmond trajectory/input archive. Original absolute analysis paths may need to be changed to the extracted paths. Original local prediction timestamps are preserved as provenance; no external preregistration identifier is asserted. The authors' new numerical data are provided under the scoped CC BY 4.0 terms documented inside the primary archive. Existing software, adapted code and force-field material retain their original provenance and terms. This release does not relicense third-party materials.
