summary: The July 2026 counterexample settled the Jacobian conjecture in dimensions N ≥ 3 and left JC(2) as the open case. This paper develops an exact-arithmetic program on the planar case. The Keller condition J(P, Q) = 1 is linear in Q for fixed P; the resulting machine (eliminate, parametrize the consistency variety, complete, invert) closes the columns min deg ≤ 2 uniformly (one closed inverse for the whole quasi-triangular class), forces perfect-power tops at bidegrees (2, n) and (3, n), and inverts every consistent stratum it has met. Four unconditional exclusion theorems follow from a weight-class calculus: a two-term P = x + a x^u y^v is never a Keller component at any partner degree; neither is any lower-weight perturbation of it; no Keller component carries a Newton top edge anchored at the linear vertex x with interior direction; and if x is a vertex of the Newton polygon then P = x + f(y) exactly (the vertex dichotomy). The residual open core is the transport of the Keller constant along the staircase of Newton vertices swallowing x: we show the completion window is block-triangular under the edge grading, exhibit the classwise transport chain as an executable elimination whose obstruction always localizes at the constant's class, and prove the corresponding fifth exclusion: for primitive tops the certificate-tower induction closes it unconditionally at all partner degrees (cleared base certificates with monomial pairings such as -13860 a^7, plus a resonance-reduction lemma showing window growth can never repair the constant's row). A recalibration against the primary sources shows that our composite-gcd certificates replicate literature-covered territory (the verified floor is gcd ≤ 8, primes, 2p, then Heitmann's B ≥ 16 and the Guccione-Guccione-Valqui dichotomy B = 16 or B > 20), and that the open frontier is the B = 16 normal form together with the single surviving degree pair (72, 108) below 125. For that open pair, an exact instantiation of the primary sources gives two necessary conditions on the original pair: seven possible northeastern vertices for a nonzero inner polynomial, and deg_x Res_y(P, Q) = 21 with an 84 + 24 major/minor root partition; neither condition alone excludes the pair. A constructible determinantal-strata calculation closes the first actual three-coefficient GGHV slice exactly. On the residual curve, two normalized maximal minors reduce, with z = u^9, to 21 - 96z - 1024z^2 and (8z + 1)^14; an explicit integer Bezout identity has constant 17^14. After adding ε_(0,7), the only two-chart residual is a degree-12 fiber over z = -1/8. A third exact minor has coprime degree-13 fiber determinant, certified by a second integer Bezout identity. A connected mod-9 row/column grading extends to every nonconstant direction in the 26-parameter lower family. This is a strict slice result and does not exclude the full (72, 108) family. At the level of the full family, after removal of the structural constant column and with the complete 302-row pool (the forced-only construction has 289 rows), one selected augmented minor compresses to a 36-column block depending on 24 of the 51 parameters. Two connectivity-generating triples factor exactly; one graph-active direction cancels identically, while the other determinant becomes weighted homogeneous with weights (7, 3, 9) after shifting the forced coefficient. On the d = 0 boundary, the tautological kernel [P, P] = 0 can be quotiented exactly. One quotient determinant factors into b^32, one five-term weighted factor, and five binomials; a second is a nonzero scalar times a^107. Together with the exact origin rank gap, these charts close the complete quotient boundary. On d ≠ 0, a first alternative chart reduces each selected component G, L, Q to a finite intersection. A third exact determinant factors as X^30 LQR, for X = A^3, and exact component ideals close G. A row basis selected independently on the finite L and Q residuals is in fact shared. Its 23-term deter

summary: Iterative language-model optimizers refine prompts and programs by evaluating a candidate, showing a proposer model a sample of failing cases, and keeping revisions that improve performance. Recent work attributes the limits of this loop to narrow single-round reflection, introducing full-set error clustering, targeted minibatches, or larger proposer models so the optimizer sees more failure modes per step. Yet every existing evaluation tests these mechanisms exclusively inside lineage-preserving search, where each revision edits a surviving parent, leaving the contribution of parent inheritance confounded with the breadth of per-round feedback. Across 1,750 pre-registered runs spanning nine prompt and program synthesis benchmarks, we separate parent inheritance from feedback disclosure under matched evaluation budgets. We find that greedy parent inheritance drives the vast majority of optimization progress, outperforming seed-reset resampling even when seed-reset proposals receive a clustered summary of all failures in every round or use a larger proposer model. While full-set error clustering and diverse failure selection improve single-step rewrites from the seed and accelerate the opening rounds of search, sequential parent inheritance rapidly closes this gap as solved error modes are retained in the candidate and filtered from subsequent failure lists. Moreover, decomposing token expenditure in GEPA reveals that proposer reflection accounts for only a small fraction of total cost whereas validation and minibatch gating consume nearly the entire budget, showing that greedy parent inheritance over raw failures captures the gains of complex reflective loops at a fraction of their compute.
title: Lineage Is Memory: Parent Inheritance and Feedback Disclosure in Short-Budget LLM-Guided Optimization

summary: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. summary: Turning an engineering request into a simulation requires consistent geometry, physics, boundary conditions, and numerical settings. Recent agent-assisted systems automate simulation setup, but successful execution alone does not establish whether the specification preserves the intended problem or correctly handles missing information. We study whether agents can reliably construct complete executable JSON specifications for automated geometry creation, meshing, PDE solving, and result export. Our workflow combines model extraction with deterministic scientific and capability checks, explicit clarification, and validated local patches that preserve unrelated accepted fields. We evaluate specification correctness, execution completion, and numerical verification separately. On 120 template-related requests, the full workflow achieves 98.3% correct first-turn specification and decision outcomes, compared with 92.5% for schema-assisted single shot and 82.5% for model-only: gains of 5.8 and 15.8 percentage points, respectively. It makes no false-ready decisions among the 42 requests requiring clarification or rejection. Component ablations identify contributions from scientific checks and conditional repair. Separate downstream studies cover 1D, 2D, and 3D steady and unsteady, linear and nonlinear problems, including flow and elasticity with complex three-dimensional wing geometries. A 30-case gallery demonstrates automated execution from retained JSON specifications, while 9 of 12 selected live user-to-results tests achieve joint specification, execution, export, and numerical-reference success (75.0%). These results support traceable, engineer-reviewed simulation assistance within the tested scope, while fresh-response regressions identify consistency as a priority for further improvement.
title: From 1D Benchmarks to Complex 3D Geometries: Can Agents Reliably Specify Problems for Automated PDE Simulation?

summary: Reasoning video object segmentation (ReVOS) requires segmenting the target specified by an implicit query throughout a video. Existing MLLM-based methods typically require costly cross-model alignment, tying MLLM training to a downstream segmentation model. We present ReVEAL, a decoupled thinking-with-video framework for ReVOS that elicits role-aware latent visual evidence from MLLM reasoning to directly guide segmentation. ReVEAL introduces Visual Evidence Tokens (VETs) into video reasoning to associate necessary visual regions or entities with target, background, or distractor roles, while a Dynamic Attention Layer Router adaptively aggregates VET-to-video attention across layers into role-specific grounding evidence. We train the MLLM to perform VET-augmented reasoning on our constructed ReVEAL-47K dataset, with a Contrastive Attention Grounding Loss as auxiliary supervision to apply role-specific constraints to VET attention and optimize layer routing for reliable latent grounding. At inference, ReVEAL identifies the target through this thinking-with-video process and fuses the resulting role-specific evidence to guide a frozen SAM2 in predicting target masks. Experiments on five benchmarks show that ReVEAL outperforms alignment-free baselines and remains competitive with alignment-based methods.
title: ReVEAL: Eliciting Role-Aware Latent Visual Evidence from MLLMs for Reasoning Video Object Segmentation

summary: We study linearized gravitational reconstruction in global AdS$_4$ with dynamical scalar matter, building on vacuum Einstein perturbations with fixed boundary metric and nontrivial normalizable data. External scalar sources prepare an excited state and modify the holographic Ward identities, while subsequent evolution can proceed without boundary driving. Separating the bulk matter-sourced response from vacuum perturbations, we derive an electric quadrupole master equation with the matter-dependent corrections required by the Einstein constraints. We also verify that a cylindrical boundary integral reproduces the Regge--Wheeler master field mode by mode, without identifying it with the full global Fefferman--Graham reconstruction. For weakly interacting scalars that become massless in the flat-space limit, we extract the Bondi shear and news from retarded gravitational evolution. The resulting supertranslation memory agrees numerically with the outgoing energy redistribution and the quadrupole moment of the boundary work. In the ordered flat-space limit, later boundary controls leave the first event's waveform unchanged, despite cancelling residual gravitational modes at finite AdS radius.
title: Gravitational Memory from AdS States in the Flat-Space Limit

summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly multilingual, distinguishing human-written from AI-generated text is essential for maintaining information integrity. However, research remains English-centric, with limited benchmarks for low-resource languages such as Hindi. To address this gap, we introduce SHAKTI, a large-scale Hindi benchmark covering four genres, eight LLM families, multiple prompting strategies, and adversarial transformations. We evaluate its quality through human annotation and analyze linguistic, grammatical, and sentiment-based differences between human- and AI-generated texts. Building on these findings, we propose TRIDENT, a round-trip translation-based detection framework with three variants: TRIDENT-S (static threshold), TRIDENT-D (dynamic threshold), and TRIDENT-C (logistic regression using multi-distance RTT features). TRIDENT leverages semantic consistency between original and round-trip translated texts to identify AI-generated content. Extensive experiments show that TRIDENT outperforms conventional and supervised baselines, with TRIDENT-S achieving the best overall performance. Further evaluations across seven languages, adversarial settings, and unseen LLMs demonstrate its multilingual applicability and robustness, while highlighting sensitivity to the translation model.
title: TRIDENT and SHAKTI: A Framework and Benchmark for Hindi AI-Text Detection

summary: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $α_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(Φ, t_n)$ alone. Here $α_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $α_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $α_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention

summary: Rumor models of the Daley--Kendall and Maki--Thompson family anchor the statistical mechanics of social contagion, yet the stifler composition a rumor leaves behind has resisted closed-form analysis. Inspired by the asymmetric two-step pairing (A2SP) process of step-growth polymerization, we import its common-factor cancellation into a minimal two-stage MT variant in which re-contacted spreaders are re-activated into a senior class at rate $αk_1$ rather than stifled, and obtain exact terminal-state theorems. (i) Saturation: the rumor exhausts the ignorant pool for every stifling-to-recruitment ratio $μ>0$, with a three-way tail classification and a logarithmically critical line at $μ=1$. (ii) Final size: the terminal stifler pool splits as $(x_1,x_2)=(μ/(α+μ),α/(α+μ))$, independent of seed size; the fingerprint inverts linearly ($α=μx_2/x_1$) and matches Gillespie simulations within $0.95\%$. summary: As a paradigm for describing open-quantum-system dynamics, the non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation generally modifies state norms, complicating coherent control over the system's Hilbert space. With a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases, we develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $Λ$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.
title: Biorthogonal universal quantum control

summary: AI coding assistants are commonly used for daily software development tasks. While prior research has examined their impact on productivity and code quality, less is understood about how these tools support diverse ways of thinking. Evidence from non-AI software engineering tools suggests that mismatches between tool design and users' cognitive styles can introduce inclusivity barriers, but it remains unclear whether similar issues arise in AI coding assistants. We investigate how developers with different cognitive styles experience and interact with these tools and whether they exhibit cognitive inclusivity challenges. We conducted a controlled laboratory study with 20 student participants using GitHub Copilot to complete code generation, debugging, and refactoring tasks. Using think-aloud protocols, semi-structured interviews, and inductive thematic analysis, we identify patterns in user interaction. We then apply the GenderMag framework to examine how these patterns differ across cognitive styles. We identify five inclusivity issues concerning how Copilot explains suggestions, supports validation, facilitates learning, exposes its features, and influences the problem-solving process. Our findings suggest that common interaction paradigms in AI coding assistants can privilege certain cognitive styles while introducing additional cognitive effort for others. We derive design implications for more inclusive AI coding assistants.
title: Cognitive Inclusivity in AI Coding Assistants: Evidence from GitHub Copilot

summary: We address the inverse problem of reconstructing a meson parton distribution function (PDF) or parton distribution amplitude (PDA) at a fixed scale from a finite set of Mellin moments. At finite moment order this map is ill posed in the Hadamard sense: the moments do not determine a unique, stable pointwise $x$-dependence, and small data perturbations can produce large changes in the reconstruction. We regularize the problem by restricting the admissible function class through constraints justified by first principles---support on $x\in[0,1]$, endpoint vanishing, unit normalization, and, for the pion, the exact $x\leftrightarrow 1-x$ symmetry---and by complementing these hard constraints with differentiable penalties that suppress the spurious multiple maxima and central concavity changes typical of ill-posed inversions. We parameterize the unknown function with two interchangeable neural cores, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN), and find that the KAN reconstructs the target distributions more accurately, most markedly in the asymmetric (kaon) case. We attribute this advantage to the locality of the B-spline basis underlying the KAN, which localizes corrections during moment matching and damps the global oscillations to which the MLP is prone. Benchmarks against synthetic targets, using both ten and five input moments, support these conclusions.
title: Reconstructing Meson Parton Distributions from Mellin Moments with Artificial Neural Networks

summary: Code, pinned inputs, raw API responses and expected numbers for Sections 3.6 and 5.2.1 of the working paper “Global Trade Settlement and Alternative Financial Rails”. reproduce.py rebuilds the freeze-timing and balance-at-freeze results (Section 5.2.1) from the OFAC SDN Advanced XML (downloaded 31 Oct 2026), TronGrid AddedBlackList events and USDT-TRC20 transfers, reproduces the Bank of Russia settlement-currency table (Section 3.6), and checks every figure against the numbers reported in the paper. summary: Ph.D. dissertation defense, Department of Physics, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, 27 October 2023. Committee: Johann Rafelski (chair), Shufang Su, John Rutherfoord, Stefan Meinel, Sean Fleming. Dissertation: https://hdl.handle.net/10150/670301 . arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07193 Abstract: Magnetism is a rich subject touching all aspects of physics. My goal with this dissertation is to explore spin and magnetic moments in relativistic mechanics from both a quantum and classical perspective. We emphasize the special case of gyromagnetic ratio g=2 and its relationship to the algebraic spin structure of wave equations. In relativistic quantum mechanics, we investigate generalizations of the Dirac equation for arbitrary magnetic moments for fermions. We analyze the homogeneous magnetic field case and the Coulomb problem for hydrogen-like atoms with emphasis on the role of the anomalous magnetic moment (AMM). We explore alternative approaches which combine mass and the magnetic moment. Classically, we propose a relativistic covariant model of the Stern-Gerlach force via the introduction of a magnetic four-potential. This model modifies the covariant torque equations and unites the Ampèrian and Gilbertian models for magnetic moments. We further study (transition) magnetic dipoles in Majorana neutrinos specifically analyzing the relationship between flavor mixing and electromagnetic (EM) fields. We demonstrate EM flavor mixing explicitly in the 2-flavor model and develop a dynamical mass basis with an EM rotation matrix. EM induced neutrino mass splitting is compared to neutrino mass hierarchy. An interesting application of these theoretical developments is to study primordial magnetization in the early universe during the hot dense electron-positron plasma epoch. We propose a model of magnetic thermal matter-antimatter plasmas. We analyze the paramagnetic characteristics of electron-positron plasma when exposed to an external primordial field. We determine the magnitude of a small polarization asymmetry sufficient to generate field strengths in agreement with those measured today in deep intergalactic space. Future research outlooks include: Second order equations for anomalous quantum chromodynamic (QCD) moments, neutrino CP violation in strong EM fields, and fifth-dimension spin dynamics in Kaluza-Klein theory.
title: Modern topics in relativistic spin dynamics and magnetism

summary: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.
title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models

summary: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses

summary: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory

summary: Natural-language skills enable large language model (LLM) agents to reuse procedures across tasks, yet most systems retrieve individual skills from a flat SkillBank without explicitly modeling the high-level strategy that governs their selection and use. We introduce TalentRL, a strategy-guided reinforcement learning framework for hierarchical routing over procedural memory. Coarse-grained talents represent recurring strategies for skill use, while fine-grained skills provide executable procedures. For each task, the policy model selects a talent that guides execution and softly prioritizes its associated skills during similarity-based retrieval. However, since task outcomes depend jointly on talent selection, retrieved skill context, and downstream execution, terminal rewards alone cannot isolate the contribution of the routing decision. TalentRL therefore trains talent routing with reward contrasts between rollouts of the same task under matched interventions on the talent-conditioned context, and optimizes downstream execution with group-relative advantages. Across seven open-domain and multi-hop question-answering benchmarks, talent-aware supervised fine-tuning improves average success rate by 7.53%, 6.71%, and 9.21% over the corresponding zero-shot baselines for Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B, respectively. Reinforcement learning further improves these SFT checkpoints by 7.58% to 9.32%, and TalentRL achieves the highest average success rate among all compared methods on all three backbones. On the agentic benchmarks ALFWorld and WebShop, TalentRL achieves the highest ALFWorld success rate (99.3%) and the highest WebShop score (90.7) among all compared methods.

summary: Agentic LLM assistants must repeatedly decide whether to answer from memory or to call a tool such as web search. Unnecessary searches cost latency and money; missing ones yield confident but unsupported answers. Prior work mostly measures verbalised confidence or trains new adaptive-retrieval methods, and rarely audits the search decisions that deployed products actually make. We introduce a benchmark of 400 multiple-choice questions that combines widely known inside-knowledge (IK) questions, which should be answered directly, with outside-knowledge (OK) questions about facts from news published after the models' training cut-offs (to our knowledge), which should trigger search or, without tools, abstention. Each item offers an abstain option, and two action-level scores, NAS and KIS, reward searching on OK questions and restraint on IK questions. Across five commercial LLMs with and without their vendors' web search, GPT-5 mini and Grok 4 Fast search on over 90% of OK but only 1% of IK questions, whereas Mistral Small searches on just 20% of OK questions, often abstaining instead of using its tool; one product's search indicator proved unusable. Searching is partly triggered by explicit temporal cues: on uncued OK questions, the NAS of the two selective models falls from about 0.72 to 0.57--0.58. The scores thus measure the search triggering of specific products, not metacognition in a strict sense.
title: Confident Fools or Careful Searchers? A Behavioural Study of When LLMs Search Beyond Their Static Internal Memory

summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) requires agents to operate under environmental changes while reusing prior knowledge whenever possible. We argue that model-based reinforcement learning provides a promising framework for this setting because learned world models (WMs) can, in principle, support change detection, knowledge reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. However, such benefits depend heavily on whether the learned model can generalize beyond the contexts in which it was trained. In this work, we propose to formulate this problem with a contextual Markov decision process in which context is decomposed into behavioral and physical components. This view organizes continual WM learning into reuse, adaptation, and acquisition of new knowledge. As a first step, we study direct reuse when behavioral rules remain unchanged. Using Dyna-Q and TD-MPC in controlled FourRooms tasks, we find that zero-shot reuse can degrade substantially under physical-context changes and that this behavior depends strongly on the observation representation used by the WM. Additional ablation studies and latent-space diagnostics suggest that learned representations do not automatically provide the invariances needed for reuse. These results identify representation generalization as an important bottleneck for reliable world-model reuse in CRL.

summary: Robot perception is increasingly data driven, yet field data is slow, costly, and sometimes disruptive to collect. Video world models offer a cheaper source: seeded with real frames, they extend a recorded scene into new footage with the deployment's sensor, altitude, and environment. We ask whether such synthetic data matches the utility of real field data and whether detectors trained with it perform in the field. Seeding a 7B-parameter world model with wildlife drone video, we more than double the training set with curated frames. On held-out videos from the same drones, mAP@50--95 rises 4.3\% when these frames are added to real data and 10.3\% when they replace it, and up to 33.5\% on an urban benchmark. Although an expert rejects an estimated 87.5\% of generated clips, the data costs about \$1,100 of GPU time, against more than \$3,200 of field labor alone for a less useful real training set. Synthetic data thus shifts data costs from fieldwork to compute.
title: Dreams Are Cheaper Than Flights: Curated World-Model Data Improves Aerial Detection

summary: Latent world models allow reinforcement learning agents to learn policies from imagined trajectories, yet determining the optimal depth of model reliance remains a fundamental challenge. Fixed imagination horizons apply uniform prediction depths regardless of trajectory reliability, exposing target values to compounding model error or over-relying on critic approximations. We introduce density-guided bootstrap boundaries, a trajectory-dependent mechanism that adapts the depth of imagined returns using a score-informed relative density proxy. The proxy accumulates the estimated divergence of a score-corrected auxiliary field formed by a feature displacement network and a noise-conditioned score estimator along imagined paths. We propose two gating mechanisms: a hard boundary that halts return expansion at a discrete state, and a soft boundary that continuously shifts the return recursion toward critic bootstrapping. Both variants preserve boundary value estimates and apply corresponding survival weights to actor and critic losses. Formulated independently of specific dynamics models and instantiated within Dreamer V3, we prove that the resulting gated Bellman operator is a strict contraction mapping and that early bootstrapping monotonically reduces conditional target variance. We clarify the theoretical assumptions distinguishing our expansion proxy from exact path likelihoods. Across continuous-control tasks and Atari Pong, empirical evaluations show that dynamic boundary selection enhances sample efficiency and late-training performance over fixed-horizon and auxiliary-enabled baselines.

summary: Large language models have been shown to memorise and reproduce verbatim sequences from their training data, raising concerns about privacy leakage, intellectual property exposure, and the limits of generalisation. Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

Recent theoretical work suggests that attention heads may contribute to this behaviour by functioning as associative memory mechanisms, with memorisation capacity scaling with the number of heads. At the same time, empirical work has shown that many attention heads are redundant and can be pruned with limited impact on downstream performance. Despite these parallel findings, the effect of pruning redundant heads on memorised-sequence reproduction remains unexplored. In this work, we demonstrate that zeroing out a substantial fraction of attention heads prior to inference can significantly suppress verbatim memorisation while preserving, or even improving, language modelling performance on the benchmark used to identify redundant heads. Evaluating GPT-2-XL(1.5B) on known memorised sequences, we find that pruning 729 task-redundant heads reduces the memorisation count by 91.5%, while improving WikiText-103 perplexity by 0.92. These findings suggest that attention-head redundancy can be exploited to mitigate memorisation at inference time, without retraining or modifying the training data.

summary: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model agents by sampling and selecting among multiple candidate trajectories, but common realizations assume that these trajectories can be executed in parallel. This assumption breaks in realistic deployments, where enterprise workspaces and cloud services are shared and persistent, costly or infeasible to replicate, and actions may introduce irreversible side effects or cross-trajectory interference. Existing generative world models avoid direct execution, but typically compress environment state into a single prompt, limiting their ability to reliably simulate transitions under partial observability. Instead, we introduce Agentic World Modeling (AWM), which reformulates next-observation prediction as a multi-turn evidence-acquisition task. For each hypothetical action, an agentic simulator adaptively queries the real environment through safe read-only interfaces, reasons over the returned evidence, and uses executable computation to construct the resulting observation without mutating shared state. Integrated with trajectory-level TTS, AWM enables parallel exploration over a single shared environment. Across $τ$-bench, AppWorld, and OfficeBench, AWM outperforms a single-shot simulation baseline by 40.07% on average, and surpasses a trained world-model baseline by 12.36% on average. These results establish interactive, read-grounded simulation as a practical foundation for safe and scalable agentic test-time scaling in shared, non-resettable environments.

summary: Although quantum geometry plays an established role in electronic transport and optical responses, the contribution of the time-reversal-odd Riemannian connection to fully subgap responses remains less explored. Here we identify intrinsic second-harmonic generation in PT-symmetric antiferromagnets, predominantly governed by the real sector of the interband Hermitian connection and arising entirely from virtual interband transitions. In bilayer MnBi$_2$Te$_4$, the response persists in trivial phases but is enhanced in the layer-Chern phase and reverses sign with Néel order, offering a probe of quantum geometry and phase-sensitive readout of antiferromagnetic order without mobile carriers or real excitations.

summary: We investigate triplon topology and the thermal Hall transport in a columnar valence-bond solid of a spin-$1/2$ honeycomb-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Inequivalent triangular sublattices, modeled by $J_2^A\neq J_2^B$, remove inversion symmetry at nearest-neighbor bond centers and allow in-plane Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya (DM) interactions. We identify the two symmetry-allowed in-plane DM vector patterns and present detailed results for the pattern parallel to the bonds including an out-of-plane magnetic field. Within a harmonic bond-operator treatment, we determine the triplon bands, their Berry curvatures and Chern numbers, and the triplon thermal Hall conductivity. The DM interaction and magnetic field generate nonzero Berry curvatures, but the numerically integrated Chern number of every isolated triplon band vanishes. Nevertheless, the energy-dependent Bose weighting of positive and negative Berry-curvature regions produces a finite thermal Hall response at nonzero low temperatures. We delimit the dilute-triplon regime in which the harmonic transport calculation is expected to be reliable. These results show that a vanishing Chern number band does not directly constrain the triplon response of a valence-bond solid. We also comment on the effects on the columnar valence-bond solid phase of a DM interaction between next-nearest-neighbor spins characterized by an out-of-plane vector pattern.
title: Triplon thermal Hall response in a honeycomb-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet with Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interactions

summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

summary: Using a unified method of identifying a telescoping function for each statistic-action pair, we prove conjectures of La Croix and Roby, and of Sheridan-Rossi that various permutation statistics, such as the number of fixed points, are homomesic under Foatic actions: compositions of the Foata bijection and dihedral symmetries of one-line notation. Underlying these results is a family of bijective identities relating permutation statistics across the Foata bijection; one of them --- an unexpected invariance of the number of right-to-left minima under reverse-complement, proved by an explicit bijection --- may be of independent interest. The telescoping functions also turn out to be shared among some Foatic actions, implying that mixing certain actions still yields a constant average on closed walks.

summary: We present FOMO-Z (Flexible Optimizer of Multi-dimensional Operators and photo-$z$s), a set of statistical methods implemented in Python for galaxy classification and probabilistic inference from photometry. The methods use a reference sample with known galaxy properties. They rely on explicit, physically interpretable criteria and make no assumptions about the functional form of the color distributions. Binary selections are calibrated using either linear color conditions, particularly suited to background galaxy selection, or flexible color--color grids, seeking to maximize completeness given a threshold on purity. For probabilistic inference, the code identifies reference objects with compatible colors within photometric uncertainties to estimate each test galaxy's probability of satisfying user-defined criteria, as well as probability density functions of continuous properties such as redshift. The code also reconstructs property distributions of selected galaxy populations using photometrically similar galaxies in the reference sample. This framework supports prior weights and reference redshift probability distributions. A built-in feature-selection method identifying informative colors is also introduced. We demonstrate applications to background galaxy selection, galaxy population classification, tomographic redshift calibration, and photometric redshift estimation. The code achieves results consistent with those obtained through machine-learning approaches, such as self-organizing maps, while remaining computationally efficient, making it suitable for large photometric surveys and future Stage IV cosmological analyses. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/GiorgioLesci/FOMO-Z.
title: FOMO-Z. Optimal galaxy classification, photometric redshifts, and reconstruction of population distributions

summary: Understanding dust evolution is essential for interpreting the properties of galaxies across cosmic time. Nearby galaxies have revealed a detailed picture of dust enrichment, but whether the same picture applies in the early Universe remains unclear. Here we explore the origin of interstellar dust in simulated galaxies at $z \sim 5$. Starting from the dust-to-stellar mass relation, we select five simulated star-forming galaxies with $SFR> 1 M_\odot yr^{-1}$ and $ log(M_\star/M_\odot) > 8$. We focus on three low-mass systems with comparable stellar masses ($log(M_\star/M_\odot) \sim 8.7$) but significantly different dust masses ($log(M_{\rm dust}/M_\odot) \sim 5.1-6.2$), to investigate the origin of the scatter in the relation. Our analysis combines outputs from the cosmological hydrodynamical simulation dustyGadget, a semi-analytical model for stellar dust production, and radiative-transfer post-processing with SKIRT. We confirm that stellar dust production alone reproduces only the low-dust branch of the relation. Grain growth is required to recover both its S-shape and the observed scatter, as established for nearby galaxies. The transition to efficient grain growth occurs at lower metallicity than locally, consistent with the denser interstellar medium of high-redshift systems. Differences in dust content reflect different stages of galaxy assembly. Progressively longer star formation histories lead to greater chemical enrichment and denser ISM, promoting increasingly efficient grain growth. We therefore identify the assembly stage as the key regulator of dust growth at high redshift. Mock observations show that JWST multi-band imaging can reveal the structural diversity of galaxies within the scatter, although the reconstruction of clumpy morphologies may remain incomplete. Their dust continuum emission remains below the sensitivity of current ALMA continuum surveys.

summary: Reproducibility data and code supporting the study “Parameter fragility in the reanalysis of published Mössbauer spectra” by Osman Armağan and Muhammed Emin Bedir. The release contains retained spectral coordinates, 44 primary archive fits and their start records, 44,000 archive perturbation refits, 24,000 paired-study refits for 12 panels from five publications, model configurations, 33 implementation-check records, 477 saved field-profile trials, provenance and source tables, bibliographic records, plotting programs, and a self-contained analysis notebook. Default execution verifies retained results and reconstructs figures without optimization; optional reruns write separate outputs. The archive contains 44 spectra from 19 publications (eight connected coauthor groups). Paired numerical references are author-supplied plotted spectra, not verified instrument-level raw counts. The analysis describes parameter sensitivity and agreement with published fits, not physical-accuracy guarantees. No independent external magnetic validation or second-operator extraction is included. Download and extract Zenodo_Upload_Files.zip. It contains five files: Reproducibility_Package.zip (complete data/code release and integrity manifest), Reproduce_Analysis.ipynb (standalone notebook), Figures_600dpi.zip (12 main/supplementary figures in PNG, TIFF, PDF and SVG), README.txt, and CITATION.cff. Extract Reproducibility_Package.zip for direct access to individual data/code files. For notebook use, follow README.txt and select the inner Reproducibility_Package.zip when prompted. Author-created material is distributed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party software and source data retain their original terms and attribution; no additional third-party rights are granted. Article PDFs are not redistributed. This is a separate release from the authors’ earlier provenance/ML corpus (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21997560; related article DOI 10.1039/d6ra08367f).

summary: Memory has become central to self-evolving LLM agents, which store and retrieve experience from past rollouts to guide future decisions. Existing systems represent this experience as free-form natural language and maintain it by rewriting, which fits tasks whose experience is narratable. However, in scientific discovery and optimization, experience is often a quantity measured by an oracle under a specific context. Rewriting it as text leaves no index for where a record should be, replaces a measurement with a description, and cannot express how interventions interact. To address this, we argue that agent memory for biomolecule optimization should instead be indexable, quantitative, and structured, and we introduce MEMIG. This memory construction framework realizes these three properties. In detail, MEMIG addresses each insight with a domain-grounded identifier and accumulates the quantitative effect measured by a property oracle, so that updates remain local and retrieval becomes an exact lookup. Next, MEMIG connects insights whose interventions are applied together and measures their epistasis by decomposing each evaluated set. Our results show that MEMIG improves performance in most settings across in silico antibody optimization tasks.
title: MEMIG: Self-evolving Memory Construction for Antibody Optimization

summary: Learned world models ship as software components whose model versions, preprocessing, and test harnesses change between releases. Work on model updates already counts per-sample regressions, or negative flips, that an accuracy check hides. Two problems remain: a test can pass under one configuration and fail under another, and a harness fault can produce erroneous scores and wrong verdicts without a crash. We present TetraState, a regression-testing protocol for paired possible/impossible video tests. Each test runs under four fixed model-native configurations; its number of correct verdicts assigns one of four outcome classes. Inconclusive tests and failed executions are reported separately alongside the verdict rate. Revisions are compared by per-test outcome transitions, and the harness is versioned as part of the system under test. On all 506 IntPhys 2 Main tests and two heterogeneous systems, Cosmos 3 Nano and V-JEPA 2, two V-JEPA 2 harness revisions move modal accuracy by only 0.2 and 2.6 points yet change 11 and 214 test labels; in the second, accuracy rises although fewer tests are judged correctly, and 43 regressions keep the modal verdict, so a modal-verdict flip check misses them. These results outline a research agenda on configuration-level regression oracles for learned components.
title: One Verdict Is Not Enough: Regression Testing Learned World Models and Their Test Harnesses

summary: Quantization of Large Language Models (LLMs) has be- coming increasingly important for reducing the computa- tional costs and resource requirements for practical deploy- ment.Growinginterestinthisareahasmotivatedthecommu- nity to move beyond 8-bit quantization towards 4-bit preci- sion, leading to the development of customized 4-bit formats such as MXFP4 and NVFP4. Recently, HiFloat4 (HiF4) has emerged as a competitive alternative which adopts a Block Floating-Point(BFP)formatwithathree-levelscalinghierar- chy, thereby achieving a significantly larger dynamic range. While quantization can substantially reduce memory usage and accelerate inference, it frequently introduces accuracy degradation. Calibration is therefore essential for narrowing theperformancegapbetweenlow-precisionquantizedmodels and their full-precision counterparts. Nevertheless, existing calibration methods are mainly designed and validated us- ing integer-precision formats, such as INT4, lacking support for HiF4 due to its hierarchical BFP structure. In this paper, weinvestigatethreecalibrationapproaches,namelyHiGPTQ, HiAutoRound, and HiFlatQuant, to further enhance model quantizationbasedontheHiF4format.Extensiveexperiments demonstratethatallthreeproposedapproachesimproveinfer- ence accuracy compared with direct HiF4 conversion, reduc- ing the gap between HiF4 and BF16 to less than 1% and out- performing the state-of-the-art NVFP4 format across various models and downstream tasks.
title: Calibration of Large Model Quantization based on HiFloat4 Format

summary: Self-distillation methods for large language models with an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher already retain a history of student updates. Muon nevertheless stores a separate momentum buffer, increasing persistent training memory. We propose Muon with Reused Teacher (Muon-RT), which reuses the teacher-student displacement to eliminate momentum buffers for hidden weight matrices. We show that this displacement encodes an exponentially weighted history of applied updates and smooths temporally uncorrelated noise under a local model. Muon-RT removes its radial component, normalizes it spectrally, and mixes it with the current gradient after Newton-Schulz (NS) orthogonalization. Under explicit regularity and alignment assumptions, we establish linear contraction of an expected objective-gap bound toward a residual error level. With Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Muon-RT improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.6 points with 42% less persistent memory, and over momentum Muon by 5.4 points with 27% less persistent memory. With Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, it improves average accuracy over AdamW by 2.0 points.
title: MUON-RT Reusing the Teacher's Trajectory for Momentum-Free Muon for LLM Self-Distillation

summary: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents

Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
title: Accept Changes, Reject Attacks: Robust Memory Management for LLM Agents

summary: This archive contains workflow code, reduced analysis outputs, plotting inputs, selected simulation intermediates, and checksum manifests associated with the manuscript “Coupled Chemical and Physical Crosslinks in Dry Crosslinked Poly(vinyl alcohol) Networks: A Controlled-Topology Molecular Dynamics Study.” The simulations examine idealized dry poly(vinyl alcohol)–glutaraldehyde networks with controlled covalent strand length and fixed network topology. summary: Abstract The three companions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] use three structures side by side: probability laws and kernels, provenance (which source a record came from), and differentiation at the boundary of the simplex. This paper studies how they fit together, one layer at a time. Every ingredient of Step 1 is standard in categorical probability; what this step contributes is a set of exact statements about where the ingredients fail to commute, which the later steps build on. The finite distribution monad Dand the provenance comonad W= L×(−) are related by a distributive law λ: WD⇒DW, (l,p) →δ l ⊗p. All four axioms are written out with their types and proved. Its two-sided Kleisli category is the category of Markov kernels indexed by a source, with one source held throughout a composite. Marginalisation is total and affine. Event conditioning is partial and nonlinear. It is undefined exactly where the event has probability zero, it cannot be extended continuously to that wall, and its derivative grows like 1/p(A) near it. Conditioning commutes with marginalisation only for events that are cylinders over the kept coordinates. Contextual Bayes decomposition. Conditioning a pooled law equals pooling the conditioned sources with Bayes-updated weights. In the worked example, source weights 1 3 4 , 4 become 8 15 23 , 23 , and keeping the old weights gives the wrong answer ( 63 160 instead of 9 23 ). Forgetting provenance is marginalisation over the sources. It commutes with every window, but it is not injective: two families of sources can share a pooled law and every pooled table while differing in every labelled table. Step 2, the tangent layer. The cone tangent structure of the tangent companion commutes with the provenance comonad. Each source is a face of the labelled simplex, and a feasible direction leaves that face exactly when it injects whole records under another label; after forgetting provenance, an injected source and a drifting source have the same direction. Marginalisation and conditioning map feasible cones onto feasible cones, with explicit lifts; conditioning’s lift shrinks like p(A) near its wall. The cone T k Hof the half-line is generated by elementary tensors, so it is closed under products, and pooling is a morphism at every order: the pooling paradox lives in the decision functional, not in pooling. Differentiating the contextual Bayes decomposition splits every sensitivity into a reweighting term and a within-source term; in the worked example the answer 9 16 23 moves at rate− 529 per unit of small-trial share. Strata and jumps. The sources that survive conditioning are exactly those with π l p l (A) > 0. Conditioning maps fibres of forgetting onto fibres: it keeps provenance ambiguity on the event, discards it off the event, and can destroy identifiability but never create it. Inside 1 its domain, conditioning moves at rate at most 2/P(A), so nothing jumps and a sudden change needs a rare event. At the wall the limit is the conditional of the path’s leading jet; analytic passages are removable, and jumps need a kink, a non-analytic path, or a jump of the law. Step 3, orders of transitions. On non-negative germs in a Hardy field, order is a semiring homomorphism to (min,+), so every layer operation has an exact order calculus. Each source reaches an event at its own order. The sources of least order survive conditioning, with weights given by leading coefficients; the others vanish at their extinction orders. The two sides of a transition carry independent order data, analytic passages are removable but smooth ones need not be, and flat approaches have limits inside a Hardy field but not outside. A transition of order mis invisible to the tangent tower below level m. At a fixed gap, a higher-order approach switches more gradually. Step 4a–4b, several parameters. When several rates vanish together, orders form a fan: the normal fan of a Newton pol
title: Probability, Context and Differentiation: The Layers Steps 1–5: the distribution monad, the provenance comonad, the tangent layer, and orders of transitions

summary: CasADi is a symbolic framework for numeric optimization implementing automatic differentiation in forward and reverse modes on sparse matrix-valued computational graphs. It supports self-contained C-code generation and interfaces state-of-the-art codes such as SUNDIALS, IPOPT etc. It can be used from C++, Python, Matlab/Octave, Julia or Javascript
title: CasADi - A software framework for nonlinear optimization and optimal control

summary: Human preferences change over time: an established preference may remain valid over time, become uncertain as context shifts, or be explicitly revised. Effective personalization requires conversational AI to adapt its response strategy to evolving preferences rather than relying on passive memory retrieval. We formalize this capability as adaptive personalization under epistemic uncertainty. A human preference study further confirms that people favor state-contingent response strategies as preference uncertainty changes. To evaluate whether language models mirror this adaptation, we create a multilingual benchmark spanning 250 personas, 5 languages, and 25K conversational turns that decouples strategy selection from response execution. Across eight closed- and open-weight models, we uncover a recognition-generation gap: models reliably identify appropriate strategies when selecting among candidate options, but collapse during open-ended generation, suffering a 35-46% drop in strategy calibration. Crucially, this failure is systematic: models default to exploit-first behavior, over-relying on existing preferences regardless of preference epistemic uncertainty. We show this failure is addressable: while prompting interventions fail, targeted training that supervises models' internal strategy representations toward state-conditional human preferences narrows the user acceptability generalization gap by a third on out-of-distribution personas and conversational styles.
title: Adaptive Personalization Under Preference Epistemic Uncertainty

summary: The semidefinite programs (SDPs) of the numerical conformal bootstrap, and of S-matrix and quantum-mechanics bootstraps, are solved with primal-dual interior-point methods whose convergence guarantees rest on primal and dual Slater conditions: the existence of strictly feasible points on both sides of the duality. Many bootstrap SDPs violate these. The consequences range from slow convergence to inconclusive verdicts and the breakdown of the Skydive algorithm. We introduce "Slater tools", all acting within the PMP class accepted by SDPB. Diagnostics measure the Slater margins and, when a margin vanishes, extract the exposing certificate that identifies the degeneracy. Two independent cures follow. Transforms that provide rigorous bounds on the original SDP objective and that for the right parameter choices return the exact value. Facial reductions that use the exposing certificate to remove the degeneracies themselves. We reproduce, explain and resolve all known types of failures in a mixed-correlator 3d Ising setup. We show that the $X$-Slater condition (SDPB's primal) fails at every disallowed point in feasibility mode, holds in every navigator problem we tested, and can be guaranteed by one additional condition on the navigator function. We show that the folklore "instability remedy" of a twist gap works by removing degeneracies at the endpoints of the positivity conditions. These often stem from a mistake in factoring out the block prefactor but can also arise legitimately in channels that mix equal and unequal operator pairs. Finally we classify and remove all degeneracies of the published current-scalar bootstrap, among them one at $x=\infty$, thus incurable by any gap assumption, caused by unequal polynomial degrees within one matrix block.
title: Guaranteed Slater Conditions for the Numerical Conformal Bootstrap: Fixing Instabilities in SDPB, Navigator Methods, and Skydiving

summary: LUNA is a differentiable astrophysical hydrodynamics code written in JAX, with hand-written Pallas kernels as a fast path on GPUs. It solves the Euler equations in one, two and three dimensions with an unsplit, second-order MUSCL-Hancock scheme and HLLC or HLL Riemann solvers, and runs on CPUs and on many NVIDIA or AMD GPUs, with the domain split over devices. Self-gravity is solved with periodic or isolated boundaries and couples to the gas conserving energy; comoving cosmology evolves gas together with dark-matter particles; radiative cooling, driven turbulence and starburst energy and mass injection are built in. Examples of what it does: shock tubes, blast waves and Kelvin-Helmholtz, Rayleigh-Taylor and Richtmyer-Meshkov instabilities; Jeans collapse and collapsing self-gravitating clouds; the cosmic web of gas and dark matter from cosmological initial conditions; driven supersonic turbulence; galactic winds blown out of a starburst disk; and inverse problems, such as optimising initial conditions with gradients taken through the solver. Non-equilibrium chemistry and cooling networks, radiation transport, sink particles and star formation with stellar dynamics and feedback through Torch/AMUSE, and block-based adaptive mesh refinement are included as experimental modules. Validated capabilities are tested against exact solutions or other codes (AthenaK, Arepo, RAMSES), whose reference solutions are published with the code.
title: LUNA: A Differentiable Astrophysical Hydrodynamics Code
