summary: Why does length generalization (LG) depend so sharply on the positional encoding (PE)? Relative schemes extrapolate fixed offsets, absolute schemes fix positions, and neither handles growing offsets. We give a realizability theory for a deliberately controlled abstraction, a single positional-only attention head, that derives this well-documented empirical pattern and says precisely where it holds and breaks. The device is a simulation transfer operator $T_L$ that re-evaluates a selected length-$L_0$-realizing positional kernel on the longer grid, with a scalar $α_L \in [0,1]$ read off before any training from $(Φ, t_n)$ alone. Here $α_L$ serves as the computable witness of that taxonomy's derivation, not as a stronger empirical predictor. Our results are a relative-head deep-row characterization for kernels with a strict unique global maximizer (Theorem 2), an absolute/relative duality that derives the pattern (Proposition 4), a learned-absolute underdetermination result, and a static expressivity bound; a sufficiency theorem (Theorem 1) bridges $α_L$ to LG, and the general deterministic case is a precise open conjecture (correcting a tempting but invalid "outside-colspan" argument). Experiments confirm the structure: in the controlled single-head regime $α_L$ exactly separates the taxonomy's generalizing and non-generalizing (PE, task) cells (2625 trained-model measurements; stable at vocab 64/d=128). Together, these results turn the received PE taxonomy into a positional-kernel transfer theorem, and identify the content and depth mechanisms that escape it. The theory concerns the positional channel alone: tasks whose targets depend on token content, including the standard length-generalization suite such as addition and sorting, fall outside Theorem 2.
title: A Positional Realizability Theory of Length Generalization in Single-Head Attention

summary: Rumor models of the Daley--Kendall and Maki--Thompson family anchor the statistical mechanics of social contagion, yet the stifler composition a rumor leaves behind has resisted closed-form analysis. Inspired by the asymmetric two-step pairing (A2SP) process of step-growth polymerization, we import its common-factor cancellation into a minimal two-stage MT variant in which re-contacted spreaders are re-activated into a senior class at rate $αk_1$ rather than stifled, and obtain exact terminal-state theorems. (i) Saturation: the rumor exhausts the ignorant pool for every stifling-to-recruitment ratio $μ>0$, with a three-way tail classification and a logarithmically critical line at $μ=1$. (ii) Final size: the terminal stifler pool splits as $(x_1,x_2)=(μ/(α+μ),α/(α+μ))$, independent of seed size; the fingerprint inverts linearly ($α=μx_2/x_1$) and matches Gillespie simulations within $0.95\%$. (iii) Pooled versus history-resolved: pooled statistics are exactly $α$-free on any static graph; only the history-resolved composition carries $α$. Restoring the classic teller-retires channel breaks the exact closure beyond quantified gates (contact rates of $1$--$3\%$ of $k_1$ for spreader channels at $μ\leq1.5$, up to $32\%$ at $μ=2$), and on configuration-model networks the composition bias decays as $\langle k\rangle^{-0.71}$. An exploratory inversion of 354,930 Higgs--Twitter retweet episodes, screened by an identity check and four negative controls, yields $\hatα=2.21\%$ (joint cluster-bootstrap CI $[1.6\%,3.0\%]$; $\approx3.7\%$ after calibration at the matched threshold). Terminal compositions identify this effective re-activation rate, an upper bound on contact-coupled re-activation; the mechanism itself requires timing information beyond the terminal state.
title: Terminal-state theorems for a two-stage Maki--Thompson rumor model: final size, stifler composition, and non-identifiability from pooled statistics

summary: As a paradigm for describing open-quantum-system dynamics, the non-Hermitian Schrödinger equation generally modifies state norms, complicating coherent control over the system's Hilbert space. With a general instantaneous frame spanned by biorthogonal ancillary bases, we develop a biorthogonal quantum-control theory for discrete-variable systems governed by time-dependent non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. In particular, we derive a necessary and sufficient condition for extracting the transitionless pathways that transport parallel in ket and bra states. When this condition is satisfied by a set of projectors constructed with biorthogonal basis states, the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian becomes diagonal in the relevant biorthogonal subspace, enabling arbitrary initial state to evolve as a superposition of controlled transitionless passages. We further identify the parametric constraints under which the transformation linking the initial and final states becomes unitary. As a result, the final system state is automatically normalized even though the transitional dynamics is nonunitary. Our theory is justified by the bidirectional population transfer and a holomonic quantum gate implemented by a non-Hermitian three-level system in $Λ$ type. For the population transfer, controlled gain and loss reduce the required coherent pulse area, enabling shorter transfer times than the Hermitian benchmark with the same average Rabi frequency. Our work integrates the universal quantum control (UQC) into the biorthogonal representation, displaying full-rank passage engineering with coherent operations in non-Hermitian systems.
title: Biorthogonal universal quantum control

summary: We address the inverse problem of reconstructing a meson parton distribution function (PDF) or parton distribution amplitude (PDA) at a fixed scale from a finite set of Mellin moments. At finite moment order this map is ill posed in the Hadamard sense: the moments do not determine a unique, stable pointwise $x$-dependence, and small data perturbations can produce large changes in the reconstruction. We regularize the problem by restricting the admissible function class through constraints justified by first principles---support on $x\in[0,1]$, endpoint vanishing, unit normalization, and, for the pion, the exact $x\leftrightarrow 1-x$ symmetry---and by complementing these hard constraints with differentiable penalties that suppress the spurious multiple maxima and central concavity changes typical of ill-posed inversions. We parameterize the unknown function with two interchangeable neural cores, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and a Kolmogorov--Arnold network (KAN), and find that the KAN reconstructs the target distributions more accurately, most markedly in the asymmetric (kaon) case. We attribute this advantage to the locality of the B-spline basis underlying the KAN, which localizes corrections during moment matching and damps the global oscillations to which the MLP is prone. Benchmarks against synthetic targets, using both ten and five input moments, support these conclusions.
title: Reconstructing Meson Parton Distributions from Mellin Moments with Artificial Neural Networks

summary: Ph.D. dissertation defense, Department of Physics, University of Arizona, Tucson, AZ, 27 October 2023. Committee: Johann Rafelski (chair), Shufang Su, John Rutherfoord, Stefan Meinel, Sean Fleming. Dissertation: https://hdl.handle.net/10150/670301 . arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07193 Abstract: Magnetism is a rich subject touching all aspects of physics. My goal with this dissertation is to explore spin and magnetic moments in relativistic mechanics from both a quantum and classical perspective. We emphasize the special case of gyromagnetic ratio g=2 and its relationship to the algebraic spin structure of wave equations. In relativistic quantum mechanics, we investigate generalizations of the Dirac equation for arbitrary magnetic moments for fermions. We analyze the homogeneous magnetic field case and the Coulomb problem for hydrogen-like atoms with emphasis on the role of the anomalous magnetic moment (AMM). We explore alternative approaches which combine mass and the magnetic moment. Classically, we propose a relativistic covariant model of the Stern-Gerlach force via the introduction of a magnetic four-potential. This model modifies the covariant torque equations and unites the Ampèrian and Gilbertian models for magnetic moments. We further study (transition) magnetic dipoles in Majorana neutrinos specifically analyzing the relationship between flavor mixing and electromagnetic (EM) fields. We demonstrate EM flavor mixing explicitly in the 2-flavor model and develop a dynamical mass basis with an EM rotation matrix. EM induced neutrino mass splitting is compared to neutrino mass hierarchy. An interesting application of these theoretical developments is to study primordial magnetization in the early universe during the hot dense electron-positron plasma epoch. We propose a model of magnetic thermal matter-antimatter plasmas. We analyze the paramagnetic characteristics of electron-positron plasma when exposed to an external primordial field. We determine the magnitude of a small polarization asymmetry sufficient to generate field strengths in agreement with those measured today in deep intergalactic space. Future research outlooks include: Second order equations for anomalous quantum chromodynamic (QCD) moments, neutrino CP violation in strong EM fields, and fifth-dimension spin dynamics in Kaluza-Klein theory.
title: Modern topics in relativistic spin dynamics and magnetism

summary: Although quantum geometry plays an established role in electronic transport and optical responses, the contribution of the time-reversal-odd Riemannian connection to fully subgap responses remains less explored. Here we identify intrinsic second-harmonic generation in PT-symmetric antiferromagnets, predominantly governed by the real sector of the interband Hermitian connection and arising entirely from virtual interband transitions. In bilayer MnBi$_2$Te$_4$, the response persists in trivial phases but is enhanced in the layer-Chern phase and reverses sign with Néel order, offering a probe of quantum geometry and phase-sensitive readout of antiferromagnetic order without mobile carriers or real excitations.
title: Quantum-Geometric Subgap Second-Harmonic Generation in PT-Symmetric Antiferromagnetic Insulators

summary: We investigate triplon topology and the thermal Hall transport in a columnar valence-bond solid of a spin-$1/2$ honeycomb-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet. Inequivalent triangular sublattices, modeled by $J_2^A\neq J_2^B$, remove inversion symmetry at nearest-neighbor bond centers and allow in-plane Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya (DM) interactions. We identify the two symmetry-allowed in-plane DM vector patterns and present detailed results for the pattern parallel to the bonds including an out-of-plane magnetic field. Within a harmonic bond-operator treatment, we determine the triplon bands, their Berry curvatures and Chern numbers, and the triplon thermal Hall conductivity. The DM interaction and magnetic field generate nonzero Berry curvatures, but the numerically integrated Chern number of every isolated triplon band vanishes. Nevertheless, the energy-dependent Bose weighting of positive and negative Berry-curvature regions produces a finite thermal Hall response at nonzero low temperatures. We delimit the dilute-triplon regime in which the harmonic transport calculation is expected to be reliable. These results show that a vanishing Chern number band does not directly constrain the triplon response of a valence-bond solid. We also comment on the effects on the columnar valence-bond solid phase of a DM interaction between next-nearest-neighbor spins characterized by an out-of-plane vector pattern.
title: Triplon thermal Hall response in a honeycomb-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg antiferromagnet with Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interactions

summary: Using a unified method of identifying a telescoping function for each statistic-action pair, we prove conjectures of La Croix and Roby, and of Sheridan-Rossi that various permutation statistics, such as the number of fixed points, are homomesic under Foatic actions: compositions of the Foata bijection and dihedral symmetries of one-line notation. Underlying these results is a family of bijective identities relating permutation statistics across the Foata bijection; one of them --- an unexpected invariance of the number of right-to-left minima under reverse-complement, proved by an explicit bijection --- may be of independent interest. The telescoping functions also turn out to be shared among some Foatic actions, implying that mixing certain actions still yields a constant average on closed walks.
title: Foatic Homomesy

summary: Reproducibility data and code supporting the study “Parameter fragility in the reanalysis of published Mössbauer spectra” by Osman Armağan and Muhammed Emin Bedir. The release contains retained spectral coordinates, 44 primary archive fits and their start records, 44,000 archive perturbation refits, 24,000 paired-study refits for 12 panels from five publications, model configurations, 33 implementation-check records, 477 saved field-profile trials, provenance and source tables, bibliographic records, plotting programs, and a self-contained analysis notebook. Default execution verifies retained results and reconstructs figures without optimization; optional reruns write separate outputs. The analysis describes parameter sensitivity and agreement with published fits, not physical-accuracy guarantees. No independent external magnetic validation or second-operator extraction is included. Download and extract Zenodo_Upload_Files.zip. It contains five files: Reproducibility_Package.zip (complete data/code release and integrity manifest), Reproduce_Analysis.ipynb (standalone notebook), Figures_600dpi.zip (12 main/supplementary figures in PNG, TIFF, PDF and SVG), README.txt, and CITATION.cff. Extract Reproducibility_Package.zip for direct access to individual data/code files. For notebook use, follow README.txt and select the inner Reproducibility_Package.zip when prompted. Author-created material is distributed under CC BY 4.0. Third-party software and source data retain their original terms and attribution; no additional third-party rights are granted. Article PDFs are not redistributed. This is a separate release from the authors’ earlier provenance/ML corpus (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21997560; related article DOI 10.1039/d6ra08367f).
title: Parameter fragility in the reanalysis of published Mössbauer spectra: Reproducibility data and code

summary: Symmetry and topology, encoded in electronic wavefunctions, play a central role in the electronic properties and emergent phenomena of quantum materials. While these properties are conventionally determined by the equilibrium Hamiltonian, strong optical fields offer a fundamentally different route by reshaping the Hamiltonian on ultrafast timescales, turning symmetry and topology into dynamically controllable degrees of freedom. Graphene provides a paradigmatic platform for realizing this concept, where circularly polarized light has long been predicted to dynamically break time-reversal symmetry (TRS) and open a topologically nontrivial gap at the Dirac point. Despite extensive experimental efforts, direct observation of this Dirac gap-the defining spectroscopic signature of the dynamical TRS-breaking induced topological phase-has remained missing. Here we directly observe this light-induced Dirac gap in monolayer graphene. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that the gap emerges simultaneously with the optical field and exclusively under circularly polarized driving, directly linking its opening to dynamical TRS breaking. Together with Floquet theory, we identify the gap with a light-induced Haldane mass and reveal the associated nontrivial Floquet Berry curvature and Chern topology. By demonstrating dynamical TRS breaking in a prototypical non-magnetic material, our results establish optical driving as a route to ultrafast engineering of symmetry and topology, opening opportunities for dynamically tunable quantum matter beyond equilibrium.
title: Observation of light-induced Haldane gap in graphene

summary: Quantized charge pumping in quantum Hall systems is a bulk topological property, typically manifesting on gapless boundaries as spectral flow through chiral edge modes upon flux insertion. When the boundary is anomaly-free, it can be symmetrically gapped by symmetric mass generation (SMG) interactions. However, the effects on quantized charge pumping at an interacting gapped boundary are unclear. We address this using density-matrix renormalization group simulations of a four-leg ladder quasi-(2+1)d realization of the (1+1)d 3-4-5-0 lattice chiral fermion model with six-fermion interactions at one edge. We find gapless modes near the interacting edge for both weak and strong couplings, but the edge can be in a fully gapped SMG phase at intermediate coupling. We also identify spontaneous breaking of the model's $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry above a critical interaction strength. Across all three boundary phases, we find quantized charge pumping with the same pumped charge per flux quantum. The spatial distribution of the pumped charge varies between phases. Besides charge pumping, we study how a single injected fermion propagates under open boundary conditions. In the SMG phase, an interaction-induced flavor-mixing current develops at the endpoints of the gapped edge, which is absent in the weak- and strong-coupling limits. This current reveals a charge-redistribution mechanism unique to the SMG phase. Additionally, we propose an analogy between charge pumping in this model and a topological leptogenesis scenario in the (3+1)d Standard Model. The anomaly-free chiral U(1) symmetries of the 3-4-5-0 model play a role analogous to the baryon-minus-lepton symmetry of the Standard Model. In both settings, charge pumping can be associated with a continuous deformation along a classically defined but quantum-anomalous direction, while a discrete subgroup remains an exact quantum symmetry.

summary: Current-driven magnetic-octupole domain walls in noncollinear antiferromagnets are promising for fast spintronic devices, yet their transient dynamics are not yet fully understood. Here, we investigate spin-orbit-torque-driven domain-wall motion in Mn$_\text{3}$Sn using a multipole micromagnetic framework. The three symmetry-related 60° walls exhibit equivalent current-driven dynamics, unlike their field-driven motion. For a representative 60° wall, the post-pulse motion is governed by relaxation of the current-induced rotation of the surrounding octupole domains, with a characteristic time of approximately 33 ps quantitatively captured by a uniform-domain analytic model. By resolving spatially nonuniform texture dynamics beyond this analytic description, the simulations further reveal an additional slow relaxation in a composite 180° wall associated with the relative motion of its constituent walls. The post-pulse response also varies systematically with the exchange stiffness and magnetic anisotropies. These results identify distinct domain and internal-coordinate relaxation channels and establish the intrinsic time scales governing pulse-controlled positioning of magnetic-octupole domain walls in antiferromagnetic spintronic devices.

summary: Code for “Emergent stigmergy and pheromone-guided decisions in a foraging collective” Manoj N H (Department of Electrical Engineering, IIT Madras) and S Ganga Prasath (Department of Applied Mechanics, IIT Madras) The article poses collective foraging as an infinite-horizon optimal control problem, in which ants read and deposit a shared trail. The code solves the resulting coupled equations on a single trail and on a double bridge. Contents single_trail.ipynb : Python notebook with the steady-state and forward-in-time solvers for the single trail, the phase diagrams in colony size, diffusion, rewards and homing stiffness, and the numerical error analysis. It reproduces Figs. 1, 2, S1, S2 and S3, except the schematics in panels (a) of Figs. 1 and 2. auto_r1/ : AUTO-07p continuation of the symmetric double bridge (r = 1), giving the pitchfork in the deposition asymmetry σ, the symmetric and broken branches, and the density profiles. It also holds the scan in colony size. auto_r_neq1/ : AUTO-07p continuation of the unequal double bridge (r ≠ 1), giving the unfolding of the pitchfork in the length ratio r. results/ : stored numerical results, which the notebook reads. figures/ : figures drawn by the notebook. Requirements The notebook needs Python 3 with numpy, scipy and matplotlib. The continuation needs AUTO-07p and a Fortran compiler. Instructions are in  README.md . Variable names in the code follow the notation of the article. AUTO-07p returns no stability information, so the continuation output does not label branches as stable or unstable.
title: Emergent stigmergy and pheromone-guided decisions in a foraging collective

summary: LLM-based multi-agent system (MAS) applications can produce useful intermediate results while leaving task requirements unsatisfied. Repairing such executions requires identifying the work still needed and the completed results that can support it. We present \tool, a contribution-guided runtime repair framework for MAS applications. \tool derives expected contributions and acceptance conditions from task requirements and method specifications, and connects their dependencies in a contribution graph. Runtime checks locate unmet conditions and establish which results remain usable. These results guide action-level correction when available inputs suffice, or graph-level recovery when prerequisites or unfinished work need revision. Both repair scopes retain validated contributions and check repaired outputs before subsequent work uses them. We evaluate \tool on 30 applications across six MAS frameworks and 9,000 tasks. It detects runtime failures with 88.28\% precision and 79.18\% recall, and achieves 84.76\% task accuracy, improving over Native execution by 26.74 percentage points and the strongest of four recovery baselines by 21.28 points. Estimated deployment token consumption is 17.92\% above Native, but 24.19\% below Reflexion and 13.05\% below Iterative Rollback. Ablation results show that combining the two repair scopes achieves higher accuracy and lower token consumption than graph-level repair alone.

summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $κ$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.
title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression

summary: We disprove the analogue of Hedetniemi's conjecture for Shannon OR-capacity, which asserts that the capacity of a categorical product equals the smaller capacity of its factors. For every sufficiently large complete graph, we construct a second graph of larger capacity such that their categorical product has capacity strictly below that of the complete graph. Further constructions show that, for every real threshold above an explicit constant, both factor capacities can exceed that threshold while the product capacity lies below it. We also construct graph pairs, again with one complete factor, whose capacities tend to infinity while their product capacity is subpolynomial in the smaller factor capacity. summary: Sample-based quantum diagonalization has been used as an impurity solver in density matrix embedding theory (DMET), but always with fixed-form circuits and without comparison to classical selection at the same subspace size. We introduce GENIE, a DMET impurity solver in which a generative transformer learns the sampling circuit, trained on the quantum-selected configuration interaction energy. On N2, hydrogen chains, water and a hydrogen ring, we compare GENIE at equal determinant budget with classical selected configuration interaction (CIPSI, ASCI, heat-bath CI) and with DMET combined with sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). GENIE selects: for N2 at 200 determinants it is within a factor of 1.7 of CIPSI and 25 to 1000 times more accurate than the determinants a fixed circuit actually samples, while standard SQD reaches good energies mainly by filling the subspace. GENIE does not beat the best classical selection, and its circuits require fault-tolerant hardware. Its failures are governed by the compactness of the wavefunction relative to the budget, not by correlation strength. A cheap estimate from coupled-cluster amplitudes predicts this compactness. A router built on it never recommended GENIE where it then failed, apart from seed-to-seed variance, and it transferred unchanged to a blind test on new systems. We also identify two benchmarking pitfalls that can create apparent quantum advantages of one to two orders of magnitude.
title: GENIE: learned quantum circuits as embedding impurity solvers, and why compactness, not correlation strength, decides when they work

summary: This paper leverages the higher-order kinematic derivatives of serial robots to achieve efficient, aspect-preserving real-time inverse kinematics. First, a family of higher-order solvers is derived, with a necessary orientation-error correction map, yielding the QuIK4 and QuIK5 methods with fourth- and fifth-order convergence. Second, an aspect-preserving step limiter extrapolates the Jacobian determinant along the step to predict and avoid singularities, shortening steps only when they head toward a singularity rather than when the current iterate is ill-conditioned. Third, a Hermite-interpolation certifier verifies the aspect of each answer, and a certified restart algorithm recovers failures from proven same-aspect seeds. The proposed methods are shown to outperform prior methods, reducing failures by up to four orders of magnitude and nearly eliminating aspect switching at tracking-level errors. A C++ library is released with ROS 2 integration.

summary: Whether a language model was trained on a document matters for copyright, privacy, and benchmark contamination. Yet most membership-inference (MI) evaluations on language models collect members and non-members after the fact, so success may reflect distribution shift and failure is inconclusive. We re-ran OLMo 2 1B's official 50-billion-token mid-training stage, replacing selected training chunks with documents from 7,814 pairs matched on domain and difficulty. For each pair, a coin flip determined which document was inserted and which was held out. The run released by the Allen Institute for AI (AI2) from the same seed saw identical data everywhere else and serves as the counterfactual. One exposure raises a previously unseen document's likelihood on average but rarely identifies it. Using the counterfactual as reference, the reference ratio has an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.767 but, with one threshold across domains, catches 3.8% of members at a 1% false-positive rate (FPR). In contrast, 13 matched pairs give a paired test 80% power at the 5% level to detect training on a collection, given same-domain non-members and a close reference. summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have made significant progress in spatial reasoning, particularly by integrating RGB images with depth data, which is often assumed to faithfully reflect physical distances. However, mirrors violate this assumption: they distort depth readings while reproducing object appearances, making reflections difficult to distinguish from real objects. As existing benchmarks rarely consider such reflective scenarios, VLM performance in mirror scenes remains largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce a mirror-centric RGB-D dataset from reflective scenes to evaluate the spatial reasoning capabilities of state-of-the-art VLMs in these scenarios. Specifically, we collect 1,011 RGB-D images from 525 real-world scenes, spanning diverse indoor and outdoor environments, six reflective surface types, and both daytime and nighttime conditions. All images are annotated with reflective surface region masks and mask annotations for both directly observed and mirror-reflected objects. Then, we curate a benchmark named MIRA-Bench (Mirror-Induced Reasoning Ambiguity Benchmark), comprising 14,140 QA pairs across eight sub-tasks organized into three cognitive levels: Reflection-aware Perception, Spatial Reasoning, and Scene-level Decision-making. We evaluate state-of-the-art VLMs on MIRA-Bench and find consistent failures across tasks: models misclassify whether objects are directly observed or reflected, fail to match reflected instances to their real-world counterparts, and produce erroneous spatial inferences. Remarkably, providing depth data actually degrades reasoning performance, implying that VLMs cannot identify incorrect depth in mirror scenes. The code and data are available at https://github.com/EvaYin-cloud/MIRA-Bench
title: When Depth Lies: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models on Mirror-Induced RGB-D Ambiguity

However, mirrors violate this assumption: they distort depth readings while reproducing object appearances, making reflections difficult to distinguish from real objects. summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.

summary: We study repeated, team-associated selling around sharp collapses of Pump.fun tokens in several deliberately selected data windows, separating the measurement from claims of fraud, common ownership or realized profit. Because token prices derived from trade amounts are not fully reliable, we compare a price-based screen with a screen that uses only the bonding-curve reserve and SOL amounts; most price-based episodes are also found by the reserve screen. Episodes concentrate in groups well beyond a within-hour label-shuffle benchmark, and most of them are collapses sold by a single creator wallet. The recorded own-token cash flow of the identified groups is positive in most windows and negative in a few, but the sign of the negative results is fragile: it changes with the screen, with the definition of a group, with the length of the window and with trading costs of about two per cent per side. A daily SOL price covariate shows no association with the incidence of episodes. An agent-based simulation of a team exit on a bonding curve, extended with a latent attention to each token and calibrated to marginal moments of the data, shows that the team's result depends mainly on the attention that tokens attract, on fees and on the team's own trading, that continual trading by the team is costly and that reacting to the inflow of other traders adds little. The model reproduces the sign of group-level results but not the early exits that are common in the data. Missing token transfers, verified migration labels and human-labelled validation prevent identifying operator profit or fraud prevalence.
title: Serial Rug-Pull-Like Exits on Pump.fun: Team-Level Evidence and Its Sensitivity to Team Construction

summary: Deploying 6G network slices across administrative domains requires an online decision for each arriving request: which domain hosts each virtual network function, how traffic crosses domain boundaries, and whether the slice is admitted. This joint decision problem is NP-hard under continuous arrivals. Experiments on a parametrized family of multi-domain topologies show that no fixed planning strategy dominates across all regimes: the performance ranking reverses between topology classes, and feasible placements exist for most rejected requests but remain undiscovered. These findings identify the plan layer as the decisive performance lever. We introduce ORION, a hierarchical orchestrator in which two LLM agents translate service intents into structured requests and generate abstract placement plans. A cooperative multi-agent RL coordinator selects the cross-domain partition, treating the plan as a persistent soft prior, while per-domain agents place the functions. ORION main contribution lies at the plan layer: an outcome-driven episodic memory that records, for each completed attempt, the network-condition profile, the proposed plan, and its verified feasibility outcome. The memory feeds verified successes and labelled failures back to the planner, thereby closing the adaptation loop using deployment feasibility rather than a scalar reward assigned to the planner's own proposals. To isolate the effect of the plan quality, we evaluate the planner on held-out topology families while keeping the downstream selection and execution mechanisms fixed. Under this controlled setting, the proposed memory improves admission by $4.6$--$11.5$ percentage points over the same planner without memory, while importance-based retention accounts for most of the improvement over a first-in-first-out store.

summary: Web agents increasingly edit images by calling open editing models in a critique-and-retry loop, and these models differ in cost by more than an order of magnitude. After every rejected edit, a service must decide whether to retry the same model, escalate to another or give up. Existing routers pick one model per request, and cascades escalate in a fixed order. However, both treat a retry as an independent draw. We identify sticky failures, meaning that a retry after a failure succeeds only 17-53% as often as a first try across six open models, three benchmarks and two judges. Based on this finding, we propose RetryRoute, a retry-aware router that estimates each model's chance of success given the request's failure history. It plans retries, escalations and abandonment over failure states and adds live queue waits to the cost, so the same plan becomes load-aware dispatch. At the main budget, RetryRoute's success under the in-loop judge exceeds the strongest of eleven prior baselines by 2.8 points on average over eight groups. On a GPU serving testbed it raises the share of edits delivered within the service-level objective by 5.0-6.3 points over the best prior baseline at every load.
title: RetryRoute: Retry-Aware Model Routing for Agentic Image Editing Services

summary: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agentic paradigm Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks execution sufficiency, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Extensive experiments across challenging spatial reasoning benchmarks show that PEPS consistently improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that explicit requirement commitment can make tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more execution-efficient.

summary: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. The gains are largest where the benchmark is far from the policy's training data: wrapping a general-purpose policy, the evolved harness yields a specialist that often outperforms even the finetuned version. Intuitive control strategies are automatically designed, such as lifting a jammed arm clear or reaching in horizontally when an obstacle blocks the way from above. The harness also evolves its own persistent memory, carrying learned experience, such as effective grasp depths, into later decisions. These results suggest that substantial headroom in robotic manipulation lies in the agent harness, and its design can be effectively automated and optimized without weight updates.
title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory

summary: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io

summary: Quantum correlations can be used to improve sensing precision beyond classical limits, yet the correlated resource states needed can be challenging to prepare and preserve. Here, we study the family of weighted hypergraph states and identify subclasses characterized by their underlying graph topology that exhibit enhanced metrological performance. Using the quantum Fisher information and a novel Dicke state basis representation, we show that these subclasses outperform both separable and standard weighted graph state benchmarks over broad ranges of edge weights corresponding to weak controlled operations between qubits representing the vertices of the graph. We provide analytical formulas for an arbitrary number $N$ of qubits, supplemented by a general study, while focusing a detailed analysis on the example case of $N=4$. By identifying the critical probabilities for local dephasing, we show that adding higher-order weighted hyperedges for $N$ qubits can enhance metrological robustness, allowing the resulting states to retain a quantum advantage at higher noise levels. These probe states exhibit favorable scaling, enhanced precision, and noise tolerance. Our findings establish weighted hypergraph states as viable, structurally tunable and robust resources for quantum-enhanced metrology.
title: Weighted hypergraph states as a resource for quantum metrology

summary: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.

summary: A panoramic video captures all directions around the camera, but relevant evidence can appear in different directions and at different times. Understanding it requires models to connect observations across the viewing sphere and time. We introduce PanoVideoBench, the first manually annotated benchmark for comprehensive panoramic video understanding. Its 1,000 questions span five categories and 15 question types, with diagnostic annotations for target search and panoramic capabilities. Evaluation of 11 proprietary, open-source, and panoramic-specialized models identifies cross-view tracking and sphere-time evidence integration as their weakest capabilities. To strengthen these capabilities, we construct PanoVideoCoT, the first reasoning dataset grounded in real panoramic video, through sphere-time-grounded synthesis that converts verified panoramic observations and successful agentic explorations into 13,465 QA-CoT pairs. Starting from a general video MLLM, PanoVideoReasoner learns from this corpus through Panoramic CoT SFT and Evidence-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation, a panoramic instantiation of Vision-OPD's OPSD in which the teacher uses verified perspective views to guide student-generated trajectories. It reaches 55.7% on PanoVideoBench, improving the backbone by 12.5 points and the previous SOTA by 2.6. The gains concentrate on the same spatial, cross-view, and temporal capabilities exposed by the benchmark, showing that grounded sphere-time supervision can equip a general video MLLM with panoramic reasoning.
title: Think in 360°: Benchmarking and Bootstrapping Panoramic Video Reasoning

summary: Automatic generation control (AGC) stabilizes frequency and scheduled power exchanges among interconnected areas, yet its reliance on communication networks introduces cyber-vulnerabilities. This work examines coordinated AGC cyber-attacks in the presence of remedial action schemes (RAS) and identifies operating conditions under which an attacker can drive grid frequency beyond safe limits while evading RAS. A feedback-based attack policy is used to manipulate AGC signals and steer system frequency toward unsafe trajectories. Then, a large nested-loop parametric sweep---spanning attacked-area inertia relative to its interconnected neighboring area, AGC capacity versus maximum tie-line transfer, AGC update rate, load damping, and bi-directional power transfers---generates over 1.45 million scenarios. These are classified using a decision tree to establish guidelines to distinguish successful from unsuccessful attacks based on frequency deviations. The resulting vulnerability guidelines are validated on a three-area system using phasor-domain simulations with IEEE 9-bus area models, detailed turbine--governor dynamics, and under/over-frequency load and generation shedding. Results show that specific combinations of AGC capacity, inertia distribution, and pre-attack tie-line loading increase the likelihood of successful attacks, offering operators actionable criteria for identifying vulnerable operating conditions.
title: System-Level Factors Influencing AGC Cyber-Attack Success and RAS Vulnerability in Multi-Area Grids

summary: Automatic generation control (AGC) stabilizes frequency and scheduled power exchanges among interconnected areas, yet its reliance on communication networks introduces cyber-vulnerabilities. This work examines coordinated AGC cyber-attacks in the presence of remedial action schemes (RAS) and identifies operating conditions under which an attacker can drive grid frequency beyond safe limits while evading RAS. A feedback-based attack policy is used to manipulate AGC signals and steer system frequency toward unsafe trajectories. Then, a large nested-loop parametric sweep---spanning attacked-area inertia relative to its interconnected neighboring area, AGC capacity versus maximum tie-line transfer, AGC update rate, load damping, and bi-directional power transfers---generates over 1.45 million scenarios. These are classified using a decision tree to establish guidelines to distinguish successful from unsuccessful attacks based on frequency deviations. The resulting vulnerability guidelines are validated on a three-area system using phasor-domain simulations with IEEE 9-bus area models, detailed turbine--governor dynamics, and under/over-frequency load and generation shedding. Results show that specific combinations of AGC capacity, inertia distribution, and pre-attack tie-line loading increase the likelihood of successful attacks, offering operators actionable criteria for identifying vulnerable operating conditions.

summary: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15$\times$ end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25$\times$ on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5$\times$ target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluationintegrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.
title: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity

summary: An approximation can reproduce an energy while missing its response, or satisfy an error tolerance without being certified by a given bound. We formulate observable-specific validity records for scientific artificial intelligence (AI) that link a reduction to its reference model, error measure, tolerance, parameter domain, and transformations or interventions. Explicit displacement and velocity certificates for a singularly perturbed oscillator recover distinct convergence orders and provide sufficient validity guarantees. Exact Hubbard dimer relations resolve the different coupling domains accepted by energy and response criteria. Across 16 repeated neural fits, imposing dimensional homogeneity reduces energy scale transfer error from 52.3% to 0.0768% and raises the median fraction jointly satisfying gap and response tolerances from zero to 100%. Paired transformations verify the protected scaling relation, while a coupling crossover identifies the additional information needed for response transfer. A causal model recovers a positive intervention response beneath a strong negative observational association. For two mechanisms observed with Gaussian noise whose responses first differ at order $x^k$, we derive an exact fixed control query requirement scaling as $x^{-2k}$ and verify its full success curve numerically. Together with a 256-task evaluation interface, these results provide independently checkable tests of controlled approximation, physical transfer, and mechanism discrimination in scientific AI.
title: Observable-Specific Validity Tests for Scientific AI: Controlled Approximations and Intervention Response

summary: This dataset contains the anonymized replication data associated with the paper:   "Can Contract Lifecycle Data Support the Monitoring Objectives of the Proposed EU Public Procurement Act? Evidence from Greece".   The dataset contains 206,143 direct-award contract lifecycles issued by 123 contracting authorities in the Greek healthcare sector during 2019–2024.   The public dataset supports reproduction of the published empirical findings, including:   • Lifecycle monitoring indicators (L1–L5) • Indicator prevalence statistics • Signal accumulation patterns • Indicator overlap analysis   All direct identifiers have been removed or irreversibly transformed through anonymization procedures.   The dataset supports results reproducibility rather than full reconstruction of the original procurement lifecycle processing pipeline.

summary: This record contains the Python programs, model inputs and manuscript assets behind the paper "Cooling and heating load reduction and economic feasibility of green roofs: A simulation study of five Chinese cities" (Qu and Chen). The study simulates an identical three-storey office building in five Chinese cities (Harbin, Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Kunming) with EnergyPlus and adds a 30-year incremental life-cycle economic assessment. Contents: three archives and one folder of six result bundles, each unpacking to one top-level directory. code.zip holds the twenty programs for case generation, simulation control, analysis and plotting, with the run order documented in README.txt; inputs.zip holds the weather-file note and the placeholder for the model files; manuscript_assets.zip holds the six figures and eleven tables as they appear in the submitted manuscript; the six bundles under outputs/ hold the analysis results - annual and monthly loads, case parameters, rooftop thermal statistics, the life-cycle economics and the sensitivity scans - together with the EnergyPlus table report and the full eplusout.sql result database of each run and its logs. The per-surface hourly dumps and the plain-text eplusout.eso files were omitted to keep the deposit compact; the SQLite eplusout.sql database, the zone-level hourly series and every table used in the manuscript are retained, so all reported quantities can be reproduced or re-queried. Restoring those two groups would add about 118 MB and take the deposit past the 120 MB upload limit. The EnergyPlus input model files (.idf) are not included: they contain the detailed geometric and construction information of the prototype and form part of an ongoing study; they can be obtained from the corresponding author on reasonable request. summary: Building stock retrofitting is essential to achieve the ambitious sustainability goals of the building sector due to its high energy consumption rates. The evaluation of the various building interventions shall be holistically assessed in terms of environmental and costing impact. The aim of this paper is twofold: First, it presents the innovative characteristics of a developed online tool (Virtual intEgrated platfoRm on LIfe cycle AnalYsis - VERIFY) able to perform dynamic life cycle analysis and global warming impact assessments by capitalizing on the well-known LCA and LCC methodologies, applicable in the case of building renovation. VERIFY is able to analyse dynamic life cycle inventories that consider the temporal profiles of energy consumption, and the timedependent temperature changes, while being also interoperable in terms of exchanging data with other available energy simulation engines, or even using real-time monitoring data from sensors, processing any data time granulation. Second, the paper evaluates, from a life cycle perspective, the impact of specific energy retrofitting measures, meeting the Passive House Standard, for the case of a multi-family residential building in Athens, Greece. The proposed energy-retrofitting scenario examines actions related to the deep retrofitting of the building envelope and the upgrade of the thermal components as well as to the incorporation of clean electricity generation based on renewable energy systems; all aiming to drastically reduce the environmental impact of the building, rendering it almost near zero energy. Through the planned infrastructure installations, the primary energy needs and CO2eq emissions were reduced by 91 % and by 95 % respectively, while for a building oper­ational lifespan of 25 years, savings up to 515 k€ compared to the baseline scenario, can be achieved.
title: Аn integrated life cycle assessment and life cycle costing approach towards sustainable building renovation via a dynamic online tool

summary: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.
title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences

summary: Looping re-applies a block of layers so that each token passes through the block more than once. Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.
title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?

Adding a loop to a trained model is attractive because it leaves the parameter count, and hence the disk size, the memory footprint and the training cost unchanged. Unfortunately, every generated token pays for the loop. Re-applying m of N layers makes each token about (N+m)/N times as expensive. Loops that a model learns during large-scale pretraining justify this price, but whether loops added after pretraining justify this cost remains unclear. We compare a looped model with two simple baselines. We first compare it with the same model trained identically without the loop (equal parameters). Secondly, we compare it with the best unlooped use of the same inference floating-point operations (equal FLOPs). Across Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 models from 0.8B to 9B parameters, only the looped 0.8B model beats both baselines. At 4B and 9B, the looped model does not beat the first baseline, i.e. the same model trained without the loop. This is not because the benchmarks are too easy, since on the same benchmarks the unlooped 9B model still scores up to 13 points higher than the 4B model, showing that there is ample room for improvement. Introducing loops in an already pretrained model therefore only pays for small models with a fixed parameter budget.
title: There Is No Free Loop: When Does Looping a Trained Model Pay for Its Inference Compute?

summary: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

summary: Linear attention scales linearly with sequence length, but its finite-state memory can limit long-context retrieval. In gated linear recurrences, memory retention depends on state decay, which is shaped jointly by gate parameters A_log and dt_bias and by input activations. In controlled Gated DeltaNet (GDN) experiments, both parameters remain highly correlated with their initial values after training, highlighting the importance of initialization. Therefore, we introduce Dual-Axis Memory Initialization (DAMI), which jointly configures these parameters before training. DAMI assigns geometric timescales across heads for varied retrieval distances and a low-high-low input-sensitivity profile across layers. A small activation sample calibrates the GDN-family implementation to match both behavioral targets without adding trainable parameters. Across GDN, KDA, GDN2, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, DAMI improves average RULER-style retrieval accuracy by 5.29 to 16.71 percentage points over the corresponding random-initialization baselines. Performance on language modeling, commonsense reasoning, and 2K real-world retrieval remains broadly comparable to those baselines. Our code is available at https://speedai.com/research/dami.
title: DAMI: Dual-Axis Memory Initialization for Enhanced Long-Context Retrieval in Gated Linear Attention

summary: Transformers retain an explicit history of the sequence, allowing attention to directly retrieve past representations. However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.
title: Dynamical Memory Transformer: Selective Recurrent Memories with Constant Cost Attention

However, the size of the KV-Cache and the cost of a new token increase with the context length. State Space Models compress the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, at the cost of reduced addressability. We present the Dynamical Memory Transformer (DMT), a hybrid architecture that separates sequence encoding from information reading. The encoder uses several memory units, each implemented by a dynamical system with a complex diagonal recurrent matrix. An input-dependent leak rate controls their updates. The decoder then uses attention to read and combine their outputs, without going through the token history. The formulation of the recurrence allows an associative scan with O(T ) total work and O(log T ) parallel depth, with fixed dimensions. During autoregressive inference, the recurrent states and the convolution cache remain fixed in size. We compare DMT with Mamba and Transformer on cognitive and language modeling tasks, and show its strengths and limitations: DMT achieves the best results on several cognitive tasks and language modeling performance close to that of Transformer, but remains behind Mamba in language modeling. On selective copy, DMT also shows stronger length extrapolation than Mamba and Transformer. These results demonstrate that parallel dynamical memory units are a promising mechanism for retaining and using information over sequences.

summary: Vector Quantization (VQ) is a rapidly evolving technique for compressing Large Language Model (LLM) weights, reducing memory usage, and speeding up inference. However, extreme compression deteriorates model performance, which is challenging to recover due to the discrete nature of VQ parameters. Existing methods employ training-free approaches that are limited to layer-wise reconstruction loss minimization. To address this limitation, we propose TVQ, a novel method that leverages straight-through estimation to enable gradient descent-based optimization of vector-quantized LLMs. By reformulating VQ LLM optimization with trainable latent weights, TVQ enables arbitrary objective minimization. We constitute our approach by applying TVQ in a block-wise knowledge distillation paradigm, which balances quality and training efficiency, and propose several practical solutions to accelerate training. In experiments on modern LLMs, we demonstrate that TVQ is compatible with modern VQ schemes. As a result, TVQ achieves state-of-the-art quality in low-bit post-training quantization settings with a modest training budget and straightforward PyTorch implementation. For instance, TVQ achieves near-lossless 2-bit quantization for LLaMA2-70B with only 1% accuracy drop on popular Question-Answering benchmarks.

summary: Deep neural networks for time series classification (TSC) are trained almost exclusively by error backpropagation, which imposes update locking and the weight-transport problem. Backpropagation-free learning rules such as Direct Feedback Alignment (DFA), Direct Random Target Projection (DRTP), and the diffusion-inspired NoProp relax these constraints but have been evaluated almost exclusively on 2D image benchmarks. We adapt these three learners to univariate TSC with 1D convolutional architectures and present the first systematic study of them across 112 datasets from the UCR time series archive, with one hyperparameter-optimized configuration per method. The optimized learners reach mean F1 scores of 0.76 to 0.79, below ROCKET (0.83) and InceptionTime (0.84). We propose an analysis framework that relates the per-dataset gap to InceptionTime to dataset properties and tests convolutional feature learning by replacing the flatten readout with global average pooling, measured as a difference-in-differences (DD) against a backpropagation control on the identical architecture. Intra-class temporal variability is the dataset property most consistently associated with the gap for all three learners (partial Spearman $ρ$ from $0.28$ to $0.40$). Pooling harms DFA and DRTP more than backpropagation (DD $-0.025$ and $-0.055$), consistent with near-random convolutional features, whereas NoProp tolerates pooling as backpropagation does (DD $+0.013$). Relative to backpropagation on the same architectures, DRTP reduces training floating-point operations (FLOPs) by 33% and trains faster only on series longer than about 700 time steps, DFA yields no computational reduction, and NoProp reduces peak memory by 38% at the cost of 48% longer training.
title: Backpropagation-free Deep Learning for Time-Series Classification

summary: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.
title: When the Past Shapes Action: Understanding Embodied Memory

summary: Recent advances in generative foundation models have expanded the capabilities of embodied AI, enabling increasingly general navigation, manipulation, and long-horizon task execution. However, effective interaction with dynamic environments requires more than only strong perception and reasoning: agents must act with partial knowledge and retain, retrieve, and update information from past observations, actions, and experiences. This survey examines embodied memory as a mechanism for preserving decision-relevant information beyond the current observation. We organize existing approaches along two complementary dimensions: six fundamental memory requirements, spanning world-state persistence, task progress, belief maintenance, and experiential learning; and eight architectural categories, including recurrent states, fast weights, visual and symbolic representations, spatial memory, and experience-based systems. We analyze their capabilities and limitations, and examine how existing benchmarks evaluate memory-dependent behavior, distinguishing genuine use of historical information from general task performance. Finally, we identify open challenges in selecting relevant experiences, maintaining consistent beliefs in changing environments, and consolidating knowledge across episodes. Our analysis provides a framework for understanding memory as an essential component of reliable, adaptive, and lifelong-horizon embodied intelligence.

summary:
Robot policy learning is dominated by zeroth-order methods such as PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box and pay for it with enormous sample counts. First-order policy learning differentiates through the dynamics, but on contact-rich whole-body control it has rarely worked: its gradients explode. A recent world-model method showed that derivative information can make humanoid motion tracking far more efficient, using surrogate gradients of a learned model. We show that exact gradients of the simulator itself do better, once two obstacles are removed. Exact gradients contain rare unbounded samples, because contact dynamics is not differentiable everywhere and its derivative diverges near some events; and they are expensive, because the simulator's adjoint has to replay the contact solve. $
abla$Mimic bounds these samples with median-relative per-sample gradient clipping at every step of the backward pass, and reuses each costly simulated window by multistep regression onto gradient-derived action targets, which bounds every action target independently of the gradient scale. NablaEngine, a differentiable GPU simulation engine for the Unitree G1, removes the cost: it computes MuJoCo's full contact dynamics with fused per-world kernels and the adjoint of a whole control step as a single megakernel, with analytic gradients that match float64 finite differences, $11.5	imes$ faster than the available MuJoCo Warp adjoint. On whole-body tracking of all 40 LAFAN1 clips with one policy on one GPU, $
abla$Mimic reaches the score reported by the state-of-the-art world-model method, 0.82, in 20 minutes instead of 1.2 h, and 0.874 in 1.8 h. SHAC, the standard first-order baseline, stops on exploding gradients within minutes. We release NablaEngine and $
abla$Mimic as open-source infrastructure for first-order humanoid policy learning.
title: $\nabla$Mimic: Ultra-Efficient Humanoid Control with Differentiable Simulation

summary: Long-context diffusion repeatedly pays for both token interaction and feed-forward computation. We formulate these costs as two separate budgets: the edges available to an attention graph and the experts activated for each token. This view connects local, dilated, and global attention with conditional expert computation without assuming that sparsity alone preserves document-level information. We specify normalized masked attention, distinguish denoising depth from sampling iterations, and derive graph and compute bounds. A reported sparse-expert configuration, denoted DualBudget, is analyzed across scientific summarization, multi-hop question answering, dialogue, and sentence-pair prediction. All supplied table measurements are retained. The length study shows gains over the listed baselines through 16K, together with measurable degradation as length increases. Ablations reveal mixed changes across the three reported scores, while the cost record indicates a 20% reduction relative to DiffuSeq under an unspecified timing convention. The analysis separates these observations from unmeasured claims about training speed, absorbing states, global coherence, and deployment memory.
title: Sparse Text Diffusion under Dual Budgets: Context Connectivity and Expert Activation

summary: As observed by Kienzle and the second author, rank-two $\mathcal{O}(3)$-twisted Higgs bundles on the projective line encode all hyperbolic crystals of genus two: the spectral curves are the unit cells, and the Hitchin fibers are the abelian Brillouin zones. In a uniform magnetic field of two flux quanta, the lowest Landau level is one-dimensional at every nonzero momentum, and, as found by Iengo and Li, its dimension jumps to two at the zero momentum. We identify the states of the lowest Landau level with the Baker--Akhiezer sections of the Higgs bundles, and their zeros, the vortices, with the Baker--Akhiezer divisors. A family of nonzero momenta limits to the zero momentum exactly when each of the two vortices approaches the image of the other under the spatial inversion, and the states of the jumped level are labeled by the directions of limiting. On the Higgs bundle side, the zero momentum is the point where the Hitchin fiber intersects the Hitchin section. Such a family of Higgs bundles limits to the Hitchin section, thereby crossing to a lower stratum of the \BB stratification, an example of the phenomenon investigated in terms of Baker--Akhiezer divisors by the first author with Figiel and Teschner.
title: Baker--Akhiezer sections from Higgs bundles and Landau levels in hyperbolic band theory

summary: This paper is concerned with an inverse source problem for the stochastic fractional Helmholtz equation in a three-dimensional inhomogeneous medium. The source is modeled as real Gaussian spatial white noise with an unknown nonnegative strength function. For admissible frequencies, we establish well-posedness of the radiating solution in the distributional sense and show that it has a smooth representation outside the source region. For the inverse problem, by using two-point correlations of the field measured in an exterior open set at a single frequency, we prove a logarithmic stability estimate for recovering the source strength under an a priori Sobolev bound. As a uniform Hölder stability estimate is unavailable for the general admissible class, by assuming the difference between two source strengths has a fixed sign, we improve the stability to Hölder continuity with an optimal Hölder exponent. The analysis combines scattering theory and quantitative continuation for the fractional Laplacian using the Caffarelli-Silvestre extension.
title: Inverse source problem for the stochastic fractional Helmholtz equation in inhomogeneous media
