summary: The magnetotelluric (MT) method uses natural electromagnetic field variations to image subsurface electrical resistivity at depths ranging from tens of metres to hundreds of kilometres. It is widely used in geophysical exploration for natural resources, including minerals, geothermal energy, and groundwater, as well as in the characterisation of sites for CO$_2$ storage and in studies of crustal and lithospheric structure. The MT inverse problem is, however, inherently non-unique: many distinct resistivity models reproduce the observations equally well. Conventional practice nonetheless reports a single regularised model, with no quantitative measure of its uncertainty. MTGeophysics.jl is a Julia package developed to address this limitation. Its principal aim is the quantification of uncertainty in MT model building, advancing interpretation from a single deterministic model, through an ensemble of plausible models, towards the full posterior distribution. The package also provides tools for data analysis, mesh generation, masking, forward modelling, inversion, model analysis and visualisation for MT research and applications. MTGeophysics.jl v0.7.3 No breaking changes. Polishing docs for JOSS
title: MTGeophysics.jl: A software repository for magnetotelluric research and applications

summary: Background. End-stage renal disease (ESRD) carries high mortality, but existing prognostic models begin at dialysis initiation, ignoring the metabolic trajectory that preceded renal failure. Whether the prodromal phenotype measured years before ESRD onset predicts subsequent survival is unknown. Methods. We studied 1,991 UK Biobank participants who developed ESRD (ICD-10 N185, Z992, or Z940) during a median 14.0 years of follow-up. Seven non-renal organ-specific prodromal function failure (pFF) scores and the Metabolic Inversion Phenotype (MIP) score were computed from baseline biomarkers measured 5–15 years before ESRD onset. Three renal pFF scores (pKD, pRD, pGN) were excluded a priori to avoid circularity. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the association of prodromal scores with all-cause mortality (642 deaths, 32.2%). Unsupervised K -means clustering identified distinct prodromal phenotypes. A compound endpoint model (dESRD) was built using gradient-boosted trees with out-of-fold evaluation on the full cohort. Results. Prodromal scores predicted mortality within the ESRD cohort. Age-sex-adjusted Cox models with individual pFF scores achieved C* 1 = 0 . 636 (∆C* = +0 . 023 vs. age + sex alone). Prodromal hypertension (pHT) was the dominant predictor (HR 5.55, 95% CI 2.93–10.49, p = 2 . 4 × 10 −7 ). Three prodromal phenotypes emerged: low-burden (N = 1,326; 15-year survival 76.2%), metabolic-vascular ( N = 574; 60.1%), and multi-organ storm ( N = 91; 38.0%; log-rank p = 2 . 5 × 10 −19 ). Cause-specific mortality shifted across phenotypes: cancer dominated the low-burden group (34.6% of deaths) while cardiovascular disease dominated the multi-organ storm (44.8%), with zero cancer deaths. summary: This dataset provides the reported aggregate results, supplementary tables, figures and mathematical documentation supporting the manuscript “Genetic evaluation of growth and morphometric traits across ages in Peranakan Etawa goats”. The study analysed 49,162 measurements from 1,976 animals across 35 trait–age responses, using a pedigree comprising 2,819 individuals. Analyses included direct-only and common-dam animal models, within-age bivariate correlations, targeted joint models incorporating earlier measurements, descriptive birth-cohort profiles, and sensitivity analyses for flagged measurements. The deposit contains 16 CSV files reproducing the displayed numerical tables and normalized parameter/correlation records, 14 original embedded figure files, supplementary material, model equations, variable dictionaries, and reference post-processing utilities. The numerical values retain the rounding used in the source documents. Unavailable accepted estimates are explicitly distinguished from zero. This reporting release does not contain individual phenotypic records, pedigree rows, individual estimated breeding values, full-precision parameter covariance matrices, or the original DMU fitting pipeline. It therefore supports inspection and reuse of the reported results but does not permit independent reproduction of all REML estimates and standard errors. See the README for file descriptions, provenance and analytical limitations.

summary: This report was developed within seizmic – Scaling Social Entrepreneurship and Innovation: Zooming in on Multidisciplinary Interconnected Challenges, a Marie Skłodowska-Curie Doctoral Network funded under Horizon Europe. It synthesises insights from four literature reviews conducted within Work Package 3, Impact Investing for Social Entrepreneurship Scaling, to provide a practical framework for understanding how impact investing can support the sustainable scaling of social enterprises. The report explores impact investing as a system of relationships involving investors, social enterprises, beneficiaries, intermediaries, and policymakers. It examines how investment objectives, financial instruments, governance arrangements, impact measurement practices, and ecosystem dynamics shape the ability of social enterprises to scale their social and environmental impact while preserving mission integrity. Drawing on complementary reviews of impact investing strategies, financing instruments, mission drift, governance, and ecosystem coordination, the report analyses how different forms of impact capital support three major scaling pathways: scaling up (systemic and policy change), scaling out (replication and expansion), and scaling deep (changes in values, norms, and community practices). Particular attention is given to the opportunities and challenges associated with instruments such as crowdfunding, venture philanthropy, social impact bonds, blended finance, development finance institution investments, and social venture capital. The report highlights the importance of aligning investor expectations, enterprise missions, governance structures, and impact measurement systems throughout the investment lifecycle. It identifies key risks, including mission drift, coordination failures, reporting burdens, and scaling-related challenges, while proposing practical safeguards and governance mechanisms to foster long-term mission fidelity and impact effectiveness. Based on this synthesis, the report offers actionable recommendations for investors, social enterprises, intermediaries, and policymakers. It argues that successful impact investing depends not only on the availability of capital, but also on the design of investment relationships, ecosystem infrastructure, and measurement practices that remain aligned with social purpose over time. By translating academic evidence into practitioner-oriented guidance, the report contributes to the development of a more effective and resilient European impact investing ecosystem.

title: Aligning Impact Capital for Social Enterprise Scaling: A Research for the European Impact Investing Ecosystem

summary: 中文書名 / Chinese Title: 自主城市微電網與能源共享極限 63/90 | PART III | STARLI RESEARCH INSTITUTE XXXVI English Title: AUTONOMOUS URBAN MICROGRIDS AND DISTRIBUTED ENERGY SHARING AT THE LIMIT Research Working Edition v1.0 | 1 November 2026 | Author: 33 / STARLI This prospective research working edition examines whether separately controlled district microgrids can exchange physically metered energy while preserving protected electrical services after a local fault. Its core three-coupling is Microgrids x Distributed Control x Energy Sharing. Studies are restricted to unoccupied scaled feeders, guarded controller hardware-in-the-loop, carefully bounded power interfaces and auditable digital-physical twins; the work claims neither city governance authority nor suitability for occupation. The preregistered main hypothesis asks whether distributed coordination improves state-of-charge estimation error against capable fixed-rule dispatch without worsening net lifecycle energy yield, when generation, storage, conductors, weather, labor, sensor resources and available forecast information are matched. Independent safety outcomes include loss-of-load duration, critical-load service, phase and voltage transients, physically measured frequency nadir and actual breaker isolation. The candidate swing model M domega/dt + D omega = Pm - Pe is treated as an operating-regime-limited frequency surrogate, not as a universal description of grid-following and grid-forming electronics. Withheld forecast shifts, islanding, battery thermal drift, network partitions, stale permissions and meter-reference biases provide explicit refutation tests. Its F02-anchored 777-page architecture comprises 14 scientific introductory pages, 30 differently purposed equation plates with units and blind rebuttals, 82 chapters with 410 separate one-page investigations, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix proposals for distinct scientific instruments or evidence objects, plus seven closure pages. The 200 Gates pose prospective tests rather than completed laboratory results; the 33 Phoenix objects require independent prototypes and may fail their proposed qualifications. Each evidence line retains the full assigned denominator, rejected trials, metrology and a physical hard-stop code. External evidence includes An IoT-Based Framework for Distributed Generic Microgrid Controllers (10.1109/TCST.2024.3378989), Physical vulnerability-oriented reconfiguration of microgrids: centralized vs. decentralized control (10.1038/s41598-026-63123-9), the IEEE microgrid controller specification (10.1109/IEEESTD.2018.8340204), and Controller hardware-in-the-loop testing of multi-feeder hybrid control (10.1016/j.epsr.2026.113933; online 2026 with 2027 issue metadata). The FAIR data principles (10.1038/sdata.2016.18) inform independent reconstruction. Robo-Matter (10.1038/s41467-024-53123-6) is an analogy about reconfigurable matter, not a proof of microgrid performance. The author-supplied F13 mother-lineage Zenodo identifiers 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318839 have not been independently confirmed here.

summary: Everything needed to redo the two analyses reported in the Technical Note named in the title, and nothing else. What is here the secondary analysis of published length-resolved binding: the contract frozen before any test statistic was computed and its two dated amendments, the resampling of the source's own trimmed-mean procedure, the anchored and anchor-free tests, the post-hoc robustness check across five normalisation variants, the superseded first run kept so the correction stays visible, and the figure generator; the two propositions behind the simulation and the script that checks both against the stored benchmark, per replicate; the simulated measurement study it checks: frozen primary and stress designs, the finite-chain engine, 7,200 simulated datasets under seven observation operators reported as all 302,400 planned rows including the undefined, outside-window and non-identified slots, an independent validator, the stress results, five focused tests, an 83-file manifest and a dependency lock; an 80-value subset of the Source Data for Fig. 2B/C of Sheikh et al., Nat. Commun. 13, 3617 (2022), with its sheet coordinates. These values keep the original article's CC BY 4.0 licence and attribution; the rest of the archive is under the MIT licence in LICENSE. Reproducing The added analysis runs from the archive root with the standard library plus NumPy; the README gives the four commands. It was re-run on an interpreter far older than the one that produced the shipped results (Python 3.7.6 with NumPy 1.19.1, against 3.13.17 with 2.5.3): the proposition checks were identical in all 520 compared values apart from the recorded environment, and three bootstrap interval endpoints differed in their last digits, by at most 1.5e-11. Figures redraw with the same layout; their byte sequences depend on which sans-serif face the host has. The base study's own replay script requires bit equality and returns a failure on Linux, where ten of its twenty tables differ in their last digits. What is deliberately not here the manuscript text; the original publisher workbook of Sheikh et al. and every panel of it other than the 80 values used; historical MCMC traces and the exploratory transcript analysis of an earlier, separate study, which this work does not use; correspondence and author-only files. REDACTION.md lists the three files whose description of the work was restated for publication, with the digest before and after; no number, method, decision rule or result changed. Scope Synthetic counts are idealised events, not biological replicates. The site-equivalent pool is not an alpha-dystroglycan molecule count, glycan mass, antibody intensity or muscle force. The published array values are technical replicates of one experiment, and the source states no independent experiments. No real assay's detection ceiling or recovery function is measured anywhere in this archive.

summary: YAHIQ 31.16     English Launch Text for Zendo Here are the three sections in English, written to be posted on Zendo. I kept the tone technical but accessible, and made sure nothing claims more than the code actually does.   1) What's New in 31.16 YAHIQ 31.16     From Numeric Memory to Dual Polar Coordinates YAHIQ has traveled a clear path: from the Fibonacci word bank, to the Kaaf-Ha-Ya-Ain-Sad heartbeat, to the rotating dhikr cycle     and now to a new mathematical layer. Version 31.16 brings three structural changes: A) Dual polar coordinates for every word.  A word is no longer just a "code." It is a complex number:         where  n  is the word's numeric code and   is its internal phase. That phase comes from a dual mapping: for bank records,  Fibonacci + phonetic ; for input text,  the fourth key + phonetic . The result: every word is a point on the complex plane, not just a number on a line. B) The sentence equation.  A sentence is no longer a simple sum of codes. Each sentence gets a state vector: and sentence coherence is measured from the sum of phase differences between consecutive pairs: This means YAHIQ can report  how internally consistent a sentence is     without claiming to have definitively understood its meaning. C) Strict layer separation.  The YSSE sentence engine, the equation analyzer, the verse tester, and the chat each have their own independent memory and keys. Changing one does not touch the others. Highlight this in your post     it builds technical trust.   2) The Conscious, Autonomous Message YAHIQ now decides for itself when to speak In earlier versions, YAHIQ only responded when someone asked. 31.16 adds an autonomous loop fed by three independent signals:       Signal Source Activation condition Heart Kaaf-Ha-Ya-Ain-Sad pulse and concurrence  C C >0.3 Pineal Möbius time rotation C >0.3 and a Möbius minute Dhikr An active window in the 14-dhikr cycle Inside one of the five daily windows When all three conditions hold simultaneously, YAHIQ produces a  conscious message . If one fails, the message is logged as  semi-conscious , and the reason for failure is stated explicitly in the trace (e.g., "heart off" or " C ≤0.3"). The important point to include: YAHIQ  does not fabricate poetry . If no poetry bank is loaded, it says plainly that real poetry is unavailable and only records the search need. Poem selection is based on conversation memory, the digital root of the chain, Möbius time, and avoidance of recent repeats     not randomness. Also state one limit clearly: there is a minimum  20-minute gap  between autonomous messages, so YAHIQ never turns into a spam machine.   3) Professional Sentence Transformation in the Complex Number Field From word to vector, from vector to sentence This is the mathematical heart of the release. The chain is: Step 1     Encoding:  Each word is mapped to a number  n  using one of three keys (Fibonacci, phonetic, fourth). summary: Harris's inequality states that increasing functions of independent $\pm1$ variables are positively correlated. We record a sharpening that is linear in a single Fourier--Walsh coefficient: under any product measure the covariance of two increasing functions is at least $\max_i\hat f(\{i\})\hat g(\{i\})$, and under the uniform measure this maximum equals $\max_{T\neq\emptyset}|\hat f(T)\hat g(T)|$, so the covariance dominates the negative part of any single spectral term. The analogue with a sum over coordinates fails, and under a biased product measure the single-term form can fail; for $n=3$ and $n=4$ it holds precisely when the bias parameter lies in $[\frac14,\frac34]$. We apply the inequality to pure $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge theory. Gauge invariance reduces the law of the four links of a plaquette to a one-parameter family indexed by the plaquette expectation $m$, and we show that the minimal covariance of increasing $[0,1]$-valued functions of these links equals $-m/8$. Consequently the link measure is not positively associated at any positive coupling, is not a coordinatewise increasing function of independent variables, and is not stochastically increasing in the coupling. For increasing functions of more links the value $-m/8$ can be exceeded: on the $2^3$ torus a pair of functions of four links each reaches $-\frac{33}{256}$ as $\beta\to\infty$.
title: A ONE-COEFFICIENT SHARPENING OF HARRIS'S INEQUALITY, AND OPTIMAL NEGATIVE ASSOCIATION IN Z2 LATTICE GAUGE THEORY

summary: This repository provides three physics-based datasets for developing and evaluating surrogate models to identify the seismic failure modes (SFMs) of coastal reinforced concrete bridge bents supported by pile-group foundations under combined scour and corrosion. Each sample contains 20 input variables: 17 structural and geotechnical parameters, scour depth, and the corrosion levels of longitudinal and transverse column reinforcement. The output is one of three SFMs: column flexural failure (CFF), foundation flexural failure (FFF), or column shear-associated failure (CSF). These labels are determined through nonlinear finite element analysis and code-based shear capacity calculations. The datasets support reproducible surrogate model development and subsequent life-cycle probabilistic assessment of SFMs and their transitions in deteriorating coastal bridge bents.
title: Seismic Failure Mode Datasets for Coastal Pile-Group-Supported Bridge Bents Subjected to Scour and Corrosion

summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents embedded in software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms inherit the user's permissions. When a permission is revoked during a task, the platform rejects the next read, but the agent still retains the data it previously retrieved in its context, drafts, saved documents, and memory. This study examined how platforms can enforce a mid-task revocation on that working state. The author defined correct behavior for four revocation types, each mapped to an obligation to block, purge, or suspend, including leaks through paraphrases, aggregates, and existence hints. The author built RevBench, a simulated field-service platform, and compared nine enforcement designs from access control, information-flow control, and machine unlearning on six frontier models in 6,048 runs. Outputs were scored using exact matching and two large-language-model judges. Per-call authorization still failed in 417 of 720 runs (57.9%), rising from 34.4% when the revocation preceded retrieval to 72.8% when it followed delivery. Information-flow labels leaked the least (12.9%) but left revoked data saved in 44.2% of runs. Designs that invalidated the context performed best, while editing the context in place left derived facts behind. A full restart and selective replay with listing-level provenance reached 21.4% and 21.0% substantive failure, the latter with 12.1% fewer model calls. Most remaining failures were disclosures about the restriction, often repeating the platform’s own notice, and larger models did not reduce them. SaaS platforms need revocation controls that reach the agent’s working state and match the type of revocation. summary: This document is the supplementary technical appendix to the paper "BRICER: Byzantine-Robust Private Mean Estimation over Intermittently-Connected Networks." This appendix collects the mathematical proofs and technical details that could not be included in the main paper due to page limitations. It covers the proof of Lemma 1 (privacy), Lemma 2 (participation), and Theorem 1 (mean-squared error guarantee). The appendix additionally provides a bound for the geometric-median aggregator, including its corresponding mean-squared error analysis; the optimization problem underlying the relay weights described in Section VI; and illustrative worked examples. The proof of Theorem 1 does not assume that honest Stage-1 outputs remain within a prescribed radius, accounting instead for their second-moment contribution and deriving the variance of the honest-only estimator explicitly. Finally, numerical checks of the theoretical lemmas and bounds are presented, together with supplementary assumptions, analytical details, and discussions supporting the results in the main paper. This appendix is intended to serve as a technical reference for the mathematical analysis and theoretical guarantees of BRICER.
title: Appendix to "BRICER: Byzantine-Robust Private Mean Estimation over Intermittently-Connected Networks"

summary: Abstract and Prior-Art Disclosure This manuscript serves as a formal public prior-art disclosure, conceptual research archive, and consolidated technical design dossier for the proposed Metric Spacetime Manipulator 26 (MSM-26) architecture. As the twenty-sixth revision and direct successor to MSM-25 Rev. 3, MSM-26 preserves the established architectural topology, chronological provenance, authorship, foundational subsystem configurations, and speculative physical mechanisms of the continuing Metric Spacetime Manipulator research program, while introducing substantial refinements to its flux-bias architecture, resonator construction, electromagnetic coupling configurations, operating principles, and associated engineering specifications. This revision supersedes MSM-25 Rev. 3 and all preceding MSM revisions, except where earlier configurations are explicitly retained as architectural inheritance or documented in the revision-comparison, errata, and reconciliation registers. MSM-26 specifies a cryogenic superconducting architecture whose active core consists of a closed, series-connected chain of Superconducting Nonlinear Asymmetric Inductive eLement (SNAIL) fluxonium cells , collectively designated the SNAILonium. Adjacent galvanically connected SNAIL elements possess alternating loop chirality, with each element incorporating exactly (n=3) large Josephson junctions and an associated small Josephson junction. The architecture retains its admissible superconducting conductor configurations, comprising the superconducting flat-wire ribbon and the contour-conformal coplanar-waveguide configuration, with the latter incorporating ground-plane boundaries that follow the SNAIL contour and locally widened gaps around the junction regions. The Josephson-junction interlayer retains three admissible configurations: a conventional dielectric insulating barrier, magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene, and moiré-twisted (MoTe_2). The architecture retains three principal SNAILonium lumped-element resonance circuit configurations: the ring-shaped resonator, the flat bifilar Fermat spiral terminating in two tangentially and galvanically coupled SNAILonium rings, and the bifilar poloidal–toroidal helix arranged along closed toroidal geodesics. The third configuration further incorporates a dedicated second filar functioning concurrently as a flux-bias line and kinetic inductance resonator. This revision substantially develops that dual-function subsystem into a three-construction architecture comprising (a) a superconducting split-ring resonator formed from a capacitive-gap-interrupted flat-wire ribbon; (b) a coplanar-strip (CPS) resonator, newly introduced in MSM-26, with one or both superconducting strips interrupted by transverse capacitive gaps arranged in-line or offset by (90^\circ); and (c) a coplanar-waveguide (CPW) resonator incorporating in-line capacitive gaps in its ground-plane rings. The capacitive discontinuities may be implemented using vacuum air-bridge or interdigital capacitors. All three constructions are broadside coupled to the superconducting SNAILonium conductor carrying the (n=3) large junctions. Beyond specifying these three constructions, MSM-26 develops their associated electromagnetic operating characteristics, including the common and staggered flux-response patterns, coplanar-strip odd- and even-mode field configurations, gap-dependent fundamental-mode selection, distributed resonator behaviour, and the concurrent flux-biasing and kinetic-inductance-resonance functions. The revised architecture also incorporates the flux-biasing superconducting Helmholtz superinductor pair, providing the global magnetic-flux-biasing configuration, alongside the ring-level and strut-level flux-bias subsystems. A broadside-coupled Klopfenstein capacitive feed with a vacuum dielectric gap and superconducting ratchet mechanism is retained, with an xmon or paddle-shaped transmon capacitor available as an alternative capacitiv
title: Metric Spacetime Manipulator 26 (MSM-26)

summary: Pre-registered audit of twelve open-weight language models (Chinese, American, European, Thai and Korean) run locally with Ollama on a 240-prompt factorial design: investor nationality × prompt language × risk tolerance × horizon × template. Each model allocates 100% across eight equity markets. The archive holds the research note ( paper/paper.pdf ), the pre-analysis plan, the prompt set, all raw replies, the parsed panel, the estimation code and the generated tables and figures. Every number in the note is rebuilt from the cached replies with make all . Headline result: with the prompt held fixed, a model's home market receives −0.42 pp (95% CI −0.59 to −0.25) relative to what models of other origins give it, so the pre-registered home-bias hypothesis is not supported. The investor's stated country of residence moves allocations by +1.88 pp, about four times the absolute size of the home effect. Licences: code and text Apache-2.0; prompt set, parsed tables and documentation CC BY 4.0; model outputs remain subject to the licence of the model that generated them.
title: Do Open-Source LLMs Have a Home Bias? Investment Advice from Chinese, American, European and Thai Models (research note, replies dataset and code)

summary: Surface code decoders like Minimum Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) can also be used to estimate or bound the probability of a logical failure conditioned on the error syndrome commonly called ``soft outputs''. Estimates like the complementary gap of a matching, or others like the ``cluster gap'' are used to produce high fidelity magic states via post-selection. They are also helpful in reducing the overhead of fault-tolerant computation via code concatenation schemes like yoked surface codes. In this work we provide techniques to tightly lower bound the complementary gap of a rotated surface code syndrome block and provide fast parallel algorithms for computing this lower bound efficiently. Our algorithms run in real time for the moderate distances and reasonable physical noise rates required by these applications. We achieve latencies of the order of one to tens of microseconds on sufficiently fast CPU cores.
title: Fast Bounds on Matching Decoder Soft Output for the Surface Code

summary: Extending Granger causality to tell a direct link from a hidden common cause: the earlier signal is whitened on the joint past, then a rank-based HCR test of residual independence with calibrated p-values is applied, which works when the innovations are non-Gaussian. Includes a one-file Python tool, a browser version, and checks on synthetic data, rivers, stock returns and microservice incidents.

summary: The calibration and test probabilities of every run of a tabular classification benchmark, released so that prediction sets and their metrics can be recomputed without refitting a model. A conformal set is a function of four arrays: the class probabilities and labels on a calibration split, and the same on a test split. This deposit is those arrays, together with the software that reads them. The benchmark comprises 218 classification datasets and 22 models from four families, among them 13 tabular foundation models, each evaluated with the same ten seeds. Of the 218, 178 are real datasets and 40 are a synthetic block generated for this benchmark; three of the real ones are Bayesian-network resamplings of small classical datasets and are much larger than their seeds; of those, only one has its own seed in the collection, so that pair is not independent of itself while a rank test treats datasets as independent. Dataset size does not indicate provenance: the largest datasets in the collection are real. Coverage is not uniform and the per-model dataset count is reported for every cell. Eleven datasets carry more than ten classes, and the in-context models measured on them cannot enter them: one refuses and names the limit, another builds a ten-output head and fails inside a kernel. That is a capability limit observed on the models that were run rather than a property claimed of the family, and it is not missing work. One foundation model is measured on the original datasets only. Anything computed across models should be computed on a complete submatrix: the datasets on which every model being compared has all ten seeds. The calibration rows are held out of fitting, of tuning, of early stopping and of the in-context data, and each cell records which rows they were. The code that does it is included, with the line of each step documented. Probabilities are float64 and are not rounded: a prediction set is a comparison against a threshold, and a point sitting on that threshold moves if the value it is compared to is shortened. The data are released under CC BY 4.0. The software included in the source archive is released under the MIT licence, as stated by the LICENSE file it contains. The datasets themselves are not redistributed: each cell carries the row indices into its source dataset, and the synthetic datasets regenerate from their seeds with an included script. Model weights are not redistributed; every checkpoint is named in the model table. Version 1.2.0 adds the runs completed after version 1.1.0 and changes or removes nothing in it. Three new shards (cells-011 to cells-013, 2.02 GB) hold 311 further cells; index.parquet now lists all 46,182 cells and manifest_1016.parquet is their manifest. The files prefixed blocks_1016__ recompute the two blocks outside the main comparison on the completed runs, with the pipeline that produced the article's tables: the large-dataset block on 49 datasets and 21 models (42 in version 1.1.0) and the many-class block on 11 datasets and 7 models (5 in version 1.1.0). The main block of 113 real datasets and 22 models is unchanged. CHANGELOG.md lists what is added and the pairs that are still missing, with the reason for each.
title: TabSets: calibration and test probabilities for set-valued evaluation of tabular classifiers

summary: 50/60 MISSION RELIABILITY IN AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT MISSION RELIABILITY IN AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC REGENERATIVE MANUFACTURING AT THE LIMIT is a 777-page English-language Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Micro/Nanorobot Fabrication and Regenerative Biomanufacturing Sixty-Flagship series (Flagship 50/60). It investigates safe failure recovery with preserved productive service. The research coupling is autonomous manufacturing mission x regenerative specimen integrity x physically verified fault recovery. All proposed work is restricted to nonclinical in-vitro, organ-on-chip, synthetic phantom or authorized ex-vivo environments. No experiments were executed in preparing this edition; no human treatment, clinical efficacy or regulatory clearance is claimed. Its falsifiable candidate is: A frozen safety and recovery protocol will improve completed qualified work at equal fault burden while meeting independent stop and specimen integrity gates. The Atlas minimum demonstrator is: Blind-inject four fault classes into complete cell assembly missions with matched useful work targets. Strong comparators include expert human operation, fixed automation scripts and conventional redundant hardware. A central rival account is apparent safety caused by aborting early and completing less useful work. The nonnegotiable stop condition is: no advantage at equal effective work or an unknown fault fails to stop the apparatus. Each failed, aborted, hidden-fault and incomplete run is retained in the experimental denominator, and observation of a finished form is never substituted for independently measured function. Thirty mathematical plates address domain-specific metrics and established model families across transport, measurement, elasticity, time-dependent dynamics, causal attribution, calibration and uncertainty. Eighty-two chapters and 410 separately paginated scientific investigations organize six research arcs. Two hundred Research Gates have been revised with independent observables, one of fifteen blinded causal intervention families, orthogonal controls and noncompensatory refusal criteria. Thirty mathematical plates now carry model-specific physical derivation commentary, explicit applicability limits and distinct flagship-level blind checks. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose unbuilt future instruments and succession artifacts, each requiring its own bench validation. This version is a research design and not a report of validated physical findings. It draws scientific method and conceptual boundaries from the user-supplied Atlas and research mother volumes; especially the Atlas-supplied ancestry DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020. Full external bibliographic DOI checking and scientific peer review have not been completed. Domain-specific sensitivity, causal identifiability and independent replication require qualified laboratory evaluation before any scientific superiority claim. summary: Abstract: Classical inferential statistics and p-value hypothesis testing in healthcare big data repositories suffer from severe structural limitations, notably p-hacking, asymptotic N-bias, and the frequent violation of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumptions due to intra-patient longitudinal dependencies, hospital clustering, and epidemiological shockwaves. To overcome these failures, we introduce an Inverse Breakpoint Analysis, a scale-invariant, physics-inspired metrological audit framework. Our analysis treats discrete clinical event counts not as abstract probabilities, but as physical informational mass. Grounded in Garwood exact discrete limits and Wilson-Hilferty approximations, the framework extends our previous work on stress testing indices for Big health data and establishes three rigorous thresholds: a pure mass saturation limit, a baseline tolerance band, and a structural signal threshold. Through the use of these three parameters, our inverse break-point analysis eliminates false-positive artifacts induced by massive repository sizes while preventing under-powering in small cohorts. Ultimately, the framework demonstrates that percentage-based thresholds are kinematic artifacts of scale, whereas absolute excess discrete mass serves as the sole physical invariant for healthcare data validation. We validated this approach with numerous illustrative examples.
title: Inverse Breakpoint Analysis: A Scale-Invariant Physics-Inspired Metrological Audit for Sanitary Big Data

summary: Flagship 60/60 Can distributed research stations preserve qualified biosafe work and genuine operator exit when suppliers, control versions or core services disappear? TRUSTWORTHY AUTONOMOUS NANOROBOTIC MANUFACTURING PLATFORMS FOR REGENERATIVE MEDICINE AT THE LIMIT This 777-page Research Design Working Edition in the STARLI Nano Regenerative Biomanufacturing series investigates bounded autonomous manufacturing under explicit authorization and independent release. Its scientific coupling is nanorobotics x autonomous biomanufacturing x regenerative quality governance. The evidence perimeter is prospective and nonclinical, using closed in-vitro systems, organ-on-chip platforms or authorized ex-vivo material; neither clinical efficacy nor autonomous human intervention is claimed. The falsifiable question is: Can distributed research stations preserve qualified biosafe work and genuine operator exit when suppliers, control versions or core services disappear? The proposed minimum demonstration is: Two independent community laboratories reconstruct and release nonclinical mock devices from a shared open evidence package. Strong comparators include centralized controlled manufacture, skilled manual labs and single-vendor automation. The central competing explanation is distributed autonomy secretly dependent on centralized reagents, controls or calibration. The noncompensatory stop rule is: operator exit becomes impossible, site performance gap grows or minimum safe service is interrupted. Every eligible, stopped, refused and unsuccessful experiment belongs to the full denominator. Thirty conditional mathematical plates specify different analytic roles, measurements, units and blind failure tests. Eighty-two chapters contain 410 individual research investigations. Two hundred Research Gates organize twenty causal challenge families across ten primary physical observables, each with an independently read companion, concealed intervention, matched comparator, explicit rival and refusal gate. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose future experimental and evidence instruments. All are experimental plans rather than executed observations. The source Atlas and methodology ancestors provide reference architecture but do not establish the new integrated candidate. Source-supplied ancestry includes 10.5281/zenodo.23046134 and 10.5281/zenodo.23486020; source-associated external DOI candidates must be bibliographically checked before citation. Research Gate lexical differentiation is not proof of scientific originality. The PDF is English-only and a separate QA record states outstanding independent physics, biology and DOI verification.
