summary: High-dimensional data from multiple sources often combine shared structure with source-specific variation. We study heterogeneous principal component analysis, which seeks to recover common and private principal subspaces when their dimensions are unknown. {We propose \emph{Feature Extraction (FE)}, a novel data-driven framework with two steps. First, the Eigenvector-based Spike-Count (ESC) estimator determines the number of principal components (PC) in each source using only sample eigenvector information, rather than eigenvalue-based criteria. Second, FE identifies the locations of common features by comparing bias-corrected inner products between sample eigenvectors across sources. These matches yield estimates of the common and source-specific subspaces without iterative optimization. We establish the consistency of our estimators under a spiked covariance model in a high-dimensional regime where the dimension and sample size grow proportionally. Simulations and applications to federated image data and U.S. housing prices demonstrate the performance of FE in rank recovery, subspace estimation, and data reconstruction.} Code is available at https://github.com/liwenbo-research/HeterogeneousPCA
title: Features Extraction Across Multi-Source Heterogeneous Data

summary: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.
title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition

summary: Distribution feeders host managed electric vehicle charging through control loops, a site energy management system enforcing a connection-point limit and a demand response aggregator dispatching curtailment, that act on telemetry the charging stations report about themselves. An adversary controlling authorised but compromised reporting sources can move those loops without switching any physical load and without defeating any transport control. We define the undetected harm frontier, the greatest feeder harm reachable while raising no alarm under a given validation setup, and show that a bound on it exists only when at least one reference in the validation chain has provenance independent of the compromised source. We classify grid-edge telemetry into four provenance classes and evaluate seven validation setups on seven published distribution test systems by quasi-static time-series power flow, parameterised by measurements from a live OCPP 2.0.1 stack. Five of the seven setups, including textbook weighted-least-squares bad data detection, trace an identical frontier and constrain the adversary not at all. The two that bound the harm are exactly the two holding an independent measurement, which is the taxonomy's prediction. Under the unanchored setups the attack crosses the statutory voltage floor on IEEE 33-bus, crosses the conductor thermal rating on four of six networks robustly across random realisations, inflates apparent hosting capacity by 7.5 percent, and misallocates settlement. The mitigation this implies is not a better detector but the acquisition of one measurement the adversary does not produce.
title: False Data Injection from Authorized EV Chargers on Distribution Feeders

summary: Visual mental imagery (VMI) decoding uses brain activity to reconstruct internally generated visual scenes, providing a potential pathway for externalizing internal experiences and developing neuroprosthetic communication interfaces. However, progress is limited by the lack of dedicated, training-scale VMI datasets. Current VMI paradigms often rely on visual prompts or short-term memory images, introducing visual and mnemonic confounds that make it difficult to disentangle neural activity associated with endogenous image construction from signals driven by prior or concurrent visual input. Furthermore, existing VMI datasets offer limited descriptive control over individual visual attributes, making it difficult to systematically assess fine grained visual details. To address these gaps, we introduce AVID, the first dedicated training-scale 5.0 Tesla functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) resource for auditory-induced VMI decoding. AVID comprises approximately 67 hours of dense recordings from nine participants. The dataset is structured into two complementary splits: a scene-level complex split using naturalistic Mandarin descriptions and a controlled simple split with explicitly specified visual attributes. We further formalize a standardized evaluation protocol that decouples source-image consistency from semantic alignment, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of imagery reconstruction. Baseline qualitative and quantitative results show that current reconstruction pipelines remain limited on AVID, although the most successful reconstructions preserve recognizable scene level semantics from spoken descriptions. By combining dedicated training-scale neural recordings and standardized evaluation resources, AVID provides both a data foundation for imagery-specific model development and a benchmark for evaluating VMI decoding with substantially reduced sensory contamination.
title: AVID: A 5T fMRI Dataset for Benchmarking Auditory-induced Visual Mental Imagery Decoding

summary: Interactive world generation requires both accurate local control and stable scene consistency over long rollouts. Existing methods improve local generation through camera or geometry conditioning and extend historical context with memory mechanisms. However, long-horizon exploration remains challenging as target-view guidance becomes incomplete and inconsistencies accumulate across repeated scene updates. We present \textbf{GSExplorer}, a generation--reconstruction framework built around a persistent 3D Gaussian world state. At each step, the current 3DGS scene provides multimodal rendering conditions for a condition-driven video generator, while camera geometry is injected through a separate Relative Ray Encoding branch. Generated videos are then fed back to a SLAM-based reconstruction backend, where inconsistency filtering prevents conflicting content from corrupting the scene and cross-chunk bundle adjustment improves spatial alignment across generation steps. We further design a data-construction pipeline that reproduces realistic 3DGS degradation during scene extrapolation, yielding 293K training pairs of degraded multimodal renderings and real target videos. GSExplorer achieves the best overall performance among the compared methods on both single-step and three-step WorldScore evaluation, with strong camera control and consistency across both settings, including a Camera Control score of 99.07 in single-step extrapolation. On 481-frame leave-and-return rollouts, it also shows strong revisit consistency, demonstrating the value of maintaining a reliable 3D world state for continued exploration.
title: GSExplorer: Interactive World Generation with a Persistent 3D Gaussian World State

summary: The Neptunian desert and savanna are separated by a ridge, an overdensity at orbital periods of approximately 3-6 d identified with Kepler. Like the hot Jupiter pileup at larger radii, this feature has been linked to the accumulation of successful outcomes of high-eccentricity migration (HEM). We revisit the ridge independently using TESS occurrence posteriors for FGK main-sequence stars. We quantify its excess over adjacent regions and compare six occurrence profiles using leave-one-out cross-validation and Bayesian evidence. For planets with radii of approximately 5-8 $R_\oplus$, the ridge has twice the occurrence density of the denser neighbouring region ($J=2.05^{+0.52}_{-0.44}$), with 99.9% posterior support (one-sided Gaussian equivalent of $3.1σ$). This contrast agrees with the discovery study and earlier Kepler occurrence measurements. Both predictive performance and Bayesian evidence strongly favour profiles peaking within the ridge over a single power law. The lognormal is preferred, suggesting a narrower inner wing and a more extended outer wing, although evidence for asymmetry remains weak. In the same period window, the analysis recovers the hot Jupiter pileup (approximately 10-16 $R_\oplus$) with a contrast consistent with that of the ridge and excludes an analogous excess among sub-Neptunes (approximately 2-4 $R_\oplus$) with $3.4σ$ posterior support. TESS thus provides an independent detection of the Neptunian ridge. Its possible asymmetry would be compatible with HEM, in which tidal disruption could produce a sharper inner edge and variations in circularisation efficiency a more gradual outer decline. Establishing whether the ridge has this shape requires more precise occurrence measurements, with PLATO's expected planet yield offering a promising opportunity to help unveil its morphology.
title: The Neptunian ridge through the lens of TESS

summary: One way to compare two graphs $G_1, G_2$ is to check whether there is some graph $H$ in a graph class $\mathcal{H}$, such that the number of homomorphisms from $H$ to $G_1$ is not equal to that from $H$ to $G_2$. This is the field of homomorphism distinguishability which has gained a lot of traction in recent years. In this paper, we study the case where $\mathcal{H}$ is the class of graphs of treewidth $k$. This has connections to important concepts in logic, machine learning, combinatorial optimization and proof complexity. In particular, Dvořák showed that $G_1$ and $G_2$ can be distinguished by a homomorphism count from a graph of treewidth $k$ iff $G_1$ and $G_2$ are distinguishable by the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm. While the relation between the iteration number of this algorithm and the depth of the tree-decomposition of a distinguishing graph is understood, our understanding of the \emph{size} of $H$ is limited. We show a $2^{Ω(n^{k/2})}$ lower bound on the size of a graph of treewidth $k$ required to distinguish two graphs of order $n$. This bound is proved via a new combinatorial game along with a construction which uses a recent compression technique for CFI graphs. It is almost tight to the known $2^{O(n^{k+1})}$ upper bound and is an exponential improvement on the previous best known lower bound.
title: An Almost-tight Size Lower Bound for Bounded Treewidth Homomorphism-Distinguishability

summary: We construct a finite-support quantum theory of gravity from a discrete causal spin chain and three axioms, without taking spacetime, a metric, or classical geometry as microscopic inputs. The fundamental degrees of freedom are operator-valued, and causal composition closes under an extended SO(5,1) algebra. Algebraic localization introduces parallel index structures and fixes four-indexed extended tetrads as identification maps. Localizing the first-order transport already generated by causal composition on that carrier fixes the covariant derivative without an independent connection, and its commutator defines curvature. The quadratic invariant F² separates an intrinsic algebraic curvature, giving the time-dependent scalar Λ(t), from the sectors that yield the Einstein–Hilbert and Euler terms after symmetry breaking. A derived Higgs-like transition then produces ordinary tetrad geometry and General Relativity. With the inherited chain normalization, it gives the a priori dimensionless result μ_SB/M_P = 5/(16√11), with no fitted threshold; conversion to GeV uses the measured Planck scale. The broken phase has a finite physical mode sector whose spin-2 excitations are collective tetrad fluctuations rather than fundamental spacetime quanta. The Supplement proves finiteness of the physical one-loop tetrad self-energy and each fixed graph, gives constructive finite-matrix definitions of the physical spectrum and all projected vertices, and proves exact unitary evolution on the invariant terminal-occupancy space. Numerical diagonalization, evaluation of infrared loop residuals, and convergence of any auxiliary continuum/decompactification diagrammatic reorganization remain open. Geometry and spacetime are therefore derived concepts in a finite-support, background-independent gravitational construction.

The microscopic input is a closed, bi-infinite ordered history of binary choices; coarse-grained histories use local binary projectors and a decoherence functional; amplitudes compose unitarily between nearest-neighbor sites. Their faithful amplitude realization forces a four-component complex carrier; unresolved crossing order with antiunitary reversal yields Grassmann history variables. The coherent-state functional integral is primary, not the quantization of a prior classical field theory. Bilinear closure gives the unique local noncompact algebra SO(4,1), while coarse-grained spin sums generate the collective SO(5,1) sector, whose infrared İnönü–Wigner contraction yields the Poincaré group. Local spinors, Clifford closure, transport generators, and Poincaré invariance thus arise from causal composition rather than background symmetry. The same representation supplies the homogeneous cosmological limit. The compact orbital sector of the Hilbert space representation has no preferred position or direction, giving the cosmological principle; its infrared contraction fixes spatial flatness. Coherence loss in the resulting shell ensemble defines entropy, a thermodynamic arrow, and Gibbs temperature. The noncompact radial sector supplies the timelike support depth for homogeneous vacuum curvature. Inverse square scaling of this depth gives Λ(t) ∝ t⁻² before saturation. Summed-history interference stops opening new resolved radial sectors at log₁₀ n⋆ = 60.3884215, saturating the timelike curvature radius. summary: We show that a pre-geometric axiom set generates structures normally assumed in relativistic physics. The microscopic input is a closed, bi-infinite ordered history of binary choices; coarse-grained histories use local binary projectors and a decoherence functional; amplitudes compose unitarily between nearest-neighbor sites. No spacetime manifold, metric, connection, Lorentz group, or action principle is assumed. Four independent binary-projector implementations furnish {I, P, T, PT}. Their faithful amplitude realization forces a four-component complex carrier; unresolved crossing order with antiunitary reversal yields Grassmann history variables. The coherent-state functional integral is primary, not the quantization of a prior classical field theory. Bilinear closure gives the unique local noncompact algebra SO(4,1), while coarse-grained spin sums generate the collective SO(5,1) sector, whose infrared İnönü–Wigner contraction yields the Poincaré group. Local spinors, Clifford closure, transport generators, and Poincaré invariance thus arise from causal composition rather than background symmetry. The same representation supplies the homogeneous cosmological limit. summary: Microbiome Repo — data package v1.29.0 (2026-11-02) One catalog, two tiers, all ages. The catalog tables ( catalog_* ) are the curated tier: human-associated microbial communities sequenced by shotgun DNA or RNA sequencing, from every body site and at every age — 5,053 projects, 810,820 samples, 4,789,110 sample × field values — with body site, age at collection, sex, BMI, country, health condition (controlled vocabulary), antibiotic exposure, subject and timepoint recovered from archive attributes (R1), supplementary tables (R2), paper full text (R3) and abstracts (R4); every value carries a verbatim evidence quote (≤ 12 words), a labelled source, a route and a confidence. Each run is labelled DNA or RNA ( catalog_runs.nucleic_acid ), each sample says which data sets it has ( has_dna , has_rna ), and each project carries the nucleic acid of its data sets ( catalog_studies.nucleic_acid ). Coverage over all catalog samples: age 24%, sex 29%, country 89%, health condition 43%, antibiotic exposure 16%. The registry tables ( registry_* ) list every screened public study in ENA/SRA/DDBJ with a human-associated metagenome signal — 64,369 studies — with archive-only classification (host, UBERON-anchored body sites, life stages, assay, access) and the harvested BioSample tier (637,397 BioSamples with normalised site / age / sex / country). Start here. catalog_studies.parquet (one row per project: body sites, DNA / RNA, papers, methods and setting read from the paper, per-field coverage, age-category and health-condition mix, curated depth) → catalog_sample_metadata_wide.parquet (one row per sample: every field with __route / __confidence , body_site_code , age_category + basis, has_dna / has_rna ) → catalog_sample_determinations.parquet (the evidence behind every value) and catalog_runs.parquet (every run). registry_studies.parquet is the registry; registry_runs_v1.29.0.parquet (every screened run) ships as a GitHub Release asset. Infant extension. The 370 infant gut projects carry a deeper infant-field curation (delivery mode, feeding mode, preterm status, gestational age, birth weight, maternal antibiotics, probiotics, HMO supplementation, NEC). Those rows are present in the catalog_* tables ( curated_source = infant_catalog ; infant_scope = true selects them: 66,355 samples) and the deep tables ( sample_metadata_wide , sample_determinations , study_metadata_wide , cohorts , universe_studies_all , sandpiper_* , …) are in the package as well. Files | File | Rows | What it is | |---|---:|---| | catalog_studies.parquet | 5,348 | Catalog projects: body sites (sample_body_sites, body_site_primary), nucleic acid of the data sets (nucleic_acid, n_runs_dna / n_runs_rna, n_samples_dna / n_samples_rna), methods and setting read from the paper (platform, extraction_kit, library_kit, study_shape, n_participants, recruitment, settlement), registry columns + per-field coverage (cov_<field> for every pack field), age-category / health-condition distributions, sequencing summary (n_runs_total, Gbp per run, instrument models, layouts, Sandpiper share; 1.12.0), curated depth and source | | catalog_sample_metadata_wide.parquet | 864,842 | Catalog samples, one row per sample: body_site_code / body_site_class / body_site_basis, has_dna / has_rna, age category, age, sex, BMI, country, health condition, antibiotic exposure, subject, timepoint, collection date, detailed location (region / locality / site), latitude / longitude, lifestyle (+ route / confidence per field), infant-only fields, body-site class, infant_scope (== the infant catalog's catalog_scope filter) | | catalog_sample_determinations.parquet | 4,947,738 | Catalog determinations : one row per sample × field for every catalog sample (every body site, all ages) — value, normalised value, route (R1 archive attribute / R2 supplementary table / R3 paper prose / R4 abstract), confidence, verbatim evidence quote and source; infant-catalog rows copied verbatim (src_track infant_catalog) | | ca

summary: We derive the bosonic sector of the causal-chain framework. Gauge and scalar fields are not primitive continuum fields; they arise from closed double-loop spinor bilinears and enter the Minkowski-limit scalar-completed branch connection. The propagating gauge algebra is the rank-five left-right algebra SU(3)_C ⊗ SU(2)_L ⊗ SU(2)_R ⊗ U(1)_(B−L), while the scalar-completed branch connection carries sixteen active branch channels, 8_C + 3_L + 3_R + 1_L + 1_R = 16, because the single B−L line appears on both causal branches. Thus the two abelian entries are branch coefficients of one generator, not two independent U(1) groups. The ultraviolet organization is the SO(10) bilinear envelope of the sixteen-state fermion carrier; the propagating algebra is selected by closed-loop branch propagation. The universal closure normalization is g⋆ = g′⋆ = 0.500 at the Paper III scale μ_U ≡ μ_SB = 1.15035058 × 10¹⁸ GeV. After branch-normalization conversion, the three measured gauge directions of the upward scalar-completed RG check return to this same closure window, while downward running gives percent-level weak-scale gauge extractions. The continuum branch-kernel roots are v_R = 4016.1085 GeV, v_L = 260.8335 GeV, thresholds rather than benchmark right-sector pole masses. The stopped detector-current quotient annihilates the orthogonal right-vector exchange kernel below the right opening and therefore fixes the low-energy overlap to ε_R(0) = 0. Above μ_R,EW^PW = 3.9230019 TeV the pre-quotient right currents and actual W_R, Z_R gauge bosons are active, predicting a positive high-energy scattering threshold. The correlated cosmological signature is ΔN_eff^(ν_R) = 0.138439, or N_eff^right = 3.182439. The scalar-color channel also yields an even 203.6 GeV response pole and a stable odd composite with mass M_X = 3.92 TeV, derived downstream in Paper XI.
title: Causal Chain Physics VI: Emergence of Bosons, Planck Scale Coupling Convergence and Dynamical Electroweak Symmetry Breaking

summary: The Sundarbans mangrove system constitutes a globally consequential blue carbon sink, yet vertically resolved soil organic carbon (SOC) inventories, particularly at depth, remain under-constrained. This study deployed a geospatial deep-learning pipeline integrating multi-source Earth observation data (optical, SAR, and DEM-derived covariates) to spatially upscale SOC stocks to 1 m depth across the Bangladesh Sundarbans. Stratified coring across five sites positioned along the salinity–tidal inundation gradient to represent four major vegetation zones (n = 25; one pit per site × five depth intervals: 0–20, 20–40, 40–60, 60–80, 80–100 cm) captured physicochemical and SOC attributions. A Kruskal–Wallis test confirmed a positive SOC gradient with depth (H = 21.7, df = 4, p < 0.001); post-hoc Dunn’s pairwise comparisons showed 60–100 cm layers differed significantly from all shallower layers (p < 0.01, Bonferroni-adjusted), with the dominant pool residing below 40 cm, implying systematic underestimation by conventional shallow-core (<30–40 cm) assessments. To partition total ecosystem carbon and establish soil-pool dominance, above- and belowground biomass were parameterized using species-specific allometric equations, revealing high stem density but comparatively low basal area consistent with a regenerating stand structure dominated by Heritiera fomes and Sonneratia apetala. Analysis of a previously published Landsat-derived mangrove record (1988–2022) revealed net contraction in mangrove extent; loss-agent raster attribution, based on shoreline-proximity buffers, land-cover transition sequences and cyclone-track coincidence, identified chronic tidal abrasion and erosion as the primary driver rather than anthropogenic conversion or cyclonic disturbance. Benchmarking against a previously published global 30 m machine-learning SOC product revealed a 4.2-fold underestimation of SOC stocks in the Bangladesh Sundarbans, particularly in peat-enriched, anoxic substrata. Assimilation of deep-profile in situ observations with the pipeline significantly improves spatial prediction fidelity and establishes a robust baseline for Measurement, Reporting, and Verification for greenhouse gas inventories, highlighting the necessity of incorporating deep-soil carbon pools for inventorizing erosion-vulnerable seaward margins.

summary: Diversity-Plankton.R README: Functional Diversity Analyses in Synechococcus Communities Under Environmental Stress Overview This repository contains the final analyses used in the manuscript examining how functional diversity influences the growth, recovery, and temporal dynamics of experimental Synechococcus communities exposed to environmental stressors. The script quantifies relationships between both initial functional diversity (before stress exposure) and assembled functional diversity (after community assembly) with ecological responses including community growth, recovery, and changes in functional diversity through time. All analyses presented in the main text and supplementary materials are generated from this workflow. Study Objective The analyses test whether variation in functional diversity predicts the performance and resilience of microbial communities under four environmental treatments: Control Atrazine Heating Heating + Atrazine Specifically, the script evaluates whether: Initial functional diversity promotes community growth during the disturbance phase. Assembled functional diversity promotes recovery following disturbance. Functional diversity changes in response to environmental stress. The strength and direction of functional diversity effects depend on species richness and treatment context. Input Data Required files File Description all-data-with-diversity.rds Full experimental dataset containing strain composition, species composition, trait information, and functional diversity metrics across all sampling days (0–20). all-data-with-diversity-normalised.rds Normalized functional diversity dataset (Hill diversity, q = 2) restricted to experimental sampling days used for analyses. trait-summary.rds Trait-space boundaries and summary statistics used for trait visualizations. Data Processing Analyses focus on sampling days: Day 0 (pre-disturbance) Day 10 (end of disturbance phase) Day 20 (post-disturbance recovery phase) The script derives: Response variables Community growth Log-response ratio between Day 0 and Day 10 abundance: Growth = log(N10 / N0) Community recovery Log-response ratio between Day 10 and Day 20 abundance: Recovery = log(N20 / N10) Functional diversity change Change in functional diversity during disturbance: FD change = log(FD10 / FD0) Functional diversity recovery Change in functional diversity during recovery: FD recovery = log(FD20 / FD10) Community composition variables species_richness — number of species in each community strain_richness — number of strains in each community Both variables are parsed directly from species and strain composition identifiers. Statistical Analyses Four generalized least-squares (GLS) models are fitted using the nlme package. To account for treatment-specific heteroscedasticity, all models include a varIdent variance structure. Model 1: Community Growth Response: Growth Primary predictor: Initial functional diversity (diversity_0) Model 2: Community Recovery Response: Recovery Primary predictor: Assembled functional diversity (diversity_10) Model 3: Functional Diversity Change Response: FD change Primary predictor: Initial functional diversity (diversity_0) Model 4: Functional Diversity Recovery Response: FD recovery Primary predictor: Post-stress functional diversity (diversity_10) Model Structure All models include: diversity * species_richness * treatment + strain_richness where: Functional diversity is the focal predictor. Species richness modifies diversity effects. Treatment represents environmental stress context. Strain richness is included as an additive covariate. Outputs Main Text Output Description figures/fig1_trait_medians.png Median trait values for all strains and species. figures/fig2_fd_slopes.png Treatment-specific functional diversity effect sizes and confidence intervals. figures/fig3_fd_trajectories.png Functional diversity trajectories through time across treatments and diversity levels. tables/table2.xlsx T

summary: Analysis code accompanying the revised manuscript AeroJ-2026-0336. It covers: the codified ICAO CO2 limit lines L_NT(M) and L_InP(M) (40 CFR 1030.30); the structural (empty-weight) model; the transpose-pair arithmetic and the analytic induced-drag carry-over derivation; the OpenVSP/VSPAERO comparison model in its two released configurations (the forward reconstruction and the equalised-exposed-span configuration on which the Section 4.4 comparison is stated); the Monte Carlo propagation of Experiment A and the Section 4.5 mission model; the clean-sheet placement analysis; the Section 5 remedy benchmark; and the generation of Figures 1-5 with Table 4. The OpenVSP scripts generate their .vsp3 model files on run. Figure 1's freighter points are illustrative only, exactly as the figure caption states (anchored centrals, not estimator outputs, no uncertainty bands). The estimator predictions of Appendix A are not covered by this release; their record is Appendix A of the paper. The data underlying the study are the public sources cited in the paper's reference list. Requirements: Python 3.10+, NumPy, Matplotlib (figure images only); SciPy optional (pure-Python fallbacks included); OpenVSP 3.x with its Python module for the two OpenVSP scripts only.

summary: Version 1.02, 3 November 2026. Acemoglu and Restrepo (2020) estimate that one additional industrial robot per thousand workers lowers a U.S. local labor market's employment-to-population ratio by 0.39 percentage points and its hourly wages by about 0.77 percent. Rebuilding their design from raw IPUMS, IFR, and EU KLEMS data, I reproduce these estimates bit-exactly. I then ask what conventional robustness checks leave open: which industries, places, periods, and shocks actually identify the estimate? The regression spans 722 commuting zones and 19 industries, but the variation behind an instrumental-variable estimate can be far narrower. The sign is robust; the support is narrow. Negative estimates persist across conventional specification changes, 60 strong European instrument windows, alternative U.S. treatment windows, and the published periods through 2014. Yet automotive carries about 84 percent of normalized absolute Rotemberg-weight mass, and automotive exposure in six Rust Belt states supplies 95 percent of the net first-stage covariance. Without automotive, the remaining 18 industry shocks do not strongly predict U.S. robot exposure. Longer horizons, later start years, and adding Germany to the instrument all strengthen it through the same margin. The automotive component shows no detectable relation to 1970–1990 employment and wage changes, and a direct effect of the instrument would have to absorb 72 percent of the reduced form before conventional significance disappears. Inference is weaker than the regional first stage suggests. With 19 underlying industry shocks, exposure-robust first-stage F-statistics are 6.2 and 6.3 rather than 34, small-sample Anderson–Rubin tests do not reject a zero effect ( p = 0.059, 0.063), and other implementations of the same test disagree; in known-truth simulations, nominal 95-percent state-clustered intervals cover in only 60–66 percent of replications. Measurement assumptions also bind. summary: We ask whether the folded Causal Chain Physics continuum admits a traversable spacelike channel and, if not, whether matter can move onto new constituents without scanning and reconstruction. The first answer is negative. One radial ladder ends at one boundary, spacetime is the image of one extended-tetrad map, and a black-hole horizon is a local pullback of that boundary. With no second exterior or earlier carrier edge, the no-channel theorem excludes traversable wormholes, metric shortcuts, baby-universe branches, and topology-changing escape channels. A fold-symmetric black hole may occur as initial data but remains terminal in both temporal orientations. The same principle gives the positive result. Orbital recurrence can repeat an informational type, but not a physical token, whose identity follows one continuous supported map. On Paper III's finite physical sector, an exact transporter preserves every reference correlation while returning the source and carrier to a fixed blank. Local, state-independent exchanges can therefore move the protected organization without cloning or a hidden blueprint, subject to explicit capacity and latency bounds. Unlike measure-and-prepare reconstruction, standard teleportation preserves an unknown state using entanglement, a Bell record, and causal feed-forward. Direct translocation uses no measurement record or remote conditional operation: the output continues the same supported map on different constituents. Proposed tests move a reference-entangled molecular qubit through an exchange chain and a coherent bond-form through dissociation, photonic transduction, and reassociation; a superconducting precursor tests the same clean-reset condition. These are causal tests, not faster-than-light transport.
title: Causal Chain Physics XII: No Traversable Wormholes and Causal Form Translocation—Spacelike No-Go, Orbital Recurrence, and Physical Identity

summary: We derive the baryon, active-lepton, and dark-matter inventory of one scalar-completed electroweak event. The CCF covariant derivative creates the first-order wall and its chiral source; bounded-support Parisi–Wu (PW) and continuum transport are two resolutions of that source, while the weak anomaly converts the left-handed bias into baryon and lepton number. The fixed-root PW calculation gives η_B,1^PW = 5.26082 × 10⁻¹⁰; the matrix-resolved continuum reconstruction gives 5.13315 × 10⁻¹⁰. Their computed hard-scale response defines the non-Gaussian theory-resolution interval η_B = 5.26 (+0.30, −0.40) × 10⁻¹⁰, which contains the independent Paper II baryon-loading range (5.37–5.48) × 10⁻¹⁰. The same event produces the flavor-scalar active source L_ν = 4.022200 × 10⁻² (1, 1, 1) and ξ = 5.87649332 × 10⁻² (1, 1, 1). An equal right-handed counterasymmetry makes this a chiral separation rather than net lepton-number creation. On the Paper II background its direct weak-rate map gives Y_P^weak = 0.24527; counting the right and active radiation once gives Y_P^full = 0.24712. An exact reflection protects one odd closed-support scalar pole with J = 0 and M_X = 3.9230019 TeV + O(Λ_QCD). The allowed Φ_G^a B_i^a operator is a heavier transverse J = 1 excitation, not the ordinary static-source gluelump ground state. The Lorenz/support theorem gives the exact temporal-source identity J_(u,G) = 0, excluding a scalar-color Coulomb kernel and Sommerfeld ladder while retaining transverse color interactions. Deconfined freeze-out then yields Ω_X h² = 0.130 (+0.028, −0.015), overlapping the Paper II requirement 0.1230–0.1234 without a cosmological fit. This number is the abundance before the ordinary-QCD transition. The complete source, spin-ordering, and late-survival proofs are given in the Supplemental Material; post-transition finite-range scattering remains a separate connected-amplitude matching problem.

summary: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.
title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale

summary: State of the art latent dynamics world models achieve impressive performance for robot planning. But do they actually encode the physics of the world? In this paper, we show that popular world models today achieve strong results on tasks that reduce to image similarity but forget key details about objects in the scene like mass, deformation, friction, and bounciness. We achieve this by defining precisely what ought to be encoded in such a world model and introducing two new evaluation methods that can directly tease physical properties and easily scale to new ones. Our evaluation, which we call Roz, includes 10 contrastive tasks and 3 continuous tasks, totaling 1734 individual scenarios. We validate our eval on control tasks. On our own model, AnonWM, we find that performance roughly improves with training steps, while not necessarily being correlated with reconstruction MSE. We argue current model failures are a symptom of evaluation strategies (probes and planners) that are opaque, model-specific, and high-compute. Roz requires only a model that can ingest still frames or video, a way to extract latents, and a distance function between them, and it can be run in one pass. We hope future evaluations will adopt Roz's evaluation techniques. More broadly, we hope Roz can be a case study for a future where benchmarks allow rapid iteration and comparison across models.
title: Roz: A Taste Test for World Model Latents

summary: We study the block Anderson Hamiltonian \(H_L=λΨ_L+\mathcal V\) on the discrete torus \((\mathbb Z/L\mathbb Z)^d\), \(d\geq2\), where \(Ψ_L\) is the nearest-neighbor Laplacian and \(\mathcal V\) consists of independent \(W^d\times W^d\) GOE blocks. In the weak-disorder limit \(λ\to\infty\), we establish an entrywise local law, a spatial scaling limit for the squared resolvent entries, time-averaged dynamical delocalization, and lower bounds on the localization length of most bulk eigenfunctions. Particularly, we allow the block size to be fixed or grow above a polylogarithmic threshold. In sufficiently large polynomial volumes, the dynamical estimates hold for \(C_δ(λ+W/λ)\leq T\leq λ^{1+κ_d^{\rm BA}-δ}\), with a dimension-dependent exponent \(κ_d^{\rm BA}>0\), and the spreading scale is \(\sqrt{(λ^3+λW)T}\). This identifies a transition at \(W\asympλ^2\) between \(λ^{3/2}\sqrt T\) and \(\sqrt{λWT}\). The proof combines Gaussian moment estimates with deterministic stability of a matrix Dyson equation. A partial Bloch transform handles fixed blocks, while scalar reduction controls growing blocks. A Feshbach--Schur reduction of the block \(T\)-equation separates a single scalar diffusion mode from the stable internal cell modes. A renewal expansion and exact cell counting give a positive representation of the diffusion coefficient and control the fourth moment uniformly across the block-size transition. Notably, our argument does not require an enumeration of Feynman diagrams.
title: Quantum Diffusion and the Block-Size Crossover in the Block Anderson Model

summary: Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home's action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.
title: Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models

summary: Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents \emph{X-World~1.6}, advancing X-World~1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.
title: X-World 1.6: Building Controllable Virtual Cities with World Models

summary: Scientific discovery advances when evidence from different investigations is brought into contact. Yet paper-centric communication leaves experimental results fragmented, delayed, or unreported, creating a "scientific memory wall" between growing computational capabilities and the evidence accessible to AI systems. We envision a different dynamic: in a network of intelligent laboratories, a failed or overlooked experiment in one domain could trigger a hypothesis in another, whose testing generates evidence that stimulates further investigations. Such chains of information collision and empirical validation could transform isolated discovery loops into a cumulative scientific process. We propose Evolving Scientific Intelligence (ESI), an architectural blueprint for enabling these evidence-driven chain reactions. ESI preserves experimental records in shared, computable scientific memory, where evidence from different domains can be recombined into testable hypotheses. It jointly selects candidates and evaluation methods according to scientific value, reliability, and cost, then coordinates physical tests across distributed experimental nodes. Their feedback revises hypotheses and evaluators, while slower meta-control reassesses research objectives and decision criteria to guard against self-reinforcing errors and misguided optimization. We call for an Information Manhattan Project to build the infrastructure for scientific intelligence that evolves through experimentally grounded chains of discovery.
title: Evolving Scientific Intelligence: From Fragmented Evidence to Distributed Experimental Loops

summary: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via llama.cpp confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.
title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study

summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.
title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel

summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory burden of large model deployment by casting the high precision trained weights to fewer bits. While this promotes memory-efficient inference, it also incurs quantization error that impairs model performance. To compensate for quantization error, the present contribution decomposes the original trained weights into a quantized matrix, a low-rank component, and a sparse matrix that accounts for outlier rows in the weights. Due to analytical intractability and the discrete structure of the decomposition, a simulated annealing search is employed to explore candidate decompositions while avoiding poor local minima. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach across a broad suite of large language models, including Llama 3.2 1B, Llama 3.2 3B, Llama 3.1 8B, and Qwen2.5 7B, evaluated on natural language generation benchmarks using 4-bit NF4 and FP4 quantizers. The novel method can markedly outperform direct quantization while incurring minimal memory overhead.
title: Quantization of Large Models with Weight Outliers and Sparsity

summary: Existing Graphical User Interface (GUI) benchmarks predominantly rely on precise and stateless user instructions. In everyday usage, however, instructions are often \emph{vague and history-dependent}: users omit the exact details of their past operations because they no longer remember them, leaving the agent to recover the missing context from long and noisy interaction histories. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce \textbf{MemU-Bench}, a mobile benchmark of \textbf{118 vague tasks} grounded in 29 long-horizon user trajectories, where agents must distill raw interaction streams into memory and retrieve the missing context on demand, with task outcomes verified against serialized application databases. Alongside Success Rate, we incorporate Interaction Efficiency (IE) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustively searching across different applications rather than by \emph{genuinely recalling} the history. Evaluations show that without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle under such ambiguity: the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves an SPL of only 16.4\%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5\%. To address this, we further propose \textbf{AppMem}, a training-free framework that distills user history into a \emph{structured, app-centric} memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches, and selectively retrieves relevant memories via target-app inference. AppMem raises the SPL of GPT-5.5 from 15.7\% to 66.9\% (\textbf{+51.2\%}), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3\%, and delivers consistent gains across evaluated backbones.
title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions

summary: All-in-one image restoration aims to recover high-quality images from multiple degradation types using a single unified model. Recent methods improve unified restoration with hybrid attention, prompt learning, or routing mechanisms, but generally focus on enhancing degradation adaptivity while employing similar feature modeling strategies across network stages. Consequently, the distinct representation requirements of encoding and decoding under diverse degradations remain insufficiently explored. In this paper, we propose SASFormer, a Stage-Aware Selective Attention Transformer for all-in-one blind image restoration. SASFormer follows a stage-aware design principle: the encoder uses established hybrid channel-spatial attention to build robust content-preserving and degradation-aware representations, while the decoder employs adaptive selective attention for restoration-oriented reconstruction. To address the stage-specific requirements of decoder reconstruction, we develop Adaptive Selective Channel Self-Attention (ASCSA) and Adaptive Selective Spatial Self-Attention (ASSSA), enabling the decoder to dynamically identify restoration-relevant channel responses and spatial contexts. Specifically, ASCSA performs adaptive query-channel selection and attention masking, while ASSSA adaptively integrates spatial attention across multiple window sizes. Compact implicit prompts further modulate the selection process without requiring explicit degradation labels. Extensive experiments on 3-, 5-, and 11-degradation settings demonstrate that SASFormer achieves strong restoration performance with favorable parameter efficiency. Moreover, stage-wise representation analysis and ablation studies provide empirical support for the proposed stage-aware design and the effectiveness of decoder-side adaptive selection.
title: SASFormer: Stage-Aware Selective Attention Transformer for All-in-One Blind Image Restoration

summary: Memory capacity and bandwidth are major bottlenecks in LLM inference, motivating weight compression beyond conventional 4-bit quantization. Vector quantization (VQ) enables approximately 2-bit weight storage but often relies on codebooks incompatible with native FP4 computation. We introduce MXCode (MX-Native Codebook Quantization), a framework bridging ultra-low-bit VQ compression with MicroXcaling (MX)-native FP4 computation. MXCode proposes three strategies: PostScale, which quantizes learned codebooks to MXFP4; PreScale, which extracts MX scales before codebook learning; and PreScale+, which further compresses these scales using VQ. These strategies explore tradeoffs among quantization quality, scale overhead, and codebook granularity. All reconstruct MX-native W4A4 operands without materializing intermediate high-precision weights. We evaluate MXCode on Qwen3 (235B), DeepSeek-R1 (671B), and GLM-5.2 (753B) using the Microsoft MX Emulation Library. MXCode achieves approximately 2 bits per weight with competitive, workload-dependent model quality. On GB300 hardware, experiments with Qwen3 (235B) show approximately 50% lower model-load memory than Native FP4 while maintaining near-Native-FP4 serving throughput. Under memory-constrained prefix reuse, P90 TTFT improves by up to 94.5%. These results demonstrate software-based reconstruction on existing FP4 hardware and inform the development of future MX-native inference systems.
title: MXCode: Vector Quantization for MX-Native Inference at Scale

summary: Dimension reduction methods are chosen by a common claim: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local structure, and PCA preserves global structure. Checking it on given data takes local and global scores on one scale and a test that compares two maps. Both scores come from one curve. The locality profile is the chance-corrected share of each point's k nearest neighbors that a map keeps, over all neighborhood sizes. Its value at k = 10 is the local fidelity L, and its mean over 30 to 50 percent of the data is the global fidelity G. We prove that at the midpoint the profile is the agreement on which half of the data is near each point, a rank correlation of the distances. Because L and G are one statistic, two maps can be tested against each other. The LG reversal test applies to any two dimension reduction methods. It decides, with a block-jackknife p-value, whether one map is more local and the other more global, and returns the scale at which to change maps. On 156 maps of twelve datasets with up to 1.38 million points, G agrees with established global scores at 0.89 and 0.96, and 2,000 points estimate it. The test confirms the usual claim on seven datasets. On both retail datasets and both rolled-up manifolds, it finds the neighbor embeddings more global. In an agent memory of one million passages, the two maps cross at 150,000 passages (p = 2.6e-5). Applications span pathology, single cells, supply chains and AI agent memory.
title: Quantifying Local and Global Fidelity of Nonlinear Embeddings

summary: LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes. The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery. Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.
title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving

summary: Abstract Sānér establishes a recursive control architecture for task regions by placing topology, self-modeling scheduling, and certificate-governed execution under one executable resource semantics. The nine-node construction supports exact recursive expansion and addressing. Its formal system establishes capacity safety, deterministic cross-layer selection, partition safety, conditional liveness, and computable deadline and recovery bounds. Using entity-isolated validation and one-time test splits, we evaluated the shared kernels and domain adapters in executable state-transition simulations and public benchmark workloads over 32–64 independent worlds, with deployment evidence obtained from 48 physical GPU blocks and eight fresh process pairs in the official Kubernetes scheduler-performance harness. Shared kernels with explicit domain realizations established task-level all-comparator superiority, while matched Kubernetes execution established a throughput advantage over the official default scheduler. The recursive representation preserved exact adjacency with a small measured footprint as graph size increased. Mechanism evidence remains separate from direct performance claims. Boundary results and nonidentifiability tests are reported independently. Together, the proofs and matched comparisons establish Sānér as a reusable and auditable control architecture whose shared mechanisms transfer across structurally different systems tasks. Validation design The study reports 52 simulation tasks and two deployment endpoints. Simulation comparisons use matched frozen worlds, observable information, action spaces, resource ceilings, and decision-time budgets. The Kubernetes deployment uses fresh paired processes under the same official scheduling and binding boundaries. Independent-unit inference, primary endpoints, and comparison procedures follow the recorded experimental contracts. Task-level all-comparator conclusions require passage against every member of the specified comparator family. Suite-defined Holm or FDR adjustments control multiplicity. Direct performance, mechanism validation, boundary results, and nonidentifiability remain separate evidence classes. Comparator strength and field standing Comparator selection was deliberately demanding. The experiments include established scheduling methods, matched MPC and CP-SAT, public MAPF implementations, official Kubernetes scheduling, strong decentralized-learning algorithms, and mature domain-specific methods. Every direct comparison uses matched information and resources. Executed comparator implementations are identified precisely. The consensus experiment uses a HotStuff three-chain simulation and a validation-tuned partition-threshold selector. The distribution-estimation experiment uses a discounted-loss context-depth KT mixture alongside Bayesian online changepoint prediction and discounted KT estimation. Published BFTBrain and context-tree weighting provide the corresponding methodological lineages. Results overview Sānér established task-level all-comparator superiority across 38 simulation tasks. Representative findings include a 764.53% improvement over equal-degree expander control, a 208.90% improvement over Exact Diffusion, and a 33.40% improvement over the Graph500 top-down port. At 5,000 nodes, the topology-based placement adapter sustained 69,258 placements per second. Under matched official Kubernetes execution, Sānér achieved 892.80 placements per second versus 371.19 for the default scheduler, with a mean paired throughput ratio of 2.40. Exact recursive-topology representation preserved neighbor recovery at 508–716 measured bytes through 26,244 nodes. Complete self-modeling was measured independently. The full experimental result index is provided in the Additional Description. Confirmatory scope The 38 task-level conclusions cover their complete specified strong-comparator families. Other direct comparisons retain
title: Sānér, The Recursive Trinity Structure for Task Regions

summary: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-based approximate dynamic programming approach to optimize the deployment of Walker-type satellite constellations under uncertainties, including launch failures and satellite malfunctions. We formulate the problem as a Markov Decision Process that incorporates low-injection orbit launches, continuous low-thrust orbit raising, and variable satellite loads. We adopt the offline approximate value iteration solution method, using linear function approximation with basis functions and action pruning strategies to substantially reduce the computational and memory requirements for finding optimal decision policies. Preliminary results demonstrate convergence to policies with low expected costs and deployment times, both of which are lower than those of a rolling-horizon baseline, showcasing a novel application of approximate dynamic programming in space logistics.
title: Offline Approximate Value Iteration: A Reinforcement Learning Approach for Satellite Constellation Deployment

summary: Indirect prompt injection creates a distinctive risk for blue-team Large Language Model (LLM) agents in Security Operations Centers (SOCs). Malicious instructions can be embedded in telemetry, tickets, retrieval results, or memory and then propagate through alert triage, incident summarization, response recommendation, and Indicator of Compromise (IOC) extraction as locally plausible intermediate decisions. We characterize this failure mode as evidence-chain contamination of protected task state. The main challenge is task dependent: a suspicious string may be malicious control text for summarization but essential evidence for IOC extraction. To address this challenge, we propose StateFence, a task-aware evaluation and defense framework that treats severity labels, incident narratives, response policies, and IOC sets as protected states. StateFence maps indirect prompt-injection attacks into explicit, stealth, multi-hop, and persistent SOC evidence attacks, records observable propagation traces, and routes defenses according to the attacked state. Across controlled SOC cases and public-SOC validation cases, StateFence lowers attack success and reduces failures that appear only after evidence is poisoned, while preserving task utility and avoiding the indicator loss caused by task-mismatched filtering. Our findings indicate that robust blue-team LLM agents require mechanisms that preserve task-critical state under untrusted evidence.
title: StateFence: Task-State Protection Against Evidence-Chain Contamination in Blue-Team LLM Agents

summary: Memory systems for LLM agents are evaluated mostly on social dialogue, where facts accumulate and rarely change, so remembering reduces largely to finding the turn in which something was said. Financial dialogue breaks this assumption: figures are revised, stances shift without being restated, rules stated once govern later questions, and a single company is discussed under several analytical lenses. Memory systems that retrieve the passages most similar to a question, or the most recent ones, therefore return superseded values, miss rules that share no wording with the question, and cannot recover a stance spread across sessions. We present TrackMem, a per-speaker graph memory that tracks the history of figures, separates perspectives by entity and lens, and preserves each speaker's actions in chronological order. To evaluate it, we introduce FinLoCoMo, a benchmark of 15 long-horizon investment conversations with 765 questions in two splits: one following the LoCoMo categories and one targeting four failure modes. With two readers, TrackMem outperforms existing memory systems on both splits. On the failure-mode split it reaches 73.9% macro accuracy against 69.4% for the strongest baseline, with the largest gains on questions about revised figures (86.5% against 73.4%).
title: TrackMem: Tracking Evolving Beliefs in Long-Horizon Financial Dialogue

summary: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.
title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions

summary: We introduce Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence (SAI), a theory and design program for learning systems that form, preserve, revise, and compose relations while continuing to learn. SAI is built on three axioms: consequential distinctions must not become orphaned (U); identity is determined by future-faithful continuation under a declared contract (I); and unresolved defects are repaired by the least lawful local completion at the lowest admitted grade (L). We model a model, agent, tool, team, or environment boundary as a recursive semi-closed system with a Kernel-Ring representation, a Compile-Open-Participate cycle, and a typed residual comparing actual with claimed continuation. Under explicit finite or affine contracts, we establish relative consistency and conditional non-redundancy of U/I/L, characterize a contract-relative semantic quotient, construct an exact joint stochastic refinement, derive a constrained residual contraction, prove finite-horizon continued-service viability, and give an executed-intervention identification result with an observational-confounding boundary. We define GRC-Close as the generative and repair schema for this contract. The framework also gives finite contracts for action-effect-feedback loop re-entry, partial failure, duplicate-effect idempotency, replay, concurrent delivery, causal uncertainty, and threshold-radix state representation. KREIT, the Kernel-Ring Equilibrium Information Theory layer, treats information as a typed, resource-bounded distinction; the control layer authorizes, executes, audits, and updates actions across cloud-edge-end scales. These results establish a common contract-level vocabulary for representation, relation, memory, action, communication, explanation, coordination, and growth, while marking the assumptions and open boundaries required for later generalization.
title: Synergetic Autonomous Intelligence: Three Axioms for Recursive Semi-Closed Learning

summary: Orbitronics exploits orbital angular momentum to generate and manipulate angular-momentum currents for controlling magnetisation, offering new approaches to magnetic memory and logic. A quantitative description of this process requires establishing how orbital angular momentum contributes to magnetic moments and, consequently, to the gyromagnetic response that governs magnetisation dynamics. Here, we present a first-principles framework for calculating the effective gyromagnetic tensor (g') of paramagnetic metals, consistently incorporating local and itinerant orbital contributions, spin-orbit coupling, and both state- and occupation-change effects. Applying the framework to V and Pt, we find that orbital paramagnetic responses are comparable to or larger than spin contributions and substantially modify g' from the free-electron value. The atom-centered approximation can underestimate the orbital response by approximately a factor of two, while neglecting occupation changes produces significant errors in the calculated g'. Our calculated g' values for V and Pt agree with experiment, while their pronounced dependence on band filling reveals a route to engineering angular-momentum responses through electronic-structure control. The results establish the modern theory of orbital magnetism as an essential ingredient for describing gyromagnetic response and provide a framework for identifying materials with enhanced orbital functionalities.
title: Local and itinerant orbital contributions to the gyromagnetic response of paramagnetic metals

summary: Deep learning models for electronic health records achieve strong predictive performance but provide little insight into what clinical concepts they represent internally. Post-hoc attribution methods produce per-cell importance scores that lack temporal coherence, cross-variable structure, and reusability across patients. We introduce the Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoder (TI-SAE), which learns a backbone-specific, patient-shared clinical concept dictionary from a frozen predictive model's representations. Each dictionary entry (latent) is defined by learned temporal Gaussian islands (specifying when the concept is active) and a sparse variable-composition vector (specifying which variables are involved). A decoupled selector then identifies which dictionary entries drive each patient's prediction, separating representation learning from attribution. We evaluate TI-SAE across five backbone architectures spanning different representation strategies on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV (three prediction tasks each). TI-SAE produces structured clinical concepts that go beyond transient attribution heatmaps while achieving strong performance on standard faithfulness benchmarks.
title: Temporal Island Sparse Autoencoders for Interpreting Clinical Time-Series Models

summary: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds---the policy's shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt's intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce FADE (Factored Ability--Difficulty Estimation), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. FADE represents each prompt's success logit as the inner product of a whitened $K$-dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya--Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the $K$-dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank-$K$ Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, FADE consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than $0.6$\,ms per step.
title: FADE: Factored Ability--Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling

summary: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.
title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training

summary: Language models in customer-facing products must be continually updated, since the data they serve shifts over time. As retraining on the full accumulated data is impractical, each update should instead run on a small set of examples carrying the training signal of all data seen so far. The strongest current methods build this set by gradient matching, which synthesizes examples whose training gradients match those of the full data. However, they require ground-truth labels, run once on a fixed snapshot rather than on a growing stream, and are slow on large data. We introduce \textbf{OLGA}, which lifts these limitations. It distills unlabeled data by drawing the gradient matching targets from the model's own next-token predictions. Across five text classification benchmarks with phi-1.5, it improves accuracy by 10 percentage points over the strongest selection baseline using as few as five examples. OLGA also distills online data streams by keeping a running rehearsal memory of synthetic examples, which is re-distilled together with each new batch as it arrives. In the online setting, it outperforms the strongest selection-based continual baseline by 6.6 stream-AUC percentage points. Finally, our method scales to large data by pairing distillation with selection in a hybrid pipeline, letting selection handle the mild stage of compression and distillation the extreme one. It cuts runtime by 30\% versus distillation alone at similar accuracy, and beats the best selection-only pipeline by up to 12.6 percentage points.
title: Online Label-Free Gradient Matching for Continual Language Model Training

summary: Government intelligence teams need LLM agents that can analyze large, messy evidence collections, but security and cost constraints often rule out hosted frontier models and broad, hard-to-audit tool surfaces. We report CLEO: Constrained Loop for Environment Optimization, a method for fitting a minimal agent harness to a fixed, self-hostable LLM. Given an expert-validated dataset, CLEO admits only the tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components that improve accuracy while remaining general and auditable. On our held-out dataset, the CLEO harness reaches an 83.8% pass rate, within 1.2 points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline, while being two orders of magnitude smaller.
title: Optimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis

summary: Optimal control of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), in general, requires a complete history. The belief state, a distribution over hidden states, summarizes this history and provides the classical sufficient statistic to control POMDPs. However, the continuous nature of the belief space generally prevents a finite-memory controller from maintaining it exactly. This raises the question we address in this work: what must the available finite memory preserve to achieve near-optimal control performance? We study this question through an information-theoretic converse that gives a fundamental lower bound on the loss of any finite-memory controller. The analysis introduces the concept of a decision witness that characterizes belief states whose confusion would lead to unavoidable loss. Motivated by this bound, we propose RECAP, a constructive quantization method for designing representative memory states. We prove an upper bound on the optimality gap of any RECAP codebook and use the components of this bound together with the converse analysis to define the codebook objective. Experiments on 11 POMDP benchmarks demonstrate that RECAP improves over finite-memory representation baselines under the same memory budget.
title: Finite-Memory Control of POMDPs: Fundamental Limits and Efficient Design

summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient large language model (LLM) fine-tuning, and recent methods incorporate curvature-aware strategies. However, in the high-dimensional parameter space of LLMs, these methods inherently suffer from exploding gradient variance and prohibitive costs.
